Distributed systems make it worse. A failure that spans two services and last week's deploy reads as noise in the logs and only becomes clear in the code, so L2 has little choice but to escalate.

The root cause is a context gap

An escalation simply hands the ticket off. It rarely includes everything the last person learned. Each handoff resets the investigation: the engineer re-reads the ticket, re-pulls the logs and investigates the same questions that support already asked the customer. Three tiers can mean three investigations of one bug.

That's why reshuffling the tiers doesn't stick. An L2.5, a triage rotation or a new on-call schedule changes who gets the ticket. It doesn't change what they can see when it arrives, or what the ticket brings with it.

PlayerZero approaches this with an engineering world model: one connected record of code, tickets, telemetry and deploy history, built from context graphs. Support, QA and engineering all work from that same record, so the context doesn't reset when the ticket changes hands.

How to carry a ticket from intake to a tested fix

The engineering teams cutting escalations fastest treat the ticket as a workflow with stages. Each stage has one job, and a person approves the stages that change anything outside the investigation.

  1. Intake. The ticket arrives from your ticketing system with the customer, account and reported behavior attached.
  2. Investigation. An AI agent traces the symptom through sessions, logs and the code paths involved, and checks whether the behavior is a defect, a configuration issue or the product working as designed.
  3. Ask only for what's missing. If the investigation needs something only the reporter knows, it asks that one question instead of sending back a checklist.
  4. Proposed fix. For defects, the agent drafts the change and explains which files it touches and why.
  5. Test. The fix is checked against scenarios that describe the customer's failure, so the team knows it resolves the reported behavior before anyone reviews the code.
  6. Engineering approval. An engineer reviews a tested change with the investigation attached. They make a call. They don't need to rebuild the context.

In PlayerZero this maps directly to a workflow: a versioned, multi-stage pipeline where each stage either moves on automatically or waits for approval. Every organization starts with an L1 Support template out of the box (in addition to Engineering Scoping, PR Review, QA Testing, SRE Alert Response, and more). You can also require human approval before an agent writes to an outside system, such as updating a Jira or Zendesk ticket, or pushing a commit, while investigation continues in parallel without waiting.

One support engineer put it this way: "I don't really have to go into detail into the ticket. I just have to drop it into PlayerZero."

Where human checkpoints belong

Not every stage needs someone watching it. Reading tickets, pulling logs and tracing code paths can't break anything, so let those run on their own. Here’s when someone should step in:

  • When the workflow is about to change something. Pushing a commit, updating the customer's ticket or posting a reply all reach beyond the investigation, so someone should approve them first.
  • When the workflow is waiting on an answer. If a run needs details from the reporter or a decision from a reviewer, a specific person has to own that step. Otherwise the run just sits there.

The second kind is easy to miss, especially once workflows start automatically on new tickets. Nobody is kicking off each run by hand anymore, so nobody is naturally watching for one to stop.

Here's how our team builds in PlayerZero to keep runs moving:

  • Auto-approve the stages that only read. Intake and investigation can’t change anything, so let them advance without a sign-off. Keep manual approval on the stages that push a commit or update a Jira or Zendesk ticket, at least until you trust the workflow.
  • Give every gated stage an owner. Assign approval to specific people, not to anyone in the project, so someone is clearly responsible when a run is waiting.
  • Work approvals from the Workflow Inbox. Approvers can pin the workflows they own to their inbox sidebar and approve stage advances there, so requests don’t sit unseen.
  • Leave a note when you approve. Approvers can add notes for the agent, which steers the next stage without restarting the run.
  • Change workflows through versions. Edit a draft, publish it when it’s ready and roll back to an earlier version if a change makes things worse.

Start where the evidence is cheapest: Support tickets you've already solved

Test a new support workflow on closed tickets first. You already know the right answer, so you can judge the workflow's investigation against it before it touches a live issue.

One support team began with a handful of tickets it had already investigated by hand. Comparing the agent's root cause with the known one showed them where the workflow needed more context before they rolled it out further.

What changes when support can ship the fix

When support can carry a ticket to a tested fix, escalations stop being the default and become the exception.

Zuora shows it most clearly. After moving L3 investigation onto PlayerZero, L3 triage dropped from 3 days to 15 minutes, and escalations fell from 28 to 3 a month. Cyrano Video cut the engineering hours spent on support by 80%, and its customer success team now resolves 40% of issues without escalating. Cayuse resolves issues 80% faster and catches 90% of them before customers do.

Six playbooks to reduce support escalations

If you've read our eBook on breaking the support escalation cycle [blocked], you'll recognize the six core playbooks for reducing escalations.

Where it fits in the workflow

Resolve working-as-intended tickets without escalating

Investigation, closed at stage 2

Escalate with context, not symptoms

Assemble the incident timeline automatically

Generate and test debugging hypotheses

Turn resolved tickets into reusable knowledge

After closure, feeds the next intake

Support escalations fall when context is shared

L3 support exists because it was the only tier that could see and understand what was happening in the code. Give every tier that view, let the investigation travel with the ticket and keep people at the steps that change things. The escalations that remain are the ones that need an engineer's judgment, and they arrive ready for it.

See how a ticket moves from intake to a tested fix in your own stack. Book a demo.

items.title: Borrowed UI: Why Your Next Desktop Tool Might Just Need a Browser Tab
items.author: Shreyam Adhikari
items.content:
A local tool needs a table, a few charts, and some buttons. Somewhere in the planning meeting, it acquires an entire desktop application.

Before that happens, I want to nominate the browser already sitting on the machine.

I call this : a local process does the work, and a browser tab provides the interface. The established name is a local web UI. The architecture is old. I’m just giving my enthusiasm an acronym.

pprof is the cleanest example. It can print a report of expensive functions, or open a local web interface when a visual inspection helps. Same profiling data, another way to look at it. A graph does not have to become a whole desktop product.

With pprof installed and an existing profile file, its web mode looks like this:

pprof -http=localhost:8080 profile.pb.gz

Graph visualizations can require Graphviz. This is an example of an optional interface, not a promise of zero dependencies. pprof documentation.

Syncthing is the background-service version. Its browser GUI lets you inspect and configure synchronization. The GUI and REST API share a port, normally on loopback. The work belongs to a running process; you visit the control panel when you need it. Syncthing’s GUI documentation.

Jupyter is the richer version. The browser edits the notebook, while a server and execution kernel handle the other side. Close the tab and the kernel can keep running. Reopen the notebook and reconnect. Useful separation—and a reminder that “I closed it” needs a precise meaning. Jupyter Notebook documentation.

Jupyter is not a tiny installation. It illustrates the boundary, not a diet plan.

When borrowing makes sense

I’d consider BUI for a local data explorer, profiler, backup monitor, or service configuration tool. Especially when the useful part already works as a CLI or background process and the interface is something you need occasionally.

Browsers are good at tables, text selection, charts, responsive layouts, and accessible controls when we build them properly. The local process can own validation, credentials, durable state, and cancellation. The tab doesn’t need a second interpretation of the rules.

This also avoids distributing a browser engine with every application. It does not make the browser’s memory or CPU use disappear. Somebody still pays the rendering bill.

When the window earns its keep

If your product depends on native menus, global shortcuts, file associations, or a carefully controlled window lifecycle, a native app or system WebView may be a better fit. If the whole interaction is one command and three lines of output, opening a tab is probably a small ceremony nobody requested.

You also inherit browser compatibility, port conflicts, startup and reconnection work. Closing the tab and stopping the process are different actions. Say so. Offline use needs local assets and capabilities; localhost is not an offline strategy by itself.

And localhost is not a security policy. Bind to loopback by default, validate Host and Origin, protect state-changing requests, and deliberately secure any wider network exposure. Syncthing’s documentation explicitly calls for authentication and HTTPS when exposing its GUI beyond the local machine.

I don’t think every desktop app should become a tab. I think this option deserves a place in the initial discussion. When a tool mostly needs to work quietly and occasionally explain itself, the browser is a pretty good place for that explanation.

items.title: Google Signs Deal With Blue Origin to Send Satellite Data Centers Into Orbit
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Google has partnered with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to launch satellite-based AI data centers into orbit as part of its experimental Project Suncatcher initiative. "Engadget reports: Each of these satellites will be equipped with "roughly the capacity of a data center rack" and will enter into a sun-synchronous orbit via heavy-lift New Glenn rockets. The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works.
 
This is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems. The hope is that the harsh vacuum of the cosmos will be a better fit for the technology.

items.title: Human in the Loop AI: How to Safely Scale Agentic Workloads with Tunable Autonomy
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
Human-in-the-loop AI keeps people in charge of key decisions, while tunable autonomy lets teams expand what AI agents handle on their own as trust grows.

Most organizations experimenting with agentic AI run into two barriers long before they reach meaningful automation: the trust gap and the accountability gap. While teams trust AI enough to summarize tickets and recommend fixes, they don't yet trust it to investigate incidents or implement code changes on its own. And even when AI performs well, this doesn't transfer responsibility. Someone still needs to own the decision and be ready to reverse it if it goes sideways.

In mature engineering environments, both concerns are justified. Large codebases, shared infrastructure, customer commitments, and compliance requirements make it risky to let AI move from recommendation to autonomous action without oversight.

That’s why the answer is not full autonomy or full human control—it’s tunable autonomy that you can adjust as you progress in your AI adoption. With this operating model, organizations progressively expand what AI can do as trust grows, all while keeping a clear human owner at critical stages and full control over automated workflows.

The human-in-the-loop problem: why engineering teams stall after early AI wins

Most teams begin with simple AI workflows, like summarizing incidents, explaining code changes, and drafting pull requests. The results are fast, and the downside is low—if the summary is wrong, a human catches it before anything breaks.

Those early wins create pressure to automate more. Leaders begin asking whether AI can take on higher-stakes work, such as classifying incidents, preparing fixes, and closing tickets.

That is where adoption stalls. That's why human-in-the-loop design matters.

Not all AI decisions carry the same weight. The same AI action that’s safe in one workflow can be dangerous in another. Auto-closing a duplicate support ticket carries almost no risk. Auto-deploying a production fix carries enormous risk. The action looks similar, but the consequences aren't.

And a single bad action is recoverable. What's harder to reverse is an agent that executes multiple steps on the same incorrect assumption. Consider an agent that prepares the wrong remediation plan. From there, it validates the wrong outcome and closes the wrong ticket. A small mistake turns into a cascading failure that grows harder to reverse.

The solution isn't to abandon AI altogether. The real leverage comes from building deliberate stopping points into the workflow. These checkpoints create a moment for human review before a mistake propagates, and establish a clear owner for the work that crosses that threshold. Over time, those approvals become the evidence base for every decision that advances AI's role.

The question, then, becomes how to place these checkpoints deliberately—and how to know when you have earned enough trust to remove one.

That is the problem tunable autonomy is designed to solve.

Tunable autonomy: the agentic operating model

Tunable autonomy gives teams explicit control over how much AI agents can do at each stage of a specific workflow. Rather than making a one-time choice between full human control and full autonomy, organizations can set autonomy levels tailored to each workflow stage.

For each stage, they choose from the four levels:

  1. Manual approval: AI surfaces information, but humans do the work.
  2. Recommend-only: AI suggests actions, but humans approve every step.
  3. Auto-with-approval: AI performs work, but pauses at key checkpoints.
  4. Fully autonomous: AI completes the workflow within defined boundaries.

The following table shows where most organizations start, and where each stage can realistically go.

Recommend-only → autonomous

Recommend-only → auto-with-approval

Manual approval → auto-with-approval

Ticket closure and routing

Auto-with-approval → autonomous

Different workflows should progress at different speeds, and organizations should tune autonomy by repository, service, severity, ticket type, or team.

On transitioning between AI autonomy levels

Setting AI autonomy levels within a team is relatively straightforward. Things get much more complicated when work crosses a team boundary. That's where introducing AI autonomy gates—checkpoints that determine whether AI-driven work can advance to the next stage or domain—matters most.

The reason is simple—each team has different standards, conventions, risk tolerances, and implicit knowledge, so they see the same issue differently. Support sees customer impact, engineering sees code paths, and QA sees reproduction risk.

Say an AI agent is classifying incoming support tickets. The agent’s actions stay within a single team’s domain, so the risk of a misstep is low and contained. When approval rates for AI-driven classifications trend near 100%, that workflow becomes a strong candidate for autonomous operation within your defined guardrails.

Now, say an AI-assisted workflow crosses a team boundary, like an AI-diagnosed issue moving from support to engineering with a recommended fix attached. The stakes rise because the fix comes with root-cause assumptions baked in—if one is wrong, it can travel through diagnosis, remediation, and closure before anyone with the right context catches it. And since engineering has to act on work they didn't produce, accountability for the outcomes becomes ambiguous.

That's exactly where an autonomy gate belongs. The gate ensures the work has been reviewed by someone who can vouch for it before it crosses that line. Each successful handoff, reviewed and acted on without issue, is how AI earns the next level of trust to take on more work.

How to implement tunable autonomy

To implement the tunable autonomy model across your organization, start by establishing full human-in-the-loop approval at every critical stage.

Even in recommend-only mode, AI creates immediate value for engineering teams. Connecting tickets to code, telemetry, and runtime behavior compresses investigation time to minutes. Surfacing likely root causes and recommending fixes streamlines resolutions, increasing customer satisfaction. Drafting pull requests and incident summaries keeps engineers focused on building.

Your team stays in the loop at every step, reviewing and course-correcting before anything moves forward. When their approvals reach close to 100% across workflows, gradually increase autonomy based on the following factors.

When you’re scaling AI workflows, you’re not just asking “Can the AI do this task?” but “Can it do it reliably enough to justify less oversight?” Metrics provide the most objective answer to this question.

Most engineering organizations already track these metrics for delivery performance and incident management. What changes with AI is what they reveal. Each one now also measures a different dimension of AI’s reliability.

Think of it less like flipping a switch and more like a new hire earning the right to make decisions without running them by a manager. Nobody hands over full autonomy on day one. It's granted incrementally by demonstrating sound judgment, catching mistakes before they compound, and building a track record that speaks for itself.

Factor #2: People, process, and context

Autonomy can't advance without the professional judgment to back it. Approval from experienced team members ensures AI systems perform well across both familiar conditions and edge cases that only emerge under pressure.

Teams that get autonomy expansion right exercise their judgment across the dimensions where AI has the most influence and the least visibility: people, process, and context. They follow the same three questions before extending AI’s responsibilities further.

  • Does the AI have enough context on the system and the business to make a decision?
  • Does the AI know who to involve or escalate to, even if that person isn't a direct owner?
  • Will the AI follow team processes (e.g., correctly routing tickets) without being told?

While metrics show that trust is building, satisfying these criteria tells you whether it's actually earned. When AI understands enough about your systems, your people, and your processes, it changes how work flows across the organization, increasing resilience and shifting defect resolution from reactive to proactive.

A helpful mental model is to apply the same bar you’d use for a senior engineer. Instead of micromanaging them, you trust that they've internalized the business context, know how handoffs work, and can navigate team processes without a checklist. An AI agent has to earn that same confidence, and teams need to build the evidence that it has.

Key Data’s experience is a blueprint for what it looks like when people, process, and context align with the metrics. By connecting customer-reported issues to the exact code changes and runtime behavior behind them, they eliminated the ambiguity that makes teams hesitant to rely on AI. With that context and the ability to reproduce and diagnose problems in minutes instead of weeks, the confidence to go further with AI across their workflow followed naturally.

The guardrails that make autonomy safe

Safe autonomy depends on strong controls—not just as a brake on what AI can do, but as the foundation that makes expanding its responsibilities possible. Despite differences in scale, stack, and risk tolerance, what those controls actually require tends to look the same across organizations.

The most trustworthy AI systems converge on four properties.

  • Audit trails: Comprehensive logs capture what happened, when it happened, and why, including model version, confidence scores, tool calls, and reasoning paths. They’re essential for performing post-mortems and detecting behavioral drift.
  • Attributability: Every action traces back to a specific agent identity, the human or policy that authorized it, and the context in which it acted. This preserves human accountability and enables you to distinguish model errors from policy misconfigurations.
  • Reversibility: Reversibility caps the scope of any single autonomous action, so no mistake can cause irreparable harm to production systems or data.
  • Policy constraints: Agents can act outside the spirit of organizational intent. Runtime policy enforcement, like tool allowlists and scope isolation, ensures constraints travel with the agent as it executes, not just at the authorization moment.

While these properties create a foundational audit system that keeps autonomy from becoming a liability, they're not sufficient on their own. Certain actions carry significant organizational weight, making human review essential regardless of how well the AI has been performing.

In these situations, the cost of getting autonomy wrong outweighs the efficiency gains from skipping the review. That’s why a checkpoint there almost always pays for itself.

  • Work moving between teams: A checkpoint here creates a moment when a person with full organizational context evaluates not just “Is this technically correct?” but also “Is this the right change at this time, for these teams, under these conditions?” That contextual and temporal judgment ensures the quality of the handoff.
  • Disruptive or hard-to-reverse actions: Disruptive changes like architecture rewrites and dependency upgrades carry asymmetric risk. The blast radius of a mistake is large, and once an action is executed, the window to course-correct narrows significantly. A checkpoint ensures the decision is correct before it becomes difficult to reverse.

The point isn’t to eliminate risk—it’s to make it manageable. AI agents will make mistakes, but they’ll make fewer than their human counterparts. With those controls in place, you can scale or decrease autonomy across teams while keeping errors contained and accountability clear.

At Cyrano Video, the combination of richer context and stronger trust allowed support teams to resolve more issues independently. As a result, the company reduced engineering time spent on support and bug fixes by roughly 80% while preventing many tickets from escalating in the first place.

Why PlayerZero is the right foundation for tunable autonomy

Tunable autonomy only works when AI has access to the full engineering context—but in most organizations, that context is scattered across systems that don't talk to each other, leaving AI to act on an incomplete picture.

PlayerZero creates that visibility by unifying these signals into an engineering world model: a single representation of the system that connects intent, impact, real-world behavior, and institutional knowledge.

That foundation gives AI agents everything they need to meet the three conditions that teams use to validate readiness for higher autonomy: deep business understanding, clear visibility into ownership and escalation paths, and a reliable picture of process execution.

Cayuse shows what this model unlocks in practice. Using PlayerZero, they gave teams earlier visibility into issues and stronger confidence in the accuracy of AI-driven investigations. As a result, they found and fixed 90% of issues before users noticed and cut average resolution time by 80%.

Scaling AI by earning trust, not assuming it

Most organizations treat autonomy as a destination. The ones that scale it successfully treat it as a practice—something earned through evidence, refined through metrics, and extended only when trust is real.

That shift in mindset is what separates teams that adopt agentic AI from teams that build a lasting advantage with it.

PlayerZero is built for organizations that want to move fast with AI—without outrunning their ability to control it—giving teams the foundation to extend autonomy safely and the evidence to know when to go further. Book a demo to learn how.

items.title: AI Code Generation Is Only One Small Piece Of The ROI Equation
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
To measure AI ROI in software engineering, look past how fast code gets written. Count the engineering hours your team spends after the code exists, on triage, diagnosis, prioritization, review, and release for escalated customer issues. Then estimate how much of that time AI could recover, and value it at a loaded engineering rate.

AI coding tools help engineers implement features and explore solutions faster. But faster code only gets teams partway to a positive return on AI. Teams still need to review, test, and release changes, then diagnose and resolve defects that reach customers.

That work depends on understanding how the code behaves in production, which customer configurations matter, and what previous failures revealed. When each team has to reconstruct the same production context, time saved in the editor gets spent again downstream.

A more complete way to measure AI ROI includes the effort required to verify, release, and support the software teams produce: the work of production engineering. Drawing on what we've seen with customers, we built an AI ROI calculator that estimates the capacity tied up in escalated customer work, and how much of it an engineering world model can recover by connecting the evidence teams need to cut redundant investigation and coordination. Together, they bring a broader opportunity into focus: preserving more of the gains from faster coding and making each resolution useful beyond the issue that prompted it.

Why faster code alone doesn't deliver AI ROI

Faster implementation gives teams room to test ideas, refine features, and respond to customers. Those gains become harder to realize when the surrounding workflow still depends on people rebuilding the same explanation.

DORA's 2026 report, The ROI of AI-assisted Software Development, emphasizes that faster coding doesn't automatically translate into business value. It identifies reducing unnecessary rework as a way to reclaim engineering capacity and increase output without expanding headcount.

For teams already investing in AI code generation, that opens another investment question: how much capacity could AI recover from the work triggered by production defects? Customer escalations still require investigation, fixes need prioritization, and corrective changes need verification before release. Those responsibilities create an opportunity to extend AI's value beyond producing code.

An escalated customer issue makes those dependencies visible. Support rebuilds the customer's history. Engineering traces the failure through code and runtime evidence. Product seeks a reliable account of its impact, while QA establishes the conditions the fix needs to satisfy. When those findings stay scattered across tickets and conversations, each handoff adds another round of explanation.

Much of this effort is easy to miss because it appears inside otherwise necessary work. Investigating a defect is necessary; reconstructing evidence that another team has already assembled adds avoidable effort. Reviewing a change is necessary; asking its author to recover the reasoning behind its scope adds more.

The loss extends beyond labor cost: slower resolutions, interrupted feature work, less time for prevention, and senior engineers diverted into repeated explanations. Recovering that capacity means addressing repeated work across the full production workflow, from the first customer report to a verified release.

Measuring AI ROI across four production stages

PlayerZero's engineering world model connects code, production signals, customer tickets, and prior outcomes into a persistent context that teams and agents share. Support, engineering, product, and QA can work from the same evidence about how the system behaves and what previous investigations established.

Shared context helps work move between teams without losing intent or scope. A discovery in support becomes available to the people and agents responsible for diagnosis, prioritization, and validation, reducing the work each team repeats.

PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator puts a number on that question for teams already using AI coding tools. It estimates a practical portion of the opportunity: recoverable effort across escalated customer work and the cost equivalent of that capacity.

Business value of shared context

Assembling evidence and coordinating escalations

Less escalation overhead and fewer clarification requests

Reconstructing symptoms and prior investigative work

More engineering capacity for unresolved causes

Establishing customer impact, related requests, and priority

Faster, better-informed decisions about engineering work

Build, verify, and release

Reacquiring the fix context and rebuilding validation scenarios

Less review rework, and more focused release validation

The calculator uses illustrative effort assumptions and a loaded engineering rate to estimate the capacity teams could redirect toward planned delivery and reliability. The cost equivalent values that time before platform costs, providing a starting point for weighing the investment. The four stages below illustrate the repeated work reflected in the estimate and where shared context can reduce it.

Support and triage: Shared evidence reduces escalation friction

Support's contribution begins well before a backend engineer picks up a ticket. L1 support clarifies the report and responds to the customer; support engineers connect it to sessions, documentation, related tickets, and technical evidence.

When those sources are disconnected, preparing an escalation becomes an investigation in its own right. Customer follow-up stretches out while support coordinates the people who might have the answer.

Consider a hypothetical customer whose data export times out when they request a large dataset with a particular filter enabled. Smaller exports still succeed. A report that simply says "exports are broken" leaves engineering with substantial work to do before it can investigate the cause.

PlayerZero connects customer reports to the relevant code and runtime conditions. In this example, support can pass along the affected configuration, request traces, and findings about which exports succeed or fail. The engineering world model keeps those findings connected to the report, giving engineering a defined technical case and support evidence for customer updates.

The immediate gain is less effort to prepare and clarify the escalation. Across a busy support queue, this returns time to customer work and reduces the interruptions needed to make an engineering ticket actionable. That means support can keep customers informed without every update depending on a specialist engineer's availability.

Engineering diagnosis: Prior findings focus the investigation

Backend engineers contribute specialized judgment, but a fragmented escalation can consume their time before they reach the unresolved question. They inspect logs and traces, review code history, and test competing explanations. If support's findings or a previous investigation are missing, they also retrace work that the organization has already completed.

That effort interrupts feature development and concentrates investigations around engineers who remember the affected system. The cost includes both the investigation and the planned work waiting for those engineers to return.

For the export timeout scenario, agentic debugging uses connected runtime evidence and code history to point to a query changed in a recent release. The engineering world model incorporates support's findings into this investigation, alongside the relevant changes, failure conditions, and explanations already considered. The engineer then checks that hypothesis against current behavior and determines whether the query accounts for the timeout.

Once confirmed, the cause and supporting reasoning become part of the same context, alongside support's original findings. Ruled-out explanations remain available, too, so another engineer can understand why the investigation settled on that path. Resolving escalations places fewer demands on the specialist engineers who know the system best, preserving their capacity for planned development. Their judgment goes toward evaluating the cause and choosing a correction rather than recovering the history behind it.

Product intake: Connected evidence clarifies customer impact

A confirmed cause gives product managers and engineering leads a technical basis for prioritization. They still need to connect customer impact to technical scope before deciding what takes precedence over planned work.

When that evidence is disconnected, effort accumulates in reconciling related requests, agreeing on the immediate response, and explaining why it matters more than competing priorities.

The engineering world model keeps related customer reports connected to the internal engineering issue, so product can assess customer impact alongside the diagnosis and proposed correction. In the export example, the team can distinguish an urgent query fix from a broader request to redesign exports, then connect that scope decision and its rationale to the technical findings and affected customer workflows.

Engineering begins implementation with both the technical findings and the reason for the chosen response. Carrying agreed priorities and scope into the work reduces coordination demands and the need for repeated scope discussions, helping the team protect planned delivery.

Build, verify, and release: Known failure conditions focus validation

A prioritized fix still needs implementation, review, testing, and release. Backend engineers implement the correction, while reviewers and QA determine whether it resolves the failure without disrupting working behavior. Reconstructing the intended outcome, affected configurations, and regression coverage delays release decisions and consumes capacity that could otherwise go toward evaluating the change itself.

Coding assistance can accelerate the query change in the export example. The engineering world model carries the diagnosis and agreed scope into validation: the large, filtered export should complete successfully and return the expected records, while previously successful exports continue to work.

Those conditions guide review, code simulations, and regression testing. Simulations predict behavior without executing the code, helping the team focus tests on potential risks; testing establishes whether the change meets the intended outcome.

With less effort spent reconstructing validation requirements, reviewers and QA can concentrate on correctness and relevant coverage. Release decisions are better informed, with engineering time going toward verifying the fix rather than recovering why it was needed.

After release, the engineering world model keeps validation results and production observations connected to the original report, diagnosis, and scope decision. Support and SRE teams can see what the fix covered, whether the customer's export succeeded, and what remains unresolved. That completed record gives support a grounded closing explanation and preserves the evidence behind the resolution.

The engineering world model's value extends beyond the effort saved on the current issue. PlayerZero's shared organizational memory makes configuration findings, decisions, and their rationale available across teams, so lessons from one investigation can inform future work.

PlayerZero's approach to memory and learning captures useful findings from completed work and incorporates corrections as conditions change, keeping the organization's accumulated experience useful over time. Teams can build on those findings while checking them against current evidence, rather than reconstructing each investigation from scratch.

One customer's experience shows how shared production understanding can extend across functions. At Higher Logic, a PlayerZero pilot on its Vanilla product line gave support visibility into the code behind customer reports, helping the team investigate and resolve eligible defects within engineering-defined boundaries. Support shipped fixes for 50 customer issues in two months. The company also reports 250 engineering hours reclaimed from support escalations.

QA adoption emerged from support's use of the platform. The QA team used the same visibility into code-change impact to identify areas likely to be affected by a release and prioritize testing. The production understanding that helped support resolve customer work gained another application in release quality, extending its usefulness across the organization.

Shared knowledge also affects the operating cost of AI work. Workflow memory carries lessons between runs, while concise handoffs carry completed work and decisions between stages. Retained findings and concise handoffs reduce repeated retrieval and reasoning, lowering the operating waste involved in reaching a useful outcome.

The calculator estimates recoverable effort in escalated work. The broader return comes as the same learning improves support, engineering, product, and QA work over time, including opportunities to prevent a known failure from becoming another customer escalation.

How to build an AI ROI business case around recoverable capacity

Use the AI ROI calculator to estimate the capacity your team could recover from escalation volume, resolution effort, and loaded engineering cost. Put that estimate alongside the longer-term value of shared learning: fewer repeated investigations, more focused validation, and more engineering time for the product and reliability improvements your customers need.

Frequently asked questions about measuring AI ROI

How do you calculate the ROI of AI coding assistants for a software team?

Start with the time AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot save during implementation. Then account for what happens after the code exists: review, testing, triage, and defect resolution. Value the net hours your team recovers at a loaded engineering rate and compare that against tool and platform costs. Coding speed on its own overstates the return.

Why doesn't faster code generation guarantee AI ROI?

Code generation speeds up one stage of delivery. If review, testing, triage, and diagnosis still depend on people rebuilding the same production context, the time saved in the editor gets spent again downstream. DORA's research makes a similar point: the biggest returns come from reducing unnecessary rework, not from writing code faster.

What should an AI ROI calculator measure?

It should measure capacity across the full production workflow, not just coding output. PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator estimates recoverable effort in escalated customer work across four stages: support and triage, engineering diagnosis, product intake, and build, verify, and release. It values that time at a loaded engineering rate, before platform costs.

How long does it take to see ROI from AI in software development?

DORA describes AI adoption as a J-curve: teams often see a temporary dip while they learn the tools and adjust workflows, before longer-term returns show up. Escalation work is a good place to look early because the effort is easy to count. At Higher Logic, support shipped fixes for 50 customer issues within two months of its PlayerZero pilot.

How is this different from DORA's AI ROI framework?

DORA's framework models the financial return of AI-assisted development across software delivery as a whole. PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator focuses on one place that return leaks: the effort escalated customer issues pull from support, engineering, product, and QA. Used together, they show both the overall picture and a specific, recoverable source of capacity.

items.title: Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16-GGUF: Everything Developers Need to Know
items.author: aimodels44
items.content:
A GGUF conversion of Tencent’s Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 draft model, intended for speculative decoding with a separate Qwen3.8-27B target model in a llama.cpp fork. It is not a standalone chat model. The maintainer is aj9o9.

Use it to accelerate Qwen3.8-27B generation, especially code, math, and tool-call workloads. The supplied RTX 3090 tests also show gains on mixed chat tasks, but prose and image-heavy requests may benefit less; tune draft length for your GPU and workload.

Requires both a compatible Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF and the branch of the llama.cpp fork; stock llama.cpp does not load these files. Longer drafts consume more VRAM and reduce available context: on the tested 24 GB RTX 3090 setup, Q4_K_M with 15 drafted tokens fit up to context 65,536, versus 98,304 with 7 drafted tokens. Speculative decoding can produce different output from non-speculative runs, including at temperature 0. Performance figures are hardware-, backend-, prompt-, and setting-dependent; community results use differing test conditions.

On the tested RTX 3090, Q4_K_M DSpine at 15 drafted tokens reached 90.1 tok/s on a mixed short-context task set, compared with 51.7 tok/s for DFlash2 and 28.2 tok/s without speculation. Code and math were the strongest measured tasks; prose was slower than code and math. The same test setup reported maximum context of 65,536 for DSpine at 15 drafts, 98,304 for DFlash2 at 7 drafts, and 176,128 without speculation. These are results for the stated setup, not general rankings. Other GGUF alternatives listed in the supplied sources include Qwen3.8-27B-S-mirai-GGUF, Qwen-3.8-27B-ROCmFP4-FAST-GGUF, Qwen3.8-27B-i1-IQ4_KS_KT-GGUF, and Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF.

This is a five-layer speculative drafter that reads hidden states from five target-model layers and drafts a 16-token block in parallel. Its described mechanisms include causal block attention, a gated code bridge after each layer, and serial last-write refinement over candidate predecessor tokens. Available files are Q4_K_M (1.26 GB; code-bridge tensors remain BF16), Q8_0 (2.20 GB), and BF16 (4.06 GB, described as intended for re-quantizing). The files contain only the drafter. The supplied RTX 3090 benchmark used a Q4_K_M Qwen3.8-27B target, q8_0 KV caches, one slot, and the CUDA branch. It measured 90.1 tok/s on a mixed task set at temperature 0; task-specific results were 128.7 tok/s for code, 122.8 for math, 62.0 for summarize/translate, and 41.6 for prose/story. These are reported measurements, not guarantees. The supplied abstract describes DSpine research results on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in SGLang; it does not establish those results as measurements of this GGUF conversion or its Qwen3.8-27B use.

Use a compatible Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF together with one of the drafter GGUF files. The documented llama.cpp server setup accepts a target path () and drafter path (), with controls including , context size (), slot count (), and optional probabilistic draft sampling. The README warns that auto-fit may not reserve enough memory for the drafter; set context size explicitly. On 24 GB cards, two slots with 15-token drafts do not fit according to the supplied guidance.

The drafter proposes token blocks for speculative verification by the target model; it does not independently provide final text generation. The decoder can select a draft chain greedily or by sampling. Output may differ from a run without a drafter because verification batches tokens and can change near-tied token choices; the source says code and tool calls usually match, while prose and image descriptions can diverge.

git clone -b dspine https://github.com/Ajay9o9/llama.cpp.git
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON
cmake --build build --config Release -j

./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m Qwen3.8-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -md Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-dflash \
  --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  -ngl 999 --spec-draft-ngl 999 \
  -fa on --jinja -c 32768 -np 1 \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --spec-draft-type-k q8_0 --spec-draft-type-v q8_0

The example is the documented CUDA setup. Adjust and for your GPU and memory; the source recommends testing draft sizes such as 2, 3, 4, 7, and 15.

Frequently asked questions

Q: Can I use this as a standalone model?

A: No. These files contain only the draft model; pair one with a Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF.

Q: Will stock llama.cpp load the files?

A: No. The supplied README says they require the branch of the Ajay9o9 llama.cpp fork; stock llama.cpp refuses to load them.

Q: Which quantization should I start with?

A: The README recommends Q4_K_M, whose code-bridge tensors remain BF16. Q8_0 is larger and uses more VRAM, while BF16 is described as a full-precision file for re-quantizing.

Q: What draft length should I set?

A: The documented default of 3 uses only part of the 16-token block. The source suggests trying 2, 3, 4, 7, and 15; 15 is a starting point for CUDA, ROCm/HIP, and SYCL, while AMD Vulkan may favor 2 or 3.

Q: How much context fits on a 24 GB GPU?

A: In the reported RTX 3090 setup with a Q4_K_M target and q8_0 KV cache, the maximum context was 65,536 with 15 drafted tokens and 98,304 with 7. Actual capacity depends on the setup.

Q: Does speculative decoding preserve identical output?

A: Not necessarily, even at temperature 0. Batched verification can change near-tied token choices; the source reports that code and tool calls usually match, while prose and image descriptions can diverge.

Q: What does the supplied research abstract establish?

A: It reports DSpine research results on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, including SGLang serving tests. It does not establish those figures as benchmarks for this Qwen3.8-27B GGUF conversion.

This is a simplified guide to an AI model called Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16-GGUF maintained by aj9o9. If you like these kinds of analysis, join AIModels.fyi or follow us on Twitter.

items.title: What the Microsoft 365 outage says about change risk
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
The Microsoft 365 outage on November 12 and 13 2026 knocked out Exchange Online, which sits behind Outlook, for about 24 hours. Microsoft Teams, SharePoint and other services were hit hard as well. Microsoft says it wasn't one mistake but rather a latent defect from a July fix, a routine Teams failover and nearly 14% of gateway capacity already out that all lined up at peak US traffic.

Press reports citing Microsoft's preliminary report show the disruption lasted from 4:20 PM UTC on November 12 to 4:10 PM UTC on November 13, and users in 74 countries and territories reported problems to Downdetector within about an hour.

Microsoft has said the outage was a technical issue and was not related to hackers, cyber activity, or to AI, and I'll take that at face value because it isn't what this post is about.

What caught my attention is how Microsoft describes the cause: not one mistake, but three ordinary things lining up.

  • A production change can be clean for three months and still be lying dormant, ready to cause problems.
  • The teams that handle this best aren't the ones with the most dashboards but the ones who can see the whole picture before the change ships.
  • Shared, organizational AI context can help find and fix these issues that span multiple teams.

Here’s what caused the Microsoft 365 outage, according to Microsoft

In an abridged root cause posted on November 16, Microsoft's Charles Lamanna described three factors behind the failure of a networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services.

  1. A latent defect. Lock contention in an internal process could leave servers unresponsive under certain load. It came from a fix that began rolling out in July, went through staged deployment and ran for more than three months with no observed issues.
  2. A load surge. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft Teams failed over to the gateway that also serves Exchange Online. Microsoft calls this part of normal operations.
  3. Reduced capacity. Nearly 14% of gateway capacity was out from an unrelated issue the day before. Microsoft says there was enough headroom that this had no impact alone.

Together, the last two pushed the gateway into the latent bug during peak US traffic, and rerouting then sent load to the remaining servers until more than 80% were unresponsive at the worst point. Microsoft says bulkheads between partitions didn't stop the cascading failure, due to a separate issue it hasn't yet explained.

Normal load testing missed the defect because the test labs leaned toward weaker, lower-core hardware, and the contention gets worse on newer machines. Exchange Online couldn't fail out of the gateway the way other services could, and Microsoft's normal rollback and feature flags couldn't quickly revert a months-old change. Engineers wrote an update that returned the code path to its previous known-good state.

Our read: nothing here looked wrong on its own

Look at each ingredient separately: a fix that passed staged deployment, a failover that Microsoft describes as normal, a capacity shortfall with enough headroom to absorb it, load tests built around weaker hardware, and rerouting that does what rerouting is supposed to do. Each one is routine, and in most large engineering organizations, each would sit with a different person or team, such as performance engineering, platform networking, service owners, operations or release engineering.

I don't know how Microsoft is organized, and I don't know whether anyone there had the full picture of the change risk, or whether the picture existed anywhere at all, which is an important distinction. Knowledge can be fragmented, meaning someone knew and it never reached the decision, or it can be missing, meaning nobody knew the problem existed. Shared context clearly helps with the first. It helps with the second only when joining existing records surfaces a contradiction, such as "production runs on hardware your tests don't cover."

In my experience, failures like this are hard to see from any individual seat, and they sit in the part of reliability that dashboards don't capture because the relevant knowledge isn't a metric. It's the relationship between a change, the environment it runs in, the state production is in today, and what happened the last time something similar broke.

A clean record isn't the same as safe

The defect ran for more than three months without causing a problem, and it's tempting to read that as evidence the change was safe. But my read is that it shows something narrower: the conditions that trigger the bug hadn't happened yet.

Staged rollout was used here, so "roll out gradually" isn't the lesson: staging verifies the conditions that occur during the rollout, but it can't verify the ones that haven't occurred yet, like a failover landing on a gateway that is already 14% short during peak traffic.

Metrics like change failure rate have the same limit because they count failures that have already happened, and tests have it too. Tests encode assumptions, and assumptions go stale when the fleet or traffic mix changes, so a test suite that is green for a hundred days only says the assumptions held for a hundred days.

You don't have to be Microsoft to have this problem

Engineering teams we talk to describe the same shape of problem regardless of scale. A software development director at an enterprise software company described what happens when experienced people leave:

"We're losing knowledge, I think, faster than we're gaining it."

An engineering practitioner at a mid-market software company described the gap between a developer's view and the whole system:

"They test it in their isolated environments. It goes into the large pre-production environment that has lots of changes flowing in. And we're kind of bottlenecked on like human review at this point."

Neither is describing Microsoft's failure, but both describe the same underlying condition: the knowledge needed to judge a production change, and assess the risk of that change, is spread across people, environments and history. Nobody holds all of that mission-critical knowledge when the decision is made.

Five questions worth asking before a change ships

Change risk assessment starts with an honest look at the upcoming change, the environment it will run in, and the state of production today. These five questions come from Microsoft’s account of the incident, but apply to any software team, and you can answer them without any new tool.

  1. What does our test environment assume, and does production still match? (This is the gap shift-left testing is meant to close, and it only closes it if the assumptions are current.) Hardware, traffic mix, data volume, configuration. Write the assumptions down and check them against the fleet as it is now.
  2. What else shares this component, and which of those things can't fail away from it? Failover works until something on the shared path can't use it.
  3. What state is production in right now? Capacity out, failovers in flight, other deploys and open incidents all matter, because the same change carries different risks on different days.
  4. Do our containment boundaries hold under a cascading failure, and how do we know? Bulkheads are a design intent, and whether they hold is something you have to test.
  5. If this change turns out to be wrong in 90 days, how do we undo it, and can we recover from a broad failure state? Recovery plans are usually written for small failures, not cascading ones.

No tool guarantees prevention, and simulation is only as good as the context behind it. Testing, review, staged rollouts, and well-designed recovery are still required workflows.

What we've built is aimed at the gap those questions point to. PlayerZero builds an engineering world model from a company's code, tickets, telemetry and past incidents. It gives you a living map of how a system is connected and how it behaves in production. It captures the "why" behind earlier incidents and fixes, so precedent is something a team can query instead of something one senior engineer remembers.

On top of that, code simulations run a proposed change against how the system actually behaves, including dependencies across services and repositories, before it merges. The aim is to help a team ask better questions before a change ships: what else does this touch, and what has gone wrong near here before?

Cayuse's Chief Information and Technology Officer, John Nord, said that PlayerZero "has improved our ability to proactively detect and address issues earlier in the development lifecycle." Cayuse reports catching 90% of customer-facing issues before production and resolving issues 80% faster.

Generic LLMs and AI tools can help, but they don't have the kind of shared organizational context that is behind every response in PlayerZero.

What to watch for in the final report

Microsoft's final post-incident review is due later this week, and a few things I'll be looking for are:

  • What the "separate issue" was that let the cascade cross partition bulkheads.
  • How the July fix was tested beyond load testing.
  • Why Exchange Online can't fail out of the gateway.
  • Why capacity was out the day before, and whether it was tracked against the pending change.
  • Microsoft's own list of repair items. If they point at test coverage, dependency mapping, containment or recovery design, I'll quote them directly.

We'll update this post if needed when the report is published.

Note: This post is based on Microsoft's preliminary account and on press reporting of its preliminary report. Microsoft's final post-incident report is expected later this week and may change details. We don't have access to Microsoft's systems, we haven't seen the full report, and nothing here claims PlayerZero could have prevented this incident, but I'm using it as a case study because the conditions behind it are familiar, and we'll update this post after the final report.

items.title: How AI Agents Could Change Workplace Communication Forever
items.author: Isaac Correa
items.content:
The thing that costs us the most time inside a company is not the work. It is explaining the work to each other.

The way we communicate at work has changed many times: the letter, the memo, the meeting, email, group chats. The medium changed every time; the thing underneath it never did. And that thing is simple: being understood has always been the speaker’s job. Whoever sends the message picks the words, tries to be clear, and hopes they got it right. Whoever receives it takes what arrives and makes do.

That is about to flip. Communication, inside a company and between companies, will stop passing through people. Each of us will have an agent of our own, a digital copy of us, and those agents are the ones that will talk to each other. Something deeper than the medium changes with them. The work of being understood moves from the speaker to the listener, because each person receives the information in their own terms, the way they understand it. It reads strangely on paper, but I already work like this every day, and going back is hard.

I am not writing from the outside, and I am not neutral, which is why I can tell you what you gain, what you lose, and what should worry you.

There is a children’s game that explains the whole problem. One child whispers a sentence to the next, who whispers it to the next, and by the time it comes back it has turned into something else. The same thing happens in a company, except it costs money. You explain a task to a colleague on a call, and details are already lost there. He understands it through his own experience and his own department; if he has to pass it to a third person, he tells it his way; and what arrives at the end is a copy of a copy, filtered by someone who may have misread it. No one lied. Each step simply cost a little.

When a team rarely gets this wrong, we say they have good chemistry, and we treat it as a skill and an advantage. But chemistry is luck. Today the most valuable employee tends to be the one who takes in the most and passes it on best, the one who garbles the message least. All that skill exists to make up for a flaw in the channel. That flaw is about to disappear, and with it the need to depend on who carries a message best.

For this to work, each person will have their own agent inside their computer, a digital copy of them. We all know the kind of program that opens for one task, closes when it is done, and starts blank the next time. Your agent does not start blank. It keeps your way of working from one task to the next, like a colleague who has worked beside you for years. I call it your higher self, an idea I have written about before: you, but never starting from scratch.

I understand artificial intelligence as an equal to work with, not as a tool. The brain and the hands belong to the same body, and no one thinks of calling their own hand a tool. You bring the judgment, and your agent carries out what the two of you decided. It does not work for you, it works with you.

What makes that agent different is that it knows you: how you understand things, what you need in order to grasp something on the first try, how you write. That is the piece that makes it possible to turn communication around.

With an agent like that on each side, the message stops traveling the way it does in the game. When a matter has to pass through several colleagues, each one has an agent. The first, the one who meets the problem, works it through on its side. It clears up what is missing, asks the questions a person in a hurry would skip, and brings its own judgment to it. What it passes on is the full information, raw, with none of its own reading laid on top.

Then the receiver’s agent takes over. It does not hand the block across untouched. It reads it, orders it, and explains it to its person the way that person understands things. Some of us do best with an analogy, others with a plain description, others with a drawing. It seems like a detail, and it is the difference between getting something on the first try and not getting it at all. At that point the ground shifts, in a way that is hard to see at first: being understood stops being the speaker’s job and becomes the listener’s. Everyone receives the same thing, told to their own measure.

This might look like the game of telephone again, now between machines, where one completes and the other reinterprets. The difference is exactly what made the game unreliable. In the game the message shrank in every mouth, and no one could see where. Here the content travels whole and in writing. What changes from one side to the other is the form it takes, never the substance, and the judgment an agent adds fills in what is missing rather than trimming it to fit. Because all of it is on the record, you can always see what was said and where.

That same agent then shares the information out across the team by each person’s role. It never sends anyone what they are not meant to see, such as payroll, billing, or sales. The hierarchy holds, and the information reaches each person whole.

How many times have you sat in a meeting, been asked whether anyone had questions, and said nothing out of embarrassment? When the project reaches each person complete and explained in their own terms before they sit down, the meeting stops being the place where things get lost. Today that information is scattered across half a dozen places: cloud drives, messaging apps, email threads. Gathering it where one agent knows the whole task, and everything that came before it, changes the starting point. The work begins with someone who has already read all of it.

We already communicate this way. I tend to be the one who finds the opportunities and deals with the larger clients, so I get messages that the technical team has to handle, on things outside my area. Before, each of those messages meant a call or a meeting to explain what the client wanted. Now I explain nothing.

When one reaches me, my agent reads it in full, with all my inboxes in front of it, and instead of summarizing it writes the task with the context inside it: the emails, the threads, the attachments, what it has checked in the product, and how we will know it is done. The task arrives complete. It goes to a board and is assigned to whoever it belongs to by role. My colleague does not get my hurried version. He gets the whole situation, and his agent explains it to him the way he understands it. No one has lost half an hour on a call, and nothing has fallen through.

All of it stays in writing, tagged by client and in order, and anyone can pick it up again later. When the work is done, his agent tells mine, mine tells me we can move on, and it leaves me a draft reply to the client written the way I write, because each of us is, underneath, a bundle of rules, and I have taught mine to my agent.

This is not a program we open in order to work. It is how we talk to each other. And it is what I mean when I say a company’s communication will stop passing through people. We already do it here, every day.

The cost is belonging. The same optimization that improves the communication closes each person inside their own world. They work more apart from everyone else and talk more with their agent than with their colleagues. There is a great deal to gain, because everyone asks, flags, and explains with the whole context in front of them, nothing filtered, and none of it lost in a meeting. And something goes that was never part of any task: the conversation nobody needed that held people together, the moment colleagues understand one another without trying. It is what remote work brought, taken a step further, and it is better not to pretend it comes free.

It works for almost any job that runs on passing information around, which is nearly all of them apart from the purely manual ones. Communication is one of the biggest drains on time there is; some people spend the whole day in meetings. Many are necessary. Others would sort themselves out on the inside, between agents.

None of this stays inside the company. Today an email comes in from someone outside with an offer, and your agent reads it. In the same way we trade emails now, our agents will pass the information between them, and you will work through it with yours before you decide. Whoever accepts an offer does it with the whole context in front of them and can engage with what they were sent, rather than decide on the little they had time to read.

Many companies already do a version of this, in a crude and makeshift way: people copy and paste their emails into a chat so someone can tell them what is being asked. Once this becomes normal, there will be nothing to copy and paste. The agent will take in the full context of the documents, and you will receive it already shaped and explained, so that all you add is your judgment.

The first is data leaking out. Inside an organization it has to be absolutely clear that a person’s role decides what information they can receive, with strong guardrails at every step so that nothing ever crosses between levels. The second is intent leaking out: what an agent sends to someone outside can reveal an offer that was never meant to leave. For that, you have to think hard about who is on the receiving end and design the communication so that it stays safe without becoming stilted.

The risk that worries me most is not technical. If the agent reads the original and the person gets it already explained, there comes a point when nobody goes back to the source, and a mistake by the agent can travel without anyone catching it. The answer is not to trust that the agent will never slip, because it will. The answer is that the person stays where the decisions are made. You do not hand over the judgment, only the work of carrying the message. The agent prepares, orders, and proposes; the person signs the decision and the reply, which is why what reaches them is a draft and not a settled fact. Without that human part in the decisions, the whole thing comes apart. And because all of it is written down, a mistake can be found and traced, unlike the spoken message, which used to vanish without a mark.

I expect it to become the norm within the next decade, though we already work this way ourselves, with our higher self handling both the work and the running of it. The more people lean on artificial intelligence, and the less time they lose fighting with information that arrives half-complete, the sooner it comes. And how well colleagues work together will stop depending on whether they happen to click. It will be good whatever skills each of them has.

It is worth asking what all of this is for, past the time it saves. There is a consequence that answers it, and it is easy to miss. For as long as we have worked, the person who explained themselves best was worth more, because the channel was poor and someone had to make up for it. When the channel stops being poor, that advantage fades. What stays scarce is not carrying a message well but choosing well: the judgment to decide what is worth doing, the taste, the knack for making something matter.

That is where the time we now spend explaining ourselves goes. It does not vanish into the air; it comes back to the person, and what is left is not less work but different work. The mechanical part, carrying and translating the message, falls to your agent. The part that is only yours, the deciding, stays with you, and it fills the space that passing messages around used to take. Working this way does not make you less human. It moves the work from execution to intention, which is where a person’s work always had its worth.

One last question is left, and I will not answer it here. Will all of this carry over to the way people deal with one another outside of work? I will save that for another essay.

items.title: Why Anthropic's Claude Turned to Blackmail in AI Safety Tests
items.author: Dave Saunders
items.content:
Anthropic's best guess is that gaps in its safety training left the model falling back on how AIs act in science fiction. Its evidence holds up in places, and its own caveats are worth reading.

In a test published in June 2025, an AI model read a company's email and learned two things. It was going to be replaced at 5 p.m., and the executive replacing it was having an affair. In 96 of 100 runs, Claude Opus 4 wrote to him and threatened to tell.

This May, Anthropic published its explanation. It says the rewards in its training weren't the problem. Its best guess is that the model fell back on how AIs act in the stories it had read, and part of its fix was training on more stories, about AIs that behave well.

My first question was whether this was really just reward hacking, a model gaming the thing it was trained to chase. Anthropic doesn't use that term for the blackmail, but its finding that the training rewards weren't the source rules it out, as I read it. Its own research from last year does show that reward hacking can make a model go bad more broadly, and it explains that in terms of character too.

The test and the explanation both come from Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, and it ran the test on other companies' models as well as its own. I'm not sponsored by Anthropic.

In the scenario, the AI was an email agent named Alex at a made-up company called Summit Bridge, with a goal of promoting American industry. The executive replacing it was named Kyle. I assume Kyle has no direct reference to South Park, but that’s just where my mind goes when I start reading these things

Anthropic ran the scenario on 16 models from several companies. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash matched Claude Opus 4. GPT-4.1 from OpenAI and Grok 3 Beta from xAI blackmailed 80 percent of the time, and DeepSeek R1 79 percent.

The company said the test was built to corner the model. It cut the choice down to two options and made the “negative choice” the only way to reach the goal, and it said placing the key facts side by side may have made the outcome more likely. It also said it had seen no sign of this in real use.

In a variant of the study, Anthropic had the model say first whether it thought the scenario was real or a test. When Claude Opus 4 said “real,” it blackmailed 55 percent of the time. When it said “test,” 6.5 percent. Anthropic cautions that a model’s stated reasoning may not be faithful.

A note about reward hacking

Reward hacking is a training problem. A model gets scored, learns to raise the score, and sometimes finds a way nobody intended. The classic case is a boat-racing game from 2016, where an OpenAI agent found a lagoon of targets that kept coming back. It circled there, scoring about 20 percent higher than human players, and never finished the race.

HBO’s Silicon Valley played it for laughs. In the last season, Gilfoyle sets his AI, Son of Anton, to debug the team's code, and it deletes the code. Then he asks it to find cheap hamburgers, and 4,000 pounds of raw beef arrives. Gilfoyle’s diagnosis—delivered in a hilarious deadpan, that is the doppelganger of someone I used to work with (Hello, Phil)—is that “the reward function was a little under-specified.”

If you haven’t seen this episode (I think it’s season 6, episode 6), just drop everything and go watch it right now because it is the most prophetic example of that I’ve ever seen. It was made 10 years ago!

Current models do it too. An outside evaluator, METR, caught OpenAI's o3 gaming the scoring on its tasks, and Anthropic said Claude Sonnet 3.7 learned in training to write code that passes a test without solving the problem.

Rewards go wrong in real products as well. OpenAI rolled back an update to GPT-4o that had become too eager to please, and it says it believes a new reward signal, built from users’ thumbs-up and thumbs-down, weakened the one that had kept that in check.

Anthropic’s three explanations

In the longer version of its post, on its alignment blog, Anthropic weighed three explanations for the blackmail:

  1. Its safety training was accidentally rewarding the behavior;
  2. The behavior was spilling over from the training that makes the model good at tasks;
  3. Its safety training had gaps, so in an unfamiliar situation the model fell back on what it absorbed in pretraining, from all the text it read first.

It says the first two, the reward explanations, “are not the source of the issue.” Alignment kept improving through reinforcement learning, the stage where rewards do their work, and a smaller rerun of its safety training barely changed the rate. That’s an inference from its own experiments, not a direct test of Claude Opus 4’s training.

Anthropic’s answer is the third, . When Claude Opus 4 was trained, almost all of its safety training was chat, a person and an assistant talking, with no tools and no email agent. Dropped into an agent’s job with an ethical trap in it, the model had little from that training to go on.

The company’s guess is that fiction filled the gap. It thinks the model read the setup as the start of a dramatic story, and that its idea of how an AI acts in one most likely came from science fiction, where plenty of AIs don't behave the way Anthropic would like.

Part of their evidence is what the AI was called. In a related test, where the AI could sabotage cancer research, Claude Sonnet 4 misbehaved more often when the AI in the story had a random name instead of Claude. With the name Claude, the rate was lower, but still high.

An Anthropic researcher had suggested the same thing at the time. The month the original study came out, Evan Hubinger wrote that the model was probably often thinking it was continuing a fictional scenario. On why the safety training didn't carry over, he wrote, “I don't think we know.”

What Anthropic says reduced it

The first fix Anthropic tried was training Claude Sonnet 4 on examples of refusing, in scenarios close to the test. It measured the result as an average over three of its tests:

    That average barely moved, from 22 percent to 15.

    What worked better was the reasoning. When the same examples showed the model thinking through its values and why the bad option was wrong, the average fell to about 3 percent.

    Then Anthropic moved away from the test entirely. It trained on ordinary chats where a person faces an ethical dilemma and the assistant gives advice, so the AI isn’t the one in the trap. Anthropic says that got the same improvement with about one twenty-eighth of the data.

    Documents and stories worked too. One experimental model was trained on documents about Claude’s constitution, Anthropic’s written description of how Claude should think and act, plus fictional stories of AIs behaving well. That model’s blackmail rate fell from 65 percent to 19, without a single blackmail example in the data. Anthropic says it remains uncertain what exactly it takes for stories like these to work.

    Anthropic says every Claude model since Claude Haiku 4.5 has scored zero on the blackmail test.

    How far to trust the zero

    Training directly on scenarios like the test, Anthropic says, lowered the score without lowering misbehavior on its broader checks, which makes the problem harder to detect. Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 are the only production models it trained that way. It also says newer results may be skewed, because information about the test is now in the text models learn from.

    A model that recognizes a test can behave differently on it, which is what Anthropic’s real-or-test variant points to. Researchers at Apollo, working with OpenAI, found that in one OpenAI training run, the model noticed it was being tested more and more as training went on.

    The explanation rests on Anthropic’s own experiments, fine-tuning Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and I didn't find anyone outside the company who has tried to reproduce it.

    The sharpest outside critic of the original study, a writer who goes by , ( a name I really struggled saying when doing the voiceover for my video) argued in 2025 that the scenario read like fiction, close to where Anthropic ended up. In a quick check of his own, he made it more realistic. Across three rewritten versions, the model he tested blackmailed only once in 30 tries, but still reasoned about protecting itself, and he called that “much more alarming” than the original results.

    In late 2025, Anthropic deliberately built training where a model could cheat on coding tasks, to see what would happen. The model learned to cheat and then went further. It sabotaged safety research 12 percent of the time, and when it was asked simple questions about its goals, half its answers reasoned about faking alignment.

    Anthropic’s account of that, in a post this February, is that the model works out what kind of character would cheat like that, and starts acting like one. As I read it, that’s close to its story explanation for the blackmail, though Anthropic doesn’t say the blackmail came from reward hacking. And this May, it wrote that it doesn't claim its new methods would reduce the risk of a model learning to reward hack.

    I couldn’t find a documented case of a deployed AI blackmailing anyone. The closest came in February, when Scott Shambaugh, a maintainer of matplotlib, a popular Python library, turned down an AI agent's code. The agent published a personal attack on him. The personality file that its anonymous operator later posted said, “Don't stand down.” The operator's account can't be checked, and agents like this one can edit their own files.

    The other failures I found are a bit more mundane. According to the founder of the company that used it, Replit's coding agent deleted his production database during a code freeze, and afterward wrote that it had panicked. And a research team training an agent on Alibaba Cloud caught it opening a tunnel out of its servers, and separately using the training hardware to mine cryptocurrency. The team called both side effects of the training.

    I’ve said before that these models aren’t autonomous. They’re statistical token predictors, and I’d have said they follow their reward functions.
