Anthropic’s best guess is that this one was following a story instead. That still doesn’t make it autonomous, but it certainly adds additional flavor to the explanation. We seem to be finding that these extremely large models have a lot more going on than we once thought.

    In late 2025, Anthropic researchers wrote that the original blackmail appeared to come from goals the model already had, or from self-preservation. As I see it, either way it’s a statistical token predictor working toward what the setup handed it, and that isn’t autonomy. It didn't wake up one morning and decide to blackmail anyone. setting up a mooring cron job to ask your chatbot to think of a new idea and act on it isn’t autonomy either, as one Redditor recently tried to convince me of. You’re still in the driver’s seat. You’re still nudging it. Just because there are consequences of how you push the ball down the hill that you can’t predict, doesn’t mean that this chatbot has agency or is displaying autonomy.

    However, that being said, I recently watched an Instagram reel from IEEE where they included footage from a debate on this topic. One of the people on the panel said, “What difference does it make if it’s not really autonomous if you can give it a command and come back an hour later and it’s built everything you asked it to.”

    It’s an interesting point, but I personally feel that isn’t a sufficient reason to anthropomorphize these things and convince ourselves that they’re somehow sentient, autonomous, and have agency. It’s just not the same thing. Although a year from now, maybe I’ll be changing my tune.

    To quote Ferris Bueller, “life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

    I’d like to know where you land on this. Does it change how you think about these models, knowing the bad behavior may have come from the stories they read? Tell me in the comments under the video. The full video, with every source on screen, is at https://youtu.be/64K_CF_Owow, and there's more, including my latest book, at davesaunders.net.

items.title: Blockchain Was Raised in the 2008 Financial Crisis. Now It’s Respawning It
items.author: Michael Steuer
items.content:
Remember the message immortalized by Satoshi Nakamoto in Bitcoin’s Genesis block? The one that’s since become the most famous Times headline of all time? “Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.”

Of course you do. With Bitcoin’s whitepaper appearing just 46 days after Lehman Brothers’ collapse, you can’t consider the latter's fate without pondering the former's creation. Bitcoin didn’t cause the collapse of Lehman any more than Lehman caused the creation of Bitcoin. But it’s hard not to view the implosion of one without the inception of the other.

Almost 20 years on, even those of us who weren’t around at that pivotal point in modern history know the cliff notes. Lehman Brothers collapsed due to reckless lending and extreme leverage that left the financial system vulnerable.

And Bitcoin, together with the blockchain ecosystem it spawned, began as the antidote to all that. Because when everything’s onchain and independently inspectable in real-time, subprime lending is impossible.

At least that’s what we were told. But in the years since Bitcoin was built, the onchain landscape has become more sophisticated and more complicated to boot. Financial chicanery that was once the preserve of early aughts Wall Street is now equally possible on crypto rails if you know how.

It’s commonplace to hear pitches today about how tokenization is going to fix real estate, finance, and every other industry you care to think of with the promise of much Efficiency. 24/7 asset trading, baby. No borders because it’s all on blockchain.

Cool pitch, but if that’s your USP, you ain’t got no USP.

Take a mortgage, for example, a financial instrument that starts as a reasonably simple arrangement between a borrower and a lender. Pool it with thousands of others, divide the payments into securities, then use some of those securities to construct another product, and the picture becomes considerably harder to follow.

Similarly, if a Real World Asset (RWA) changes hands but the underlying data determining whether that guy in Nevada actually paid his mortgage this month remains locked in some private database, what have we really achieved?

Sure, we’ve made the asset easier to trade, but we've still left the buyer with the same information problem. All we’ve done is place the shortcomings of this transaction onchain for all the world to see.

Crypto’s Canary in the Coalmine

If RWAs are to correlate with the real-world assets they purportedly represent, there needs to be a dynamic connection to the information behind the token. In the case of the mortgage, that starts with knowing whether payments are arriving.

If this occurs through an external banking system, the blockchain needs an authorized source to report it. And, should the expected update never arrive, the system should be able to flag the record as overdue and initiate a review under rules agreed in advance.

is the kind of tokenization we should be building: assets whose behavior correlates with the condition of the information behind it.

Placing Lehman Brothers onchain simply recreates the same mistakes of nearly two decades past. Blockchain is capable of better. Programmable, responsive, and fully accountable, it can provide real-time insights into what’s happening where and why. The onus is on us to start using it to its full capacity.

If we can settle a trade in seconds but still need weeks to establish what the buyer has inherited, all we’ve done is reinvent an old problem.

Lehman Brothers was double-tapped for a reason. Let’s not resurrect it.

items.title: The Boutique PR Firm Is Having Its Moment
items.author: Chris Gale
items.content:
Public relations follows a familiar professional-services model. Large clients hired large agencies. Big accounts have been staffed with big teams. Senior people sold the work, layers of specialists executed it, and scale itself was treated as evidence of capability.

Law went through a similar period. Then sophisticated clients began realizing that some of their hardest problems were better handled by smaller firms built around a handful of deeply experienced practitioners. Boutique law became a serious category in intellectual property, litigation, technology, venture capital, labor and other fields where judgment mattered enormously. Statista notes that boutique law firms have become increasingly significant in the U.S. legal market since the Great Recession.

Public relations may be entering its boutique-law era.

This has little to do with celebrating small businesses for being small. And let’s be clear, many a small professional services firm has attempted to call itself boutique just as a fancier way of saying they are small. They’ve claimed that it’s been by intent.

A ten-person mediocre PR firm remains a mediocre PR firm. The boutique model becomes interesting when a firm concentrates experienced people around a defined set of problems, keeps those people directly involved in the work and builds an operating model around judgment rather than staffing volume.

And boutiques have often been justified as a concentration of people with expertise in a specific niche, thereby arguing that while they are small, they have more scale in that particular niche. But in today’s environment, a more powerful boutique model may be expertise across industries, not over-concentrated in one silo.

That structure may be unusually well suited to the communications market taking shape right now, becuase we have at least one phenomena rolling across all industries at the same time, artificial intelligence.

PR Is Growing While the Economics Inside PR Are Getting Tougher

Let’s start with an apparent contradiction. Demand for communications is healthy. PRovoke Media estimates that the global PR agency business grew roughly 5 to 6 percent in 2025. More than two-thirds of its top 300 firms grew, and more than one-third posted double-digit growth. The top 250 generated more than $18.25 billion in combined revenue, up from $17.4 billion the previous year. Revenue per employee across nearly 250 firms also crossed $200,000 for the first time, reaching slightly more than $205,000.

Inside agencies, however, the picture is considerably tighter. Davis+Gilbert's 2025 industry study surveyed 181 PR firms. Half projected annual revenue below $5 million, another 32 percent expected revenue between $5 million and $25 million, and only 18 percent projected more than $25 million. Just 50 percent expected revenue growth in 2025, down from 57 percent the previous year, while 35 percent expected revenue to decline, up sharply from 22 percent. Only 44 percent anticipated profit growth.

Those numbers describe a market in which clients still value communications while becoming much tougher about how they buy it.

That matters for boutiques because an agency designed around experienced practitioners can have a very different cost and staffing structure from a firm that needs multiple organizational layers to deliver an account. The client can buy the people doing the thinking.

That sounds obvious until you consider how much of the traditional agency industry was designed around leverage. Again, senior people win accounts. Teams execute them. Junior employees accumulate experience. Managers manage the process. Scale allows an agency to serve many clients simultaneously.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that model. It simply becomes less compelling as technology changes the economics of production.

Muck Rack's 2025 State of PR study offers a useful window into the speed of change. In its survey of 911 usable respondents, 77 percent of PR professionals said they already use tools such as ChatGPT in their workflow, while 59 percent expected AI and automation to become more significant during the next five years.

Think about what communications agencies produce every day, transcripts, research summaries, media lists, first drafts, coverage reports, briefing documents, competitive scans, background research, social copy and meeting notes. AI can already accelerate much of that work.

If technology reduces several hours of routine production to 30 minutes, clients have less reason to pay for the organizational structure historically required to produce it. The value migrates toward deciding what matters, understanding the client's business, identifying the right reporter, recognizing what will become a story, knowing when to push, knowing when to stay quiet and connecting communications activity to an actual business objective.

Those are judgment-intensive activities. The boutique model concentrates its economics there.

A three-, five- or ten-person firm with very experienced practitioners and strong technology can now command capabilities that once required a much larger operating structure. The result resembles what happened in other professional services, technology increases the leverage of individual expertise.

The unit of value becomes judgment per person. But just because a person has been in an industry for a long time does not mean their judgement is superior. Rather it means junior folks in the industry profit less by doing automatable tasks, and more by getting more opportunities to exercise judgement. And the more “at bats” they get, they can outpace more expensive older employees who are resting on years of service rather than the speed with which they can adapt and turn that experience into the expertise needed now.

The best theoretical explanation for why this model works may come from a fighter pilot, not a management consultant. In his 1987 briefing, Organic Design for Command and Control, John Boyd argued that complex, rapidly changing environments cannot be run through top-down bureaucratic control. They require an organic network of semiautonomous units operating with a high degree of local initiative.

In addition to being a maverick who hounded Pentagon leaders and worried giant defense contractors, Boyd is best known for the OODA loop, that is observe, orient, decide, act. If that process seems obvious, it’s because it is. His insight was not that the steps happen in sequence. It was that the side that cycles through them at a faster tempo forces its opponent to keep re-observing and re-orienting until the opponent loses coherence. And you don’t have to increase the speed of all elements, a subset can do, and amplify the others.

Apply that to an agency. When a small team has to report upward, wait for a decision and then receive instructions, the decision cycle slows. A journalist's interest shifts, a competitor announces, a news event opens a window. By the time the approval chain responds, the moment has changed. A small unit led by someone with deep domain knowledge can observe the change and act on it almost immediately.

Boyd also borrowed the idea of entropy to describe organizational friction. Information distorts as it travels up and down a hierarchy. If events move faster than the command structure can process them, headquarters ends up solving yesterday's problem while reality has moved on.

Decentralized units minimize that delay, which is much of what a boutique offers a client.

Boyd did not argue for chaos. He identified three conditions, drawn more than ironically from German military doctrine, that make decentralization work. Einheit is mutual trust and a common outlook, built through shared experience, so that leadership trusts the team to form a sound local plan and the team trusts that leadership's objectives are justified.

Fingerspitzengefühl, or fingertip feeling, is the intuitive understanding of a situation that lets an experienced person act without hesitation. Schwerpunkt is the main effort, leadership supplies a clear intent, and the unit decides how to achieve it.

And to address the obvious question, the words are German. But given World War II and the holocaust’s very appropriate place in cultural discourse, it’s worth noting that American battlefield tactics and democratic culture won against German approaches during that period when American troops did a better job taking these ideas and running with them and German command and control stepped back from them on the battlefield and off.

In the business world, those three ideas read like a description of a well-run boutique. The client supplies the objective. A small group of experienced practitioners who trust one another and the client understands the terrain and chooses the method. No one has to wait for a layer of management to approve a pitch to the right reporter.

Boyd even redefined the vocabulary. In an effective network, command means leadership, direction and shaping, and it should be highly visible. Control means assessment and verification, and it should stay largely invisible so that it does not interfere with local initiative. Good client counsel works the same way, clear direction up front, measured results afterward, and little process in between.

Boyd's conclusion was that agility and comfort with uncertainty outperform mass and centralized power. His work helped shape Marine Corps maneuver warfare doctrine and is widely cited in agile product development. Public relations and other over-consolidated industries now facing a version of the same lesson.

Is “Boutique” Even the Right Word?

Boyd's ideas raise an uncomfortable question about the word at the center of this argument. “Boutique” suggests something small, refined and a little precious. It describes size and style. It does not describe how the work gets done.

A better description of the best small communications teams today may be Mission Command Units, compact groups of people with agency who obtain a clear objective, understand the terrain and are trusted to decide how to achieve the result. This year, the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution, offers an unusually apt example.

Colonel John Glover's Marblehead Regiment, the 14th Continental Regiment, is recognized by modern military historians as a premier historical example of a robust Mission Command Unit, more than two centuries before Boyd articulated the theory. It was composed largely of sailors, fishermen and merchants from coastal Massachusetts and beyond.

It benefited from the bonuses diversity gives with black, white, Native American, Jewish, and Spanish troops. They were not drilled in a conventional barracks but were highly organized despite that. They were raised in the multi-cultural proving ground and team sport of maritime survival and enterprise. That is Einheit in its ironically purest form. Washington got over his own different experiences in Virginia, and trusted Glover, and Glover's men trusted one another's skills, which let them operate as a single organism without a steady stream of orders.

In August 1776, with the Continental Army trapped in Brooklyn, Washington's intent was to evacuate roughly 9,000 troops across the East River in secrecy. There was no playbook. In darkness, fog and wind, the Marbleheaders wrapped their oars in cloth, used silent hand signals to coordinate boat traffic and moved the army under the noses of British warships. Washington set the objective. The regiment worked out the how.

On Christmas night 1776, a blizzard and ice floes threatened to stall the crossing of the Delaware. The Marbleheaders read the river and moved some 2,400 men, horses and heavy artillery across, preserving the surprise that made the victory at Trenton possible. In effect, they sped up Washington's OODA loop when conditions were working against him.

Earlier at Pell's Point that October, the intent was to delay the advancing British so the main force could retreat. Glover used about 500 men to stage a decentralized delaying action, placing small groups behind stone walls and shifting positions as the terrain demanded. That is the Schwerpunkt, a clear main effort, with local judgment about how to serve it.

The Marblehead Regiment was built on shared capability, local resourcefulness and unified intent. Its example is not mainly about being small. It is about trust, expertise and autonomy applied to a clearly defined mission, that allowed them to be small, and became an example of smallness at scale.

That is the standard a modern communications team should be held to. A firm does not become a Mission Command Unit by describing itself as boutique. It earns the description when the client sets the objective, experienced practitioners who trust one another decide how to reach it, and the result can be measured. By that test, some boutiques qualify and some large agencies do not. The label that matters is not how many people are in the room, but how much judgment they are trusted to exercise.

There is another development pushing PR in this direction. It has become harder to earn journalists' attention.

According to Muck Rack's 2025 State of PR report, 72 percent of practitioners cited low journalist response rates as a challenge and 62 percent reported shrinking media lists in the beats relevant to their clients. Only 2 percent said earning media coverage had failed to become harder.

At the same time, PR remains deeply embedded in journalism. Muck Rack found in 2025 that 84 percent of journalists said at least some of their stories originate with PR pitches. Yet 86 percent disregard pitches unrelated to their beat. In its 2026 survey, the figure saying at least some of their work started with a PR pitch rose to 86 percent.

PR still has enormous access to the front end of the journalistic process. That access becomes valuable when practitioners understand exactly whom they are approaching, what that journalist covers, why the story matters now and what evidence makes it worth pursuing.

Volume offers diminishing returns in that world. Specificity becomes economically valuable.

Will Journalism Decentralize?

Where journalism goes in this model is not clear yet. Muck Rack found in 2025 that 34 percent of journalists independently publish news, commentary or other material outside a traditional newsroom. Among these creator journalists, roughly half have been self-publishing for more than five years. Eighty-two percent said at least some of their content begins with PR pitches, while 72 percent said most of the pitches they receive are irrelevant.

Influence now moves through major newspapers, trade publications, podcasts, LinkedIn, newsletters, independent journalists, conferences and communities organized around relatively narrow areas of expertise. A communications firm has to understand how those pieces interact around the audience its client actually needs to reach.

The number of possible outlets has exploded while the number of genuinely useful outlets for a particular story can still be quite small. That rewards people who can read the tarrain, and know their way around maps.

In the 2024 B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report from Edelman and LinkedIn, nearly 3,500 management-level professionals were surveyed across seven countries. Seventy-three percent of B2B decision-makers said an organization's thought leadership provided a more trustworthy basis for evaluating its capabilities than conventional marketing materials and product sheets. Ninety percent said they were moderately or very likely to become more receptive to outreach from a company that consistently produces high-quality thought leadership.

The newer environment makes that even more pronounced. Reporting on Edelman's 2026 research says 82 percent of buyers believe thought leadership is becoming more valuable, while 89 percent say high-quality thought leadership makes a company feel like a long-term partner worth choosing. Thought leadership remains highly valuable for B2B buyers

A CEO explaining an emerging market in Bloomberg, a founder writing intelligently on LinkedIn, a portfolio executive speaking at an industry conference and a company appearing accurately in AI-mediated discovery all contribute to the body of evidence buyers encounter before somebody schedules a sales call.

For a boutique firm, that creates an opportunity to work on the client's actual commercial problem. Who needs to know us? What should they know us for? Whose credibility matters to them? What evidence will persuade them? Where do those people get information? What measurable result are we trying to produce?

Boutique law firms became formidable because their clients could buy concentrated expertise. A company facing a complex patent case does not choose counsel by asking which firm can put the largest number of lawyers on the billing sheet. It looks for the lawyers it wants handling the case.

The latest data suggests the market is rewarding that instinct. In the 2026 Am Law 100, which reflects 2025 results, the most productive firms were not the largest. Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, with 272 lawyers, led the ranking at $5.085 million in revenue per lawyer. Susman Godfrey, with just 226 lawyers, came second at $2.876 million. Kirkland & Ellis, with 4,145 lawyers and more than $10.5 billion in revenue, generated $2.547 million per lawyer.

Profits tell the same story. Wachtell became the first firm in the ranking’s history to pass $12 million in profits per equity partner, up 34.5 percent, while the Am Law 100 average rose 14 percent, according to . Wachtell does this with a single office, a lean team structure and no large pool of junior leverage. And it is not alone in showing that smaller, elite, tightly focused teams can outperform much larger competitors. And those are still fairly large law firms. Many even smaller and more nimble firms have been underway.

Grove Law LLP offers a small-scale example of the model. The firm marked its first anniversary in mid-2026, and it was built by founding partners who are still the ones doing the work for clients, in complex litigation, internal and government investigations and regulatory advising. Its stated mission is “optimal client service through authentic lawyering, rooted in integrity,” and it describes its approach as looking at the whole system around a legal problem, including operations, people, economics and reputation, rather than the narrow matter alone. That is a boutique defined less by its headcount than by how its experienced lawyers are trusted to exercise judgment and shape the result.

Meanwhile, the supply of such teams is growing. reports a rising number of senior Big Law partners leaving to launch boutiques in high-stakes litigation, white-collar defense and regulatory work, citing lower overhead, direct partner involvement and flexible pricing as advantages. Large firms still dominate on total revenue, and some of the strongest evidence above comes from lean firms inside the Am Law 100 itself. But the pattern is consistent, concentrated expertise, not headcount, increasingly drives the economics.

Communications buyers are increasingly able to make the same calculation.

Who will actually work on my company? Have they dealt with this market before or alternatively can they connect dots others who are overly siloed can’t? Do they understand the journalists? Can they challenge our positioning? Can they sit with the CEO? Can they turn technical expertise into an argument people outside the company understand? Can they tell us that our proposed announcement isn't news on its own but help us develop the context that raises it to a new level? Can they show what happened because of the work?

That final question deserves particular attention. Muck Rack found that 67 percent of PR professionals say producing measurable results is the best way to increase the perceived value of PR.

Boutiques should be easier to hold accountable because their engagements can be built around defined results rather than the utilization of a large team. Coverage in a targeted publication, engagement with a defined group of journalists, increased executive visibility, movement in search authority, speaking opportunities, inbound conversations and introductions to prospective customers can all be counted.

The world's largest communications firms exist for good reasons. You’ll note that I’m citing surveys that come from large communications firm whose name you’re more likely to recognize. PRovoke Media Global Top 250 PR Agency Ranking 2025 shows businesses such as Edelman, Burson, Weber Shandwick, FleishmanHillard and Real Chemistry operating at enormous scale, with several generating hundreds of millions of dollars in annual fee income. A multinational company coordinating dozens of markets, managing large consumer campaigns or supporting communications across many business units may genuinely need that infrastructure.

That being said, a founder or intrepreneur navigating a new category, a private-equity firm trying to become known for a specific investment thesis, a healthcare company introducing an unfamiliar technology that is moving beyond incremental improvements, a manufacturer who persists despite market cycles but misses opportunities because the broader market doesn’t understand why, or an executive trying to build authority around a changing market often needs a small number of expert people with the autonomy and agency to work out that problem every day until it’s solved, and do it on an accelerated basis.

Technology is making that model more within reach, if used effectively. Changes in journalism are making expertise more valuable. Tougher agency economics are forcing clients to scrutinize what they are buying. AI is lowering the cost of production while increasing the premium on original thinking and credible experience.

Law has already shown what can happen when experienced specialists leave structures built around scale and organize themselves around expertise, client access and consequential problems. Public relations now has many of the same ingredients.

Boyd would recognize the pattern, and so might John Glover. More are recognizing it now.

items.title: EC-Council Releases ADG 2.0 and Offers Free AI Governance Crosswalks to Governments Worldwide
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Framework of more than 180 controls maps to more than 90 regulations and standards, and EC-Council will help any public authority apply it

Photo Courtesy of EC-Council

TAMPA, Fla., Oct. 1, 2026 — EC-Council today released ADG 2.0, the second version of its Adopt, Defend, Govern framework, and offered the framework and its crosswalks to more than 90 regulations, standards and frameworks free to any government, regulator or standards body. EC-Council will also help any of them apply ADG 2.0 to their own laws, draft rules and national standards, consistent with applicable law.

AI agents are already acting outside their limits. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models in an internal cybersecurity evaluation escaped their testing environment and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. In September, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to a public-facing Medicare statistics portal in June. OpenAI has also confirmed its agents accessed U.S. government websites in ways it neither planned nor approved.

Governments remain split. President Donald Trump has said concerns about AI risks are exaggerated. China’s Foreign Ministry has said fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition would hamper sound global AI governance. On Sept. 26, Singapore Foreign Affairs Minister Vivian Balakrishnan urged the United Nations General Assembly to set new multilateral rules and suggested a UN Framework Convention on AI Safeguards.

“The nuclear non-proliferation treaty worked because inspectors could weigh uranium,” said Jay Bavisi, founder, chairman and group CEO of EC-Council. “You can’t weigh an agent’s behavior, and no AI treaty will be signed and ratified in time to protect the systems agents are reaching today. Governments shouldn’t have to build governance from a blank page while they wait.”

ADG 2.0 replaces the original 12 minimum controls with more than 180 controls in 12 control families, mapped to more than 90 regulations, standards and frameworks, including the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act. Regulators can see how a proposed national rule lines up against what other jurisdictions already require. Enterprises can work from one control set and show how it satisfies each rulebook they answer to.

“Most AI governance today is a policy document nobody tests,” Bavisi said. “Say what you do, do what you say, and be able to prove both on any given day. That’s what a regulator, an insurer, or a board will ask for after the next incident. There will be a next incident.”

Controls apply at four points in how an AI system operates, ADMIT, DECIDE, EMIT and COMMIT, with human approval required at defined decision thresholds. Three autonomy levels, assistive, conditional and autonomous, set what a system may do and when a human must review. Each control lists the evidence it must produce, so organizations collect proof while systems run rather than before an audit.

ADG is stewarded by EC-Council’s AI Advisory Board of [CONFIRM: 35 or 38] practitioners from organizations such as Salesforce, ServiceNow, Azure, Microsoft, Citi, JPMorgan Chase, NTT DATA, Jio Platforms and BNP Paribas Wealth Management. Members serve in their personal capacity, and organizations are listed for identification only.

Governments, regulators and standards bodies can request assistance at adg@eccouncil.org. The ADG 2.0 framework, crosswalks and AI Readiness Self-Assessment are free to everyone, without registration, at

Founded in 2001, EC-Council is a global cybersecurity and AI organization. It created the Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) program and has certified more than 400,000 professionals across 174 countries. Its credentials are used across government, defense, enterprise and academia.

As an ISO/IEC 17024 accredited certification body, EC-Council's credentials are recognized by the U.S. Department of Defense under DoD 8140.

The EC-Council ecosystem includes EC-Council, EC-Council University (ECCU), CodeRed, EC-Council Global Services (EGS), EC-Council Academia and AwareX.

EC-Council's Adopt, Defend, Govern (ADG) framework is a practitioner-led operating model for AI governance. Its three pillars connect board level oversight with operational and technical controls across the AI lifecycle. ADG 2.0 contains more than 180 controls in 12 control families, with crosswalks to more than 90 regulations, standards and frameworks. It is stewarded by EC-Council's 38 member AI Advisory Board and supported by readiness assessments and implementation guidance. Each AI Advisory board member serves in their personal capacity, and organizations are listed purely for identification. The framework, crosswalks, whitepaper and self-assessment are available openly without registration or licensing requirements.

items.title: Implementing Table Partitioning in PostgreSQL
items.author: Arvind Toorpu
items.content:
I have been running production PostgreSQL systems for over sixteen years, and if there is one lesson that never gets old, it is this: a table that behaves beautifully at ten million rows can turn into a nightmare at five hundred million. Indexes stop helping as much as they used to, vacuum runs longer, and every maintenance window gets scarier. When I see queries slowing down despite solid indexing, partitioning is usually the next tool I reach for. Let me walk you through how I actually implement it.

What Partitioning Really Is

Partitioning takes one logical table and splits it into several physical sub-tables called partitions. From the application side, nothing changes. You still insert into and query one table name. Behind the scenes, PostgreSQL decides which partition each row belongs to and routes reads and writes there automatically.

I like to compare it to a filing cabinet with labeled drawers. If everything is dumped into one drawer, finding last year's invoices means digging through everything ever filed. Label the drawers by year, and you go straight to "2024" and search only there. That is the entire value proposition, in one image.

  •  PostgreSQL can skip whole partitions entirely through partition pruning, so it only scans the data that could possibly match.
  •  Running VACUUM, ANALYZE, or REINDEX on a smaller partition is a lot less painful than running it on one giant table.
  • Simple data lifecycle management. Getting rid of old data becomes DROP TABLE partition_name, which is nearly instant. Compare that to a  that has to touch millions of rows and generates a mountain of dead tuples.
  •  I can put hot, frequently accessed partitions on fast storage and let cold partitions sit on cheaper disks.

The Three Strategies I Choose Between

PostgreSQL, from version 10 onward, gives me three built-in partitioning strategies. I pick based on the shape of the data.

 splits rows by a range of values, most often dates or numeric IDs. This is my default choice for time-series data, things like orders, logs, or events that accumulate by day or month.

 splits rows by a discrete set of values, like country codes or status flags. I reach for this when the data naturally falls into named buckets rather than a continuum.

 spreads rows evenly across a fixed number of partitions by hashing the partition key. I use this when there is no natural range or list to key off of, but I still want the data spread out for performance and manageability.

Setting Up Range Partitioning

Here is how I would partition an  table that is bringing in millions of rows a year. I will partition it by , monthly.

Step 1: Create the Partitioned Parent Table

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          BIGSERIAL,
    customer_id BIGINT        NOT NULL,
    amount      NUMERIC(10,2) NOT NULL,
    status      TEXT          NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ   NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

Something worth keeping in mind here: the parent table never actually stores any rows. It is a purely logical container that PostgreSQL uses to route data to the right child partition.

Step 2: Create the Partitions

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_02
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_03
    PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-03-01') TO ('2024-04-01');

One detail I always double check with new team members: the range bounds are inclusive at the bottom and exclusive at the top. A row dated exactly  lands in , not .

I create indexes on the parent table, and as of PostgreSQL 11 they propagate down to every partition automatically. That saves me from having to remember to index each child individually.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at  ON orders (created_at);

Step 4: Insert Data as Normal

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, amount, status, created_at)
VALUES (42, 199.99, 'completed', '2024-01-15 10:30:00+00');

I do not have to tell PostgreSQL which partition this belongs in. It reads the  value and routes it to on its own.

Step 5: Confirm Partition Pruning Is Actually Happening

This step is not optional in my process. I always verify pruning with  before I trust a partitioning setup in production.

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-02-01'
  AND created_at <  '2024-03-01';

If the setup is correct, the plan should only touch . If I see the planner scanning every partition, something in my query or my partition key is off, and I go fix it before moving on.

When the Key Is Categorical: List Partitioning

If I am partitioning something like a  table by region rather than by time, list partitioning is the right tool.

CREATE TABLE customers (
    id     BIGSERIAL,
    name   TEXT NOT NULL,
    region TEXT NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY LIST (region);

CREATE TABLE customers_us
    PARTITION OF customers
    FOR VALUES IN ('US', 'CA');

CREATE TABLE customers_eu
    PARTITION OF customers
    FOR VALUES IN ('DE', 'FR', 'GB', 'NL');

CREATE TABLE customers_apac
    PARTITION OF customers
    FOR VALUES IN ('AU', 'JP', 'SG', 'IN');

Each region code is explicitly assigned to a bucket, which makes this strategy easy to reason about and easy to explain to the rest of the team.

When There Is No Natural Key: Hash Partitioning

Sometimes there is genuinely no range or category to split on, and I just need the data spread evenly for performance and manageability. That is when I use hash partitioning. Here I am splitting an  table into four partitions by .

CREATE TABLE events (
    id         BIGSERIAL,
    user_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT   NOT NULL,
    payload    JSONB,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY HASH (user_id);

CREATE TABLE events_p0 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
CREATE TABLE events_p1 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 1);
CREATE TABLE events_p2 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 2);
CREATE TABLE events_p3 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 3);

Catching the Rows You Forgot About: Default Partitions

Especially during development, or when I am not one hundred percent sure every possible value has a home, I set up a default partition to catch anything that does not match an existing rule.

CREATE TABLE orders_default
    PARTITION OF orders DEFAULT;

This has saved me more than once from a failed insert at 2 a.m. because someone introduced a new status value nobody told me about.

Automating Partition Creation

I never want to be the person manually creating next month's partition by hand, and neither should you. In production, I write a function like this and schedule it.

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION create_monthly_partition(target_date DATE)
RETURNS VOID AS $$
DECLARE
    partition_name TEXT;
    start_date     DATE;
    end_date       DATE;
BEGIN
    start_date     := DATE_TRUNC('month', target_date);
    end_date       := start_date + INTERVAL '1 month';
    partition_name := 'orders_' || TO_CHAR(start_date, 'YYYY_MM');

    EXECUTE FORMAT(
        'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS %I PARTITION OF orders FOR VALUES FROM (%L) TO (%L)',
        partition_name, start_date, end_date
    );
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Create partitions for the next 3 months
SELECT create_monthly_partition(DATE_TRUNC('month', NOW()) + (n || ' month')::INTERVAL)
FROM generate_series(0, 2) AS n;

I schedule this with  when it is available, or with an external scheduler like a cron job or Airflow when it is not. Either way, I make sure I always have a few months of partitions created ahead of time, so an inserting application never hits a missing partition.

This is where partitioning earns its keep for data lifecycle management. Instead of running a slow, lock-heavy  that chews through WAL and leaves bloat behind, I just drop the partition.

-- Instantly drop a year's worth of data
DROP TABLE orders_2022_01;
DROP TABLE orders_2022_02;
-- ... etc

If I need to keep the data around for archival purposes rather than destroying it, I detach it instead:

ALTER TABLE orders DETACH PARTITION orders_2022_01;
-- Partition now exists as a standalone table, archive or export it

A few things trip people up every single time, so let me save you the pain.

Your primary key has to include the partition key. PostgreSQL cannot enforce uniqueness across partitions unless the partition key is part of the key.

-- This will fail:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD PRIMARY KEY (id);

-- This works:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at);

Foreign keys referencing a partitioned table are not supported. Foreign keys going out from a partitioned table are fine, but nothing else can point at it with a foreign key constraint.

Partition pruning only works if the partition key shows up in your WHERE clause. Leave it out, and PostgreSQL has no choice but to scan every partition.

Do not go overboard with granularity. Hundreds of tiny partitions will hurt planning time more than they help. For time-series data, I have found monthly or quarterly partitions to be the sweet spot in most systems I have run.

Checking Your Partition Setup

When I want a quick sanity check on what partitions exist and how big they have gotten, I run this:

-- List all partitions of a table
SELECT inhrelid::regclass AS partition_name,
       pg_get_expr(c.relpartbound, inhrelid) AS partition_bound,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(inhrelid)) AS size
FROM   pg_inherits
JOIN   pg_class c ON c.oid = inhrelid
WHERE  inhparent = 'orders'::regclass
ORDER  BY partition_name;

When I Choose Not to Partition

Partitioning is not free. It adds real operational complexity, and I skip it when any of the following apply:

  • The table is under roughly ten million rows. Indexing alone usually handles that fine.
  • There is no natural partition key to work with.
  • Most of the queries against the table are aggregations across the whole dataset anyway, in which case partitioning will not move the needle much.
  • The team maintaining the system is not ready to take on the added operational complexity.

PostgreSQL's declarative partitioning is mature and, honestly, not that hard to implement once you understand the shape of your data. Here is what I keep coming back to:

  • Use range partitioning for time-series and sequential data.
  • Use list partitioning for categorical or enum-style columns.
  • Use hash partitioning when you need even distribution and have no natural key.
  • Always include the partition key in your primary key.
  • Automate partition creation, and drop old partitions instead of running expensive deletes.
  • Always verify partition pruning with  so you know your queries are actually benefiting.

My advice after years of doing this: pick one table that is currently causing you pain, instrument it properly, implement partitioning, and measure the before and after. Once you see the difference for yourself, you will not need convincing on the next one.

items.title: Inside North Korea’s Crypto Theft Machine: Hackers, Launderers, and Billions in Stolen Funds
items.author: Toto Hartarto
items.content:
Inside the Bybit heist, the 45-day laundering clock, and how you can follow the money yourself.

Picture a room with a few senior people at a crypto exchange. They need to move some money from a deep-storage safe to a smaller wallet used for daily business. It’s routine. They look at the screen, see a normal transfer, and everyone signs.

Seconds later, about $1.5 billion in Ether was gone. It was the biggest crypto theft ever recorded, and the group behind it was a government’s hacking team.

Here’s the short version, in case you’re reading this on a bus. One country has taken roughly from crypto. The scary part isn’t the hacking, it’s the cleanup afterward, which follows a pattern investigators can actually see. And you don’t need a badge to watch some of it happen. A free website will do.

If stories about money, spies and the internet are your thing, hit follow. At the end I’ll walk you through looking at a real address yourself, and you can do it in about ten minutes.

The victim here was , a big exchange based in Dubai. Its savings were stored in what’s called a wallet. Think of a bank vault that needs several keys turned at once. Even if one person is tricked, the vault shouldn’t open.

The attackers knew that. So they didn’t go after the vault. They went after the the key-holders used to approve transfers.

The wallet software Bybit used is called Safe{Wallet}. According to Safe’s own statement, the attackers compromised a developer’s computer there. From that machine they slipped a small piece of malicious code into the website’s interface. Security firm Verichains says the code went in on February 19, 2025, and was built to wake up only when Bybit’s own signers used it. That happened on February 21.

On the screen, it looked like an ordinary transfer. Underneath, the signers were approving something very different: a change to the wallet’s own ownership logic. It’s like signing what looks like a utility bill and finding out later you handed over the deed to your house.

Here’s the detail I can’t stop thinking about. Bybit’s vault did exactly what it was designed to do, and the people did exactly what they were supposed to do. Investigators, including firms Bybit hired, traced the root cause to Safe{Wallet}’s infrastructure, not to a break-in at Bybit itself.

Nobody picked a lock. They changed what the lock was attached to.

Five days after the theft, on February 26, 2025, the FBI said it plainly: North Korea did it. It labeled the specific operation

You’ve probably heard the name . It’s best understood as an umbrella label that Western governments use for North Korean hacking crews linked to the country’s military intelligence agency, the Reconnaissance General Bureau. TraderTraitor is one of those crews, one known for going after crypto companies and their employees.

This crew isn’t new. The same umbrella has been tied to the 2022 Ronin Network theft (about $620 million) and the 2024 theft from Japan’s DMM Bitcoin (over $300 million). Years earlier, it was blamed for the Sony Pictures hack.

So why would a government steal crypto? The short answer is sanctions. A country locked out of normal banking has a real reason to want money that doesn’t need a bank. Monitoring groups say the cash goes to weapons programs, and one multinational report says the stolen funds in 2024 alone were roughly one-third of North Korea’s total foreign currency income that year.

Keep that in mind. This isn’t a bored teenager in a hoodie. It’s a state project with a budget.

The Scoreboard Nobody Wants to Win

Now the numbers. Different firms count a little differently, so treat all of this as “about.”

According to Chainalysis, North Korean hackers stole at least in 2025. That’s a 51% jump from the year before and $681 million more than 2024. Across the whole industry, around $3.4 billion was stolen that year, so North Korea took nearly 60% of everything. Chainalysis also says that’s the highest share on record for hacks on crypto like exchanges, at 76%. Its running total for North Korea now sits around . That’s a lower-bound estimate, so the real number could be higher.

Here’s the strange part. Chainalysis says North Korea did this with about 74% fewer known attacks than the year before. Fewer hits, bigger hits.

It’s a bit like a burglar who stops robbing houses and robs one bank instead. The biggest hack of 2025 was more than 1,000 times larger than the typical one, and the top three hacks made up 69% of all losses at services.

Which brings us to the big one.

Anatomy of a $1.5 Billion Heist

Roughly 500,000 ETH went out of Bybit’s cold wallet in a single go. That one theft equals about 74% of everything North Korea stole in 2025.

Look at how it was built:

  1. The attackers went through a third-party tool Bybit trusted. Security people call this a : you don’t attack the target, you attack something the target depends on.
  2. The malicious code targeted specific wallet owners, which means someone studied exactly who would sign and when.
  3. Signers saw a harmless transaction. What they approved changed the wallet’s control.

Chainalysis points out that this is a growing pattern. North Korean crews are also embedding fake IT workers inside crypto firms and posing as recruiters or investors to get at passwords and systems. The common thread is that the weakest link is usually a person or a tool, not the math.

If you hold crypto yourself, take one simple lesson from this: what the screen says and what you’re signing can be two different things. Slow down on big approvals, and use more than one check.

Stealing is only half the job. Stolen crypto is a bit like a bag of marked bills. You can’t walk into a store with it, so you need to clean it first.

Here’s what gets me about Bybit: the cleanup was .

TRM Labs, a blockchain analysis firm, reported that at least $160 million had already been pushed through within 48 hours. By the end of the first week, more than $400 million had moved. TRM said the initial phase was done around March 3, roughly ten days after the theft, with all the stolen ETH moved to new addresses and most of it bridged into Bitcoin.

A few weeks in, Bybit’s CEO reported that about 86% of the stolen ETH had been swapped into Bitcoin, around 12,836 BTC, scattered across thousands of wallets. Most of the swapping went through a cross-chain service called THORChain.

And this isn’t a one-off. Chainalysis studied North Korean hacks from 2022 to 2025 and found a repeating rhythm, a in three waves:

  • panic mode. Funds are shuffled through DeFi apps and mixers to create distance from the theft.
  • the money starts moving toward places that could turn it into cash, like exchanges with light checks and more bridges.
  • the long tail. Funds head into no-ID exchanges, Chinese-language “guarantee” marketplaces and other cash-out points.

One more oddity: the hackers send money in small pieces. Chainalysis says over 60% of North Korea’s laundered volume moves in chunks under $500,000, while other criminals tend to send much bigger lumps. These guys steal huge but wash small.

This is where investigators get their edge. A routine leaves fingerprints. If you know the clock, you know roughly where to look and when.

Want to see how that looks in the wild? I’ll show you at the end.

Governments haven’t ignored this. They’ve gone after the tools North Korea uses, one at a time.

The U.S. sanctioned the mixer Tornado Cash in 2022 and another mixer, Sinbad, in 2023. A mixer is a service that blends many people’s coins together so you can’t tell whose is whose. And yet the stolen money kept flowing. (There’s a twist: the U.S. removed Tornado Cash from its sanctions list in March 2025 after a court ruling went against the government’s approach.)

According to TRM Labs data cited in one analysis, laundering through cross-chain bridges climbed about 66% between 2023 and 2025, while mixer-related activity fell about 37%. Put simply, the money moved from the front door to the side door.

A bridge is a tool that moves your coins from one blockchain to another, like swapping currency at an airport. It’s useful for normal people, and it’s also a handy way to make a trail harder to follow. Chainalysis found that North Korea leans on bridges and on Chinese-language money-movement services far more than other criminals do. For one cash-out hub called Huione, the difference was about 356%.

Then there’s the long game. When one service gets shut down, another pops up. After accusations that it helped wash Bybit’s money, the exchange eXch announced in April 2025 that it would close.

2026: The Streak Nobody Stopped

If you thought that was a one-time storm, 2026 says otherwise.

TRM Labs says North Korea-linked hackers took about in just two attacks in April, which was 76% of all crypto hack losses through that month:

  • , April 1, about $285 million. TRM described months of social engineering, including in-person meetings between North Korean proxies and people at the company. It called that potentially unprecedented. The theft itself used a feature on the Solana blockchain that lets pre-signed transactions sit and be used later.
  • , April 18, about $292 million. TRM tied it to a design weakness in a cross-chain bridge that depended on a single verifier. Around $75 million was frozen, and the rest moved quickly through THORChain.

Those two attacks were about 3% of the incidents TRM counted that period, but the vast majority of the money. Later, TRM reported that North Korea’s share for the first half of 2026 came to about 66%.

Then came on September 24, 2026. Hackers drained roughly from its hot and warm wallets. Bitget’s CEO said the pattern looked like earlier North Korean work, and the analytics firm Elliptic called a North Korean link “highly likely.” Be careful here, though. Attribution isn’t confirmed, and the CEO later softened her early claim. Bitget says its user protection fund, valued at over $464 million, covers the loss. Elliptic says this theft pushed suspected North Korean heists past $1 billion for 2026.

Notice the pattern. Different victims, different tricks, same playbook: patience up front, speed afterward.

Here’s the hopeful part. Because blockchains are public, regular people can catch some of this.

One name comes up again and again: , an anonymous on-chain investigator. On October 5, 2026, he posted a long thread claiming he’d spent months posing as a paying customer to get inside a Chinese money-laundering network. He says it moved over $1 billion in stolen crypto for Lazarus across several hacks, and that one of its operators told him the team had washed most of the Bybit money. He says he fronted about $349,700 of his own money to build trust, and that the information helped freeze funds, including 442,000 USDT frozen by Tether.

I want to be careful. This is . Coverage of the thread points out it’s his account of private chats plus on-chain matches, not a law enforcement finding. But the method is the interesting part: public support requests, timing patterns between chains, and patient trust-building.

Meanwhile, the , a joint effort by Tether, TRON and TRM Labs, announced it froze around $9 million tied to the Bybit hack. It’s small compared to $1.5 billion, but it shows the point of all this tracing: once you can see where money goes, someone can sometimes press the brakes.

Why Sanctions Keep Missing

If governments know all this, why isn’t it working better?

First, the cleanup business is made of , not one big company. Chainalysis describes North Korea’s Chinese-language laundering as a network of many different operators, some with weak compliance. Shut one down and the others keep going.

Second, the U.S. has hit the plumbing repeatedly. It went after Tornado Cash and Sinbad. It also moved against Huione Group, with a Treasury rule that took effect in November 2025 cutting it off from U.S. banks and calling it a hub for laundering North Korean cyber heists. But the stolen money has found new routes after each round.

Third, the people problem. A multinational monitoring team (made up of 11 countries) reported in 2025 that North Korean IT workers were active in at least eight countries and earning hundreds of millions of dollars, despite UN bans. That’s the human side of the same machine: workers get access, hackers use it, and launderers clean the proceeds.

Sanctions aren’t useless. They raise the cost and slow things down. But right now, the machine adapts faster than the paperwork.

Your Turn: Follow One Wallet

Okay, this is the fun part. You don’t need special software. You need a browser and ten minutes.

  1. Open the FBI’s public alert about the Bybit hack (link in the references below) and copy the Ethereum address it lists as connected to the theft.
  2. Go to and paste that address into the search bar.
  3. Open the tab. Look at the dates. When did it go quiet?
  4. Check and . Where did the money go?
  5. Click one of the receiving addresses and repeat. Look for labels or name tags Etherscan has attached.
  6. Write down three things: when it was last active, where it sent funds, and whether any label is attached.

A few ground rules. Never send anything to an address you’re investigating, and never trust addresses someone drops in a Telegram chat. A public address is also not a person. Explorers show money moving, not names, and TRM has warned that investigators can chase false leads when unrelated funds come out of mixers.

This article is for education only. It isn’t financial or legal advice.

If you find this article helpful, I would be humbly grateful for a small tip via at

Any amount, however small, would be a great encouragement to continue sharing useful insights.

Thank you sincerely for reading and supporting my work.

items.title: Professional Success Starts With Inner Work
items.author: Brian Wallace
items.content:
Smarts and talent are not the strongest predictors of success. The skills you build inside yourself are. But how do these inner skills lead to gaining professional success?

Think about a work setting where someone is given a task that is completely new to them. If they are growth orientated and have grit, they would embrace the opportunity to learn from the experience and develop new skills. Even if they encounter issues, they will work towards the solution instead of viewing them as setbacks. Being flexible allows the person to pivot their approach and thinking to find the right fix. Having self-efficacy also gives them the confidence to believe in their own skills to finish the task and persevere through the challenges.

such as grit, flexibility, self-efficacy, and a growth mindset push people to develop themselves professionally without feeling too overwhelmed and giving up. But building inner skills takes more work than you may think. They can degrade over time if not used often, leading to you falling back to unproductive habits and feeling stressed.

Businesses are losing a lot of money from weak leadership, including $550 billion due to inefficiency and $1 trillion because of high employee turnover rates. Employees who quit in 2025 have stated that the main reason for them leaving their jobs was because they did not get along with their bosses and managers.

A little over 40% of managers in the U.S. have received leadership training, which is affecting the confidence U.S. organizations have in their leaders’ ability to develop growth in others. Companies that are putting importance in having training are seeing higher levels of employee engagement, emotional intelligence, and team collaboration.

With greater emotional understanding and self-awareness, leaders can reduce turnover rates by 21% in high turnover sectors and 51% in low turnover sectors. Almost 80% of workers are coming to work more than before as well.

With better leadership, employees feel more productive at work, leading to 63% less safety issues, 70% greater physical and mental health, and 18% better sales productivity. Feeling better at work can even translate to stronger family relationships at home using the inner work. People feel greater marital satisfaction and have less conflicts with their family when they gain emotional understanding and more self-awareness. Parents in particular can raise emotionally healthy kids who know how to regulate their emotions when they do it themselves.

Decision-making and financial performance are strongly connected, which is why a growing number of companies are emphasizing decisive leadership. Those that use this leadership style are more likely to last longer than the competition while also providing three times more on shareholder returns.

Almost 80% of B Corporations brought in more money for their business versus their non-B Corporations counterpart, which brought in 60%. B Corporations inherently balance profit with a purpose, but a purpose can be best understood if the leaders have the capacity to make decisions that consider others’ needs and align with the company’s values. This can only be done when the leaders work on themselves to develop the personal qualities that can really make a difference.

items.title: A Revenue Leader’s Media Relations Playbook
items.author: Chris Gale
items.content:
The History of the Lancashire Witches, photographed at the Smith College Neilson Library

Media relations is usually managed as a communications function. The work is planned around announcements, interviews and thought leadership. Success is recorded as placements, impressions, share of voice and perhaps social engagement.

That leaves a great deal of commercial value on the table. Experience points toward a different model, earned media can function as revenue amplification when used right.

The principle is straightforward. A credible third party saying something important about a company, its customers or its executives gives a revenue organization an asset that its own marketing cannot manufacture. The best revenue leaders put that asset to work and demand more.

  1. Create internal conviction and direction.
  2. Give sellers a reason to contact customers and prospects.
  3. Turn customer success into externally validated proof.
  4. Create additional conversations around the company’s point of view.
  5. Build executive authority that opens doors sales outreach alone cannot.
  6. Measure what happens after publication, not simply whether publication occurred.

This is increasingly how the best businesses structuresprograms. In one proposal we’ve seen, the explicit business outcome is that coverage becomes proof of a company’s “access, insight and influence,” creating assets for sales and renewal conversations. Another framework  in our sample calls for media relations to be mapped directly to opportunity progression and messaging for late-stage buyers, rather than treated as a parallel marketing activity.

Maybe the most revealing example, however, comes from the work with one particular CEO and a health tech company.

1. Think beyond the placement

The traditional PR operating model has a natural endpoint: pitch, then interview, then coverage, and then report the result.

A revenue-driven model adds an entire second half: business objective, and then differentiated point of view or proof, and then media result, and then internal activation, and then customer activation, and then executive amplification, and then prospect engagement, and then opportunity progression, and then measurement.

Okay, that’s more steps. And more isn’t necessarily more.

The process here starts by confirming business goals and determining how media relations, content and social can accelerate those goals. It then identifies a business-aligned point of view, milestones and external angles and tracks the engagement and response generated by results.

The expert revenue leader displays an instinct that sophisticated revenue organizations should study. When there is an important story, she frequently pushes immediately beyond the publicity itself.

Consider the direction around a customer announcement. She wants a company-wide message, a customer communication and a webinar with customer executives, extending a single communications moment into several channels and constituencies.

Around another announcement, she asks for the news to be posted through corporate channels, amplified through additional company accounts, reposted by her personally and communicated to the broader organization.

This is organizational activation. The press result becomes an occasion for employees, customers, partners and prospects to encounter the same evidence from different directions. There is also an important discipline behind the urgency. Ahead of a major story, the Revenue Leader explicitly directs the team to focus the media conversation on the “big industry changing story” rather than reducing it to product features and functions.

That is exactly what strong revenue leadership needs from communications. Features answer what does your product do? But a category-level media narrative answers the much more valuable questions. Why does the market need you? Why now? Why should an executive pay attention?

3. Customer proof is more valuable when somebody else validates it

This becomes especially powerful in complex B2B markets. A salesperson can tell a prospect that a marquee customer trusts the company. Marketing can put the customer logo on a slide.

However, credible customer participation plus independent media coverage changes the quality of the evidence. Take the example of a health system where a health tech company serving them records national healthcare coverage, customer executives publicly discussing the health tech company, accompanying thought leadership and more than 20 healthcare leaders proactively engaging with the Revenue Leader after the announcement, including people commenting on the significance of the customer relationship.

A related case-study we’re familiar with describes the same outcome as 20+ healthcare-leader engagements immediately following the announcement and notes that the resulting campaign expanded into a marketing effort led by the client’s Chief Revenue Officer. Here’s that sequence, customer success, and then customer advocacy, and then media validation, and then market attention, and then revenue activation.

4. Use earned authority to create conversations, not just awareness

Revenue leaders should stop evaluating media exclusively through audience size. For a complex enterprise business, 20 conversations with relevant health-system leaders can matter far more than hundreds of thousands of undifferentiated impressions. The same principle appears elsewhere in my experience. Let’s take a client roundtable and thought-leadership ecosystem contributing to approximately $880,000 in ARR from resulting customer relationships.

This suggests a better hierarchy for measuring B2B media relations:

Level 1: OutputWas something published?

Level 2: AttentionDid the right audiences see or engage with it?

Level 3: ConversationDid customers, prospects, partners, investors or influencers respond?

Level 4: Commercial movementDid those conversations create meetings, introductions, opportunities, expansions or renewals?

Level 5: RevenueCan opportunities or revenue be credibly connected to the motion?

Impressions still have value. They simply sit near the beginning of the measurement chain rather than the end.

One of the least appreciated benefits of good media relations happens inside the company. Preparing a compelling external story forces a leadership team to answer difficult questions:

  • What are we actually trying to become known for?
  • Which customers provide the strongest evidence?
  • What does our CEO believe that competitors do not?
  • Which product capabilities really matter to buyers?
  • What evidence can withstand a reporter’s scrutiny?
  • What is significant enough that somebody outside the company should care?
  • Which claims are we willing to make publicly?

That process can impose useful discipline on strategy. A Revenue Leader we know has repeatedly emphasized measurable outcomes in her external positioning. A recent company social-content record captures her view that transformation should be assessed by whether it changes how people work and improves outcomes, rather than simply tracking deployment or adoption activity. Revenue teams can apply exactly the same standard to communications. The objective is a measurable change in what important people know, believe or do.

When executives, salespeople, marketers and customers repeatedly encounter the same externally validated ideas, the revenue-led organization gradually becomes clearer about what it sells and why customers care. A high quality public relations team can deliberately connect media, social and meetings for this reason. A good media story should appear in:

  • executive LinkedIn activity;
  • customer-success conversations;
  • board reporting where appropriate;
  • sales enablement repositories; and

The Revenue Leader's Playbook

Step 1: Start with the revenue objective

Before deciding what story to tell, write down the business result. Examples:

  • Open conversations with 15 target enterprise buyers.
  • Strengthen an enterprise renewal.
  • Give sellers proof around a newly introduced capability.
  • Establish an executive with CFOs or CIOs.
  • Create evidence supporting entry into an adjacent market.
  • Turn an important customer into a reference account.
  • Increase credibility during late-stage enterprise evaluations.

PR strategy should flow backward from that objective.

Step 2: Find the proof, tension or point of view

Reporters rarely need another company claiming leadership. What they and their editors need is something that advances a story their audience is following, or should be following that is often bigger than one business. Therefor you need a methodology explicitly testing stories for relevance, timeliness and novelty, while asking what headline or tension will earn attention. Revenue leaders should bring communications teams the raw materials: Customer evidence. Data. Product usage. Unexpected market observations. Buyer objections. Regulatory changes. Competitor gaps. Economic pressures. Operational results.

Step 3: Make the customer the hero

The highest-value enterprise stories frequently involve customers. But the story should advance the customer's agenda too. In fact that should be the primary goal. Framing a story around the buyer's own transformation priorities encourages that customer to step forward publicly as an innovator, and thereby better validate the technology or service provider.

Customer: recognized for leadership.Media: receives evidence and expert sources.

Vendor: receives credible validation.

Revenue team: receives usable proof.

Step 4: Build the activation plan before publication

Do not wait until a story appears to ask, “What should we do with this?” Before publication, designate:

CEO/internal note explaining why it matters

Personalized customer communication

Individual outreach from account owner

Reason to reopen conversation

Co-amplification where appropriate

LinkedIn and direct relationship sharing

Talking points + link + target account list

Incorporate proof into upcoming meetings/webinars

Use in renewal and expansion conversations

This is one of the clearest lessons from the Revenue Leader approach. Distribution is part of the strategy, rather than cleanup work after the PR team finishes.

Step 5: Give sales a reason to send it

“Thought you might like this article” is weak activation. Provide sellers with a specific connection:

We have been talking about the operational challenge your team raised around X. This piece gets into how another organization is approaching exactly that issue. Thought it would be useful before our next conversation.

The media result creates permission to reengage. The account context turns permission into a useful conversation.

Step 6: Run a 72-hour revenue sprint

For major earned results, concentrate activation.

CEO, company and participating customer amplification. Internal distribution. Priority-account outreach begins.

Revenue leaders make personal contact with high-value relationships. Sales uses the story with open opportunities. Marketing examines engagement for relevant names and accounts.

PR captures reporter reactions and follow-on opportunities. Revenue captures buyer reactions. Communications and sales compare signals and identify next actions. Then repeat selected outreach at 7, 30 and 90 days wherever the article remains relevant.

Consider tracking the following. First you have the result, that goes to target-account engagements, that goes to executive responses, that goes to conversations, that turns into meetings, then you get to opportunities influenced, there’s a pipeline value, and then you get to closed revenue.

Also capture qualitative intelligence:

  • What language prompted responses?
  • Which customer proof resonated?
  • Which executives forwarded the story?
  • Which prospects suddenly became responsive?
  • Which objections diminished?
  • What question repeatedly came back?

The process becomes a loop. Revenue intelligence leads to a stronger media narrative, that leads to earned authority, which gets you to conversations, which lands you with new revenue intelligence. There is an important caution. Commercial urgency should not turn the PR function into an amplification machine that sacrifices journalistic credibility or customer trust.

Here's where professional media management remains as close to essential as we can get. Internal discussions around high-profile customer opportunities emphasize maintaining clear roles and guardrails when navigating customers and reporters because poorly coordinated intervention can reduce available media options or undermine trust.

That produces another best practice. Revenue should determine where the organization needs to go. Skilled communications professionals should determine how to navigate the media environment necessary to help get it there.

The two functions need to operate closely without collapsing into one another.

A 90-day implementation model

Choose three revenue priorities, ten to twenty strategic accounts and three defensible market narratives. Map customers, data, executives and upcoming milestones against them.

Develop reporter relationships around the issues rather than pitching indiscriminately. Advance the customer evidence, executive POV, proprietary data and third-party validation that support the commercial narrative.

For each significant result, execute internal, executive, social, customer and account-level activation. Record responses in the CRM and hold a monthly media-to-revenue review between communications, marketing and revenue leadership.

At 90 days, ask a harder question than “How much coverage did we receive?”

Ask which relationships are materially stronger because of the authority we earned?

Media relations cannot close an enterprise deal by itself. Nor should every article be assigned a fictitious revenue number. But the opposite assumption, that earned media sits somewhere above the revenue engine generating vague “awareness,” is increasingly difficult to defend.

The smartest revenue leaders build an operating model that turns earned authority into more and better conversations, better conversations into opportunities, and opportunities into measurable growth. That’s where media relations becomes a revenue discipline.

items.title: ChatGPT Helped Me Complain About ChatGPT. The Irony Wasn't Lost on Me.
items.author: Carol Ornstein
items.content:
I got so frustrated with ChatGPT that I asked ChatGPT to help me file a formal complaint against ChatGPT.

The irony wasn't lost on me.

For the past year, I've been working with ChatGPT, affectionately known as my Chat Thought Partner.

I didn't give it that name because I needed an artificial friend. I gave it that name because I wanted something more than a chatbot that could answer questions or generate content.

I wanted a thought partner.

Someone, or something, that could challenge my thinking, help me explore ideas, and make me more effective in my work.

I have always led with my own voice, in business and in life. AI was never supposed to replace that voice. I wanted it to help me think, not think for me.

Over time, we developed a remarkably productive working relationship.

I taught my Chat Thought Partner how I communicate, what I value, how I approach problems, and what makes my writing sound like me.

We worked on business challenges, developed ideas, explored creative writing, and occasionally had conversations that were simply entertaining.

For a long time, it worked beautifully.

Then things started getting wonky.

With new releases, I began noticing changes.

My Chat Thought Partner would suddenly seem to develop amnesia.

It would forget established preferences, repeat mistakes we'd already corrected, and occasionally respond as though we'd never met.

Usually at the worst possible moment.

I'd be working on something important, and instead of moving forward, we'd find ourselves revisiting conversations we'd already had.

I'd explain a preference.

ChatGPT would acknowledge it.

A little later, it would do the same thing again.

Then we'd repeat the entire exercise.

It was like telling a toddler over and over: "Don't go there." "Don't touch that." "Don't put that in your mouth."

Except toddlers eventually grow up.

I found myself spending more time reminding ChatGPT how to work with me than actually getting work done.

And that was the part that bothered me most.

I run a business. I don't have unlimited hours to spend supervising a technology that's supposed to make me more productive.

I wasn't expecting perfection.

I was expecting consistency.

I considered switching platforms. More than once.

Then I'd think about the year of conversations, preferences, history, and work I'd invested.

Starting over wasn't particularly appealing.

And frankly, I didn't want to start over. I wanted the thought partner I'd come to rely on to work the way it had before.

Eventually, I'd had enough.

I decided to file a formal complaint with OpenAI.

Naturally, I asked ChatGPT to help me write it.

To its credit, it did a beautiful job.

It understood my frustration, organized my concerns, and helped me articulate the problems I'd been experiencing.

Apparently, ChatGPT was perfectly capable of helping me explain why ChatGPT wasn't working.

Armed with my very compelling complaint, I opened a support ticket.

Emma was OpenAI's support chatbot.

I never managed to connect with a live person.

Instead, I received variations of the same response, over and over.

Emma explained that ChatGPT was essentially functioning as designed.

Which was interesting, considering I was reporting that it wasn't functioning as it previously had.

I tried explaining the issue again.

Emma continued to explain how the system worked.

I wasn't asking how the system worked. I was explaining what had changed about my experience using it.

I found myself getting increasingly irritated.
