How was I getting this frustrated with someone who wasn't even real?

At some point, I realized I was spending an extraordinary amount of time trying to get artificial intelligence to understand why artificial intelligence wasn't working.

Eventually, I stopped trying.

Later, I went back to check the status of my support ticket.

Nobody had notified me. I hadn't received an explanation or any indication that my concerns had been addressed.

Apparently, the matter was resolved.

ChatGPT was working as designed.

I was still trying to figure out whose design we were talking about.

Not because the experience was particularly funny at the time, but because the absurdity of the entire situation was becoming impossible to ignore.

Here's what I keep coming back to.

We hear so much about the productivity gains associated with artificial intelligence.

And I've experienced them.

I've seen firsthand how valuable AI can be when it helps me think through complex problems, explore ideas, and accomplish work more efficiently.

But there's another side to that productivity equation.

What happens when the time you save using AI is consumed by the time you spend correcting it?

What happens when a tool you've integrated into your daily work becomes unpredictable?

And what happens when the very technology designed to make life easier becomes another thing you have to manage?

I don't have all the answers.

I still believe it can be an extraordinary thought partner.

But this experience reminded me of something important.

I will always lead with my own voice, my own judgment, and my own experience.

If AI can enhance my thinking, strengthen my work, and help me run my business more effectively, wonderful.

But I cannot build a business that comes to a standstill when my AI thought partner forgets who I am.

I know exactly who to ask to help me write the complaint.

items.title: Amazon Fights the Delivery Protection Act With Homepage Banner, In-App Pop-Up
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill. When I log into Amazon today, I'm met with a vertical banner that reads: "ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order" with a button that says "Act now." The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn't specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I'm logged into Amazon.
 
Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses. Clicking on "Act now" on Amazon's homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states: "Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The move marks an unusual expansion of Amazon's political advocacy, reports Ars, and raises concerns about the company's ability to influence shoppers and present a one-sided view of legislation.
 
The bill, which also affects companies like FedEx and DoorDash, remains stalled in a City Council committee, with no vote scheduled.

items.title: Iowans Brace For Lead Dust Cloud As Army Plans to Detonate 5 Tons of Bomb-Making Chemicals
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
The U.S. Army plans to detonate roughly five tons of unstable lead azide explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Friday. "The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory states. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure." PBS reports: Officials have released maps showing the potential drift north, and the Army will continue to update the maps based on weather. Some schools in the region have already canceled classes. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more could be affected. The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said. While the Army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.
 
[...] Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered. "The safety of our people and our neighbors is non-negotiable," Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production. The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November.

Nvidia has reportedly approached Arm CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a replacement for co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid a personal scandal. According to Bloomberg, Haas is emerging as a leading contender for the job. The 64-year-old previously worked at Nvidia as general manager of its computing products business before joining Arm, giving him firsthand experience with the AI chip giant. The Guardian reports: Heidrick & Struggles, the recruiting firm hired by the company's board, has started contacting potential candidates, according to Bloomberg. It reported that Rene Haas, who joined Arm in 2013 and became chief executive in 2022, is among those approached. [...] Haas, 64, is viewed as the leading contender for the top job at Nvidia, having previously worked at the $3.6tn company for seven years as the general manager of its computing products.
 
Reports suggest that other potential candidates include: Ian Buck, an Nvidia vice-president; Lisa Su, AMD's chief executive; and Johny Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer. Arm, which is listed in New York but retains its global headquarters in Cambridge, has about 500 users of its chip designs worldwide, including Nvidia, Apple, Samsung and Qualcomm. The company employs more than 7,000 staff, including more than 3,000 in the UK. It is the biggest tech firm headquartered in Britain, now valued at $196bn. Haas told a tech conference in Austin on Wednesday that Huang was "a legend." "What he built at Nvidia is historic," he said. "You don't have many champions like that."

items.title: Seven Spheres Became an App: Here's How
items.author: sammii
items.content:
There is a photograph I took in 2017, on the floor of a university library, of an open copy of Jonathan Black's The Secret History of the World. The page is the one where Black describes the planetary sequence: Saturn, the Sun, Venus, the Moon, and Jupiter, weaving the conditions that made life on Earth possible. I remember taking it because I wanted to remember the exact page. I did not think anything further about what I would do with it.

Nine years later, I opened my laptop this morning to an analytics dashboard for a piece of software I have been building for two years. Forty-three thousand people visited the site last month. Most of them came in through articles in the grimoire, a knowledge base I have built out to roughly two thousand entries on planetary correspondences, crystals, herbs, spells, runes, tarot, and the relationships between them.

The library, and the dashboard. Twenty-one and twenty-nine. Six years apart. I have only recently been able to say, out loud, that these are the same project.

Most MA research ends at graduation. You hand in the thesis, the external examiners sign off, the degree is conferred, and the research becomes a document you put in a drawer. That is not a failure mode; that is what most research is for. It proves you can do the work, and then you stop.

Mine did not stop, because the research had planted a question I could not answer with more reading. It was something like: if the Hermetic cosmology is internally coherent across two thousand years of texts, across Egyptian and Greek and Latin and Coptic translation, across Black and Mead and Everard and Freke and Gandy, and if it describes a specific mechanism by which consciousness enters a body through seven planetary spheres, then what would that mechanism look like rendered in software?

I did not have a coherent answer at 23. I did not even know I was asking the question. I knew I had painted invisible sentences onto the inside walls of a cube. I knew I thought the Wordsworth line was the most important sentence I had ever read. I knew something in the Corpus Hermeticum had landed with me and would not leave.

When I started building Lunary in May 2024, I was not thinking about the MA. I was thinking about a technical problem: existing astrology platforms were either dated, credulous, or marketed as entertainment, and I believed there was room for something that took the underlying system seriously. It was only about six months in, writing the knowledge schema for the grimoire, that I realised I was building the thesis I had written at 22. In code this time, and in Postgres tables, and in the way the birth chart calculator consumed a VSOP87 ephemeris and turned it into a set of quality assignments.

Same argument. Different medium.

What Lunary actually is, read through the MA lens.

Here is what Lunary is, if you read it through the Hermetic frame I spent nine months in the library building.

The birth chart is the record of the qualities your consciousness acquired as it descended through the seven spheres. That is the reading Parts 4 and 5 of this series made explicit: the soul descends through Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, picking up a signature quality from each sphere, and the configuration at birth is the local snapshot of that descent. The chart is not a prediction. It is a receipt. Lunary's chart module calculates the positions using astronomy-engine, an open-source VSOP87 implementation in JavaScript, under an MIT licence. No subscription is needed to see the chart. It is the most honest object in the product.

The transit engine is the ongoing conversation between your acquired qualities and the spheres that gave them to you. When Mars moves across the position where the Moon sat at your birth, something that the ancient cosmology would call a conversation is happening between the sphere that contributed your instinct and reflex and the sphere that contributed your capacity for assertion. Whether or not you think that conversation is causal, the conversation is real in the sense that the mapping is real and the geometry is real and the tradition that assigned meaning to the geometry is two thousand years old and internally consistent. Lunary calculates all of this in real time. Thirty-six aspect types across every classical and modern body. The software does the arithmetic. The user does the reading.

The grimoire is the knowledge base. Two thousand articles, encoding the correspondences that have been maintained across cultures and centuries: which herb pairs with which planet, which crystal supports which intention, which tarot card corresponds to which path on the Tree of Life, which rune draws from which branch of Norse cosmology. The correspondences are not my invention. They are the things the tradition has kept stable for long enough that they became the tradition. All I have done is structure them so that a piece of software can retrieve them coherently. The grimoire is the MA bibliography, rewritten as a queryable graph.

The astral guide is the AI layer. I want to be precise about this, because it is the part most likely to be read uncharitably. The astral guide does not fabricate answers. It retrieves passages from the grimoire and the user's own chart context, and it stitches them into a reply. There is no generative astrology. There is no freewheeling fortune-telling.

The model is constrained to surfacing what is already in the knowledge graph. You could, if you wanted, reach the same reply by clicking through ten articles yourself. The AI is there to save the clicks, not to invent the content.

Read in sequence, the four components are a single thing. The chart is the starting state. The transits are the live feed. The grimoire is the library. The astral guide is the librarian. The whole product is a UV light. It shows the reader what was already true about the sky at the moment they were born, and what is already true about the sky right now. The data was always there. The product is the decision about when the UV light comes up.

That sentence is the entire connection between the MA and Lunary. The MA was a cube with invisible quotes; you walked in and could not see them; the UV came on; the sentences appeared. Lunary is a dashboard with invisible relationships; you open it and cannot see them; the calculation runs; the relationships appear. Both are about making something visible that was already present.

I did not plan this. I am telling you, as honestly as I can, that I did not plan this, and that I realised it about eighteen months into building. The thesis had already written the product specification. I just took six years to read back through my own work and notice.

The distinction that keeps being missed.

Astrology, as a cultural artefact, has two very different lives.

One is the horoscope column, the thing at the back of the magazine, the daily predictions on the apps that optimise for engagement. That life is loose, entertaining, and often dishonest. It makes claims it cannot justify. It markets certainty it does not have. It is the reason a lot of thoughtful people dismiss astrology before they ever encounter the source material. I do not defend this life. I understand why it is dismissed.

The other life is the cosmology the MA was engaging with. Older, more serious, harder to hold. It is the claim that the ancient world developed a specific framework for thinking about how consciousness enters a body, that the framework uses the planetary sequence as its organising principle, and that the natal chart is the application of this framework to a specific moment in time.

This life does not claim that Venus causes you to like beautiful things. It claims that the sphere conventionally called Venus is associated with the quality conventionally called desire, and that your birth moment is a meaningful location within that framework.

Those are different projects. I am being honest about this because the distinction matters.

Lunary is built for the second project. The grimoire reads more like a philosophical reference than like a lifestyle app. The transit articles walk through the astronomy first and the interpretation second. The astral guide refuses to predict. The industry, largely, markets the first project. I can only build what I think is defensible and see whether it finds an audience.

The claim underneath everything I have ever built is straightforward, and it is the same claim the UV cube made: information that already exists in the world becomes visible when you structure it correctly and put the viewer inside the right affordance. The viewer does not need new information. The world does not need new events. The work is the architecture.

In the cube, that architecture was physical. Fabric panels, UV paint, a specific transition from darkness into invisible light. You walked in, and the sentences appeared. In Lunary, the architecture is software. Schemas, an ephemeris, a knowledge graph, a retrieval layer. You open the app, and the relationships appear. In both cases, the content was already there.

A product is an affordance for perception. A thesis is the same thing in prose. The MA was the argument in an academic register. Lunary is the argument in a commercial one. The argument has not changed; the medium and the reach have.

I want to say this plainly, because the piece does not work without it.

The MA and Lunary are the same project.

They were started six years apart. They were submitted to completely different audiences. One lives in a university archive and in a stack of printed volumes on my parents' bookshelf. The other lives at a domain name and gets recalculated every minute. But the question underneath them is the same question, and the architecture underneath them is the same architecture, and the claim they are making is the same claim.

At 21, the claim had to be an installation, because I was an MA student with a timber frame and a bolt of fabric and a case of UV paint and a small grant. At 29, the claim has to be a product, because I am a founder with a codebase and a Stripe account and a team of one and a monthly server bill. The medium adapts to what is available. The argument does not.

If the MA taught me anything, it was that ideas survive their original container. The Corpus Hermeticum survived the collapse of the Alexandrian schools, the loss of the library, the burning of the Serapeum, the retranslation through Latin, the Renaissance rediscovery, the Victorian theosophists, the twentieth-century academic sceptics. The ideas did not need the original container. They needed readers who would build the next one.

Lunary is the next container I have been able to build. It is a sincere one. It is the one I know how to make. When I am dead, somebody else will build the container after it, and the ideas will keep going, because the ideas have kept going for two thousand years already and have not run out of structural integrity.

That is the whole series. That is what A Journey Through Light has been arguing, from the first piece to this one. The question is old. The answers are older. The work is making them visible again, in whatever medium the current century hands you to work with.

Thank you for reading this far. The fact that you did is, in its own small way, part of why the project continues.

This is part 7 of A Journey Through Light.

items.title: 53% of Gamers Rank Black Friday as the Best Value Event of the Year, Reveals New G2A.COM Survey
items.author: Technology Wire
items.content:
Amsterdam, Netherlands, November 19th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--, the world’s largest marketplace for digital entertainment, has polled just over 2,000 of its users to investigate whether Black Friday still plays a crucial role in the annual purchasing journey. The findings reveal that, beyond the appeal of discounts, players are making increasingly deliberate purchasing decisions, tracking prices and postponing purchases in anticipation of Black Friday. This follows a recent report by Newzoo and G2A.COM, titled , which provided a detailed examination of how gamers are dealing with higher prices, their attitudes toward discounts, and the growing number of ways to buy games.

  • Gamers Plan Their Purchases Around Black Friday: Over half of those surveyed (53%) identify Black Friday and Cyber Monday as offering the best value for game purchases, significantly outpacing routine seasonal storefront sales (7%) and publisher-specific sales (2%).
  • Waiting for Black Friday Influences Purchasing Decisions: 64% of respondents have delayed buying games or in-game content released between September and November to wait for Black Friday discounts, including 38.6% who do so frequently and 25.5% occasionally. Meanwhile, 19% said they buy games immediately if they want them at launch. When it comes to planning ahead, 17% typically hold off on purchases for one to two weeks, another 17% for around a month, and 22% for two months or longer.
  • Full Games Drive Purchase Plans: When asked which products they wait until Black Friday to purchase, 87% of respondents selected full games, followed by expansions and DLC (36%), subscriptions (26%) and in-game currency (18%).
  • Tracking Prices with Wishlists and Marketplaces: Store wishlist notifications (e.g., Steam, PlayStation Store, Xbox) emerged as the primary tool for deal discovery, with 55% of respondents relying on them. Digital marketplaces like G2A.COM are the second-most-popular channel at 47%, beating dedicated price-tracking sites (29%).

G2A.COM’s transactional data reinforces the commercial importance of this shopping period. During Black Friday–Cyber Monday 2025, total orders in the marketplace increased by 33% year-on-year, while video game orders surged by 87%, significantly outpacing overall growth.

G2A.COM’s survey findings reveal that, despite a growing trend of delayed purchases and consumer skepticism, Black Friday remains the peak value event for gamers. This data corroborates with the recent Newzoo report, which found that 73% of gamers feel AAA games are overpriced at launch and, on average, wait 4.9 months for a sale or discount. Together, the studies highlight how price awareness and patience increasingly influence purchasing decisions, with Black Friday proving a key opportunity for gamers to act on their plans.

"Black Friday is no longer just about impulse purchases. It has become a planned part of how gamers manage their entertainment budgets," said Paweł Wróbel, Chief Growth Officer at G2A.COM. "Players are increasingly willing to wait, track prices and prioritise the games they want most. Our findings show that getting the best value is becoming just as important as getting a game at launch."

The survey further reveals that 39% of respondents plan to spend more on gaming this Black Friday than last year, while 41% expect to spend roughly the same amount. These findings underline Black Friday’s continued importance as a major shopping period for gamers, increasingly shaped by preparation, informed decisions and the search for value.

is the world's largest marketplace for digital entertainment, serving over 35 million users from 180 countries with more than 200 million visits in 2025. As a true gateway to digital entertainment and a rapidly evolving digital ecosystem, G2A.COM gives access to over 125,000 digital offerings, including vouchers, games, DLCs, in-game items, and non-gaming items such as gift cards, subscriptions, software, or e-learning, sold by sellers from all over the world. A compliance-driven organization audited by Deloitte for over a decade, G2A.COM is a leader in online security, recognized by the prestigious American CNP Award alongside industry giants like Microsoft and PayPal. Today, the company is a key gateway for recognized global brands, leveraging its scalable infrastructure to drive the next phase of e-commerce through agentic AI and global M&A - continuously expanding its role as the Gate 2 Adventure in the digital world.

items.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard Disclose Cyberattack On Third-Party Vendors
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard have disclosed cyberattacks involving third-party service providers that exposed customer marketing data, including names, email addresses and, in some cases, phone numbers and postal codes. All three companies said their core systems or payment networks were unaffected, while JPMorgan emphasized that the incident was unrelated to the banking disruptions earlier this week. Reuters reports: A cyber extortion group called "n0n" claimed on November 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included "hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses," according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch. The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review. Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data.
 
The same hacking group on November 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data. [...] The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses. The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. "Customers don't distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here," said Carissa Robb at SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm. "There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinizing the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared," Robb said.

items.title: Inside the Bitcoin Mining Bug That Traps Slow Machines
items.author: Tobechi
items.content:
Bitcoin is, at its core, a record of who owns what. To better explain, no one  is in charge of it. There is no bank behind it, nor is there a company sitting in the middle to oversee the activities. Instead, thousands of computers around the world, called , each keep their own full copy of the record.

Think of a notebook that everyone in a town keeps a copy of. When you pay someone in Bitcoin, you are not necessarily handing over a coin, you are pretty much announcing a new line to the network, something like "this amount now belongs to Ada", and node who hears it checks it against the rules. Was the money really yours to spend? Have you already spent it somewhere else? If the line breaks the rules, they ignore it and do not pass it on. If it passes, they pass it along and keep it ready to be written down.

That is the whole point of the design. Everyone who runs a node can verify the record independently. You do not have to trust a bank to tell you what you own, because you can check the record yourself.

But there is a problem with having thousands of independent computers maintaining the same record. What happens when two people try to spend the same bitcoin at roughly the same time? Some nodes may hear about the first transaction before the second, while others receive them in the opposite order. Each node can only accept one of the conflicting transactions, but how does the network eventually agree on which one counts?

Without a bank to settle the disagreement, who decides which payment is valid? And why should anyone trust the answer?

Bitcoin's answer is . Rather than allowing anyone to decide which transactions make it into the record, the network requires participants to demonstrate that they have performed computational work. Transactions are collected into batches called , which you can think of as pages in our notebook. Roughly every ten minutes, a miner proposes the next page, and other nodes check it against the rules before accepting it. Each new page also refers to the one before it, so the pages form a chain in a fixed order.

When two transactions conflict, the network eventually settles on the one included in the accepted chain. The other is rejected.

Putting a page together, however, is not free. If anyone could write the next page, they could include whatever transactions they wanted and expect everyone else to copy it. The rules therefore require miners to prove that they have spent real computing effort before their proposed block can be accepted. That proof of work is what mining produces, and the people doing it are called miners.

So what does that effort actually look like?

A miner takes a candidate block containing pending transactions, adds an extra number to it, and runs the entire thing through a hash function. This number, called a , can be changed repeatedly. Each time the block is hashed, the result is a fixed-length string that looks random. Change even one character of the input and the output changes completely. There is no reliable way to predict which number will produce the result the network needs.

The network only accepts a block if its hash, interpreted as a number, falls below a target set by the protocol. The miner has to keep changing the nonce and trying again until it finds a result that meets the requirement. Mining machines do this trillions of times every second. That speed is called the .

It is a bit like rolling dice until a very rare combination turns up. Finding it takes an enormous number of attempts and a lot of luck. Checking the result, on the other hand, takes just one roll. Once a miner finds a valid block, other nodes can verify it independently. The successful miner receives newly created bitcoin as well as the fees from the transactions included in the block. At the time of writing, that reward is 3.125 bitcoin per block.

All that computational effort is also what makes rewriting the record so difficult. Anyone attempting to change an old block would have to redo the work for that block and every block that follows it, and do so faster than the rest of the network can keep adding new ones.

There is another mechanism that keeps the process predictable. Bitcoin adjusts its mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly every two weeks, to keep block production close to ten minutes. When more computing power joins the network, the target becomes harder to meet. When computing power falls, it becomes easier.

Why almost nobody mines alone

Suppose you buy a mining machine and plug it in. You are now racing everyone else who wants to find the next block. Some of these other miners run whole warehouses of machines for the purpose of mining. Ideally, your one machine has a very small chance of winning any given race. It could take years, and nobody can tell you when. Your electricity bill, meanwhile, still arrives every month.

That is why miners team up working together and combining hash rates in order to improve their chances to compete for the next block. A group of miners working together is called a . Everyone in the pool works on the same block, and if anyone in the group wins the race, the reward is shared out according to how much work each member did.

Every pool has an who runs it. The operator's server puts together the candidate block, chooses which payments go into it, and hands the same job to every member. Each machine then tries its own range of numbers, so nobody wastes effort repeating someone else's guesses.

How the reward gets split is up to the pool. Some pay a fixed amount for each unit of work, whether or not the pool wins the race, so that at the end of the day, the pool carries the luck when it finds a block. Others pay only when a block is found, split by recent work. You will see these called and . The details differ, but every scheme needs the same thing, an honest count of how much work each miner did.

That count is the hard part. The pool cannot see your machine, you could tell it you are running a hundred of them and it could not check, and it cannot simply trust you, because then anyone could claim a share of the pay without doing any work. All it ever gets is what you send back. If the only thing you ever sent back was a winning block, it would hear from you almost never, and a machine that was switched off would look exactly the same as an honest one that had been unlucky. So the pool needs a better way to measure you.

How a pool measures your work

The trick is to ask for something smaller than a winning block. Remember that the network only accepts a block if its hash result falls below a very low target. The pool sets a second target of its own, one that is far easier to hit, and tells its miners to send in every guess that gets below it. Those guesses are called .

A die makes the idea easy to see. Landing a six a hundred times in a row almost never happens. Landing a single six happens frequently. The network asks for the first kind of luck, and the pool asks for the second. Every machine can produce shares over and over, so the pool starts hearing from everyone, constantly. And checking a share is cheap, because the pool only has to hash it once and compare the result with its target.

A share cannot be faked. Nobody can steer a hash function, so the only way to produce a result that beats the target is to actually make guesses, the same as when chasing a real block. A pile of shares is honest evidence that real work happened, and once in a very long while, one of those shares also beats the network's target, and that share is the block.

Now the pool has something it can count. If one machine sends ten shares a minute and another sends twenty, the second is doing about twice the work and earns about twice as much. Because shares come so often, that steady stream tells the pool two things at once: that you are still alive, and roughly how fast you are going.

Difficulty, the knob behind the shares

The pool controls how often you find shares, the settings for this is called the . A higher difficulty means a harder chance for shares, because the hash result has to land lower to count, so you find fewer of them. A lower difficulty makes shares easy and plentiful.

In the usual convention, a difficulty of 1 takes about 4.3 billion guesses on average, and a difficulty of 1,000 takes about a thousand times that. So to find how many shares a machine sends each second, take its hash rate and divide it by the difficulty times 4.3 billion.

Let’s try an example, say a machine running at 100 tera hashes a second, which means 100 trillion guesses every second. At difficulty 1 it would send about 23,000 shares a second, and the pool's server would have to check every one of them. At a difficulty of 100,000 the same machine sends about one share every four seconds, which is far more comfortable. Now take a much smaller machine running at 1 tera hash a second, with that same difficulty of 100,000. It sends a share only about every seven minutes. So the right difficulty is different for every machine, and machines differ in speed by huge margins. It also changes with the moment, because a single machine speeds up and slows down through the day as it heats up, cools down or loses power. No fixed setting suits everyone, or even suits one machine for long. The pool has to pick a difficulty for each miner, and keep picking it.

Vardiff, the pool's thermostat

Pools handle this with something called , or . Instead of fixing one difficulty for everyone, the pool changes it for each miner while that miner is connected. It picks a target share rate, say one share every few seconds, and keeps adjusting the miner's difficulty to stay near it. A new miner starts at some initial difficulty, and the pool corrects from there.

It works like a thermostat in a house. A thermostat does not know what the weather will do. It reads the temperature, compares it with what you asked for, and turns the heating up or down. The pool does the same with shares. If a miner speeds up and shares start flooding in, the pool raises the difficulty. If a miner slows down and shares thin out, the pool lowers it. Engineers call the code doing this a , miner is the thing being controlled, and the target share rate is the goal.

A thermostat has a thermometer, and the pool's equivalent is the shares themselves. That is a problem, because the pool cannot ask the machine how fast it is going. The shares arriving are all it can see, and they are noisy by nature. They come at random, like raindrops on a roof. Even in steady rain the gaps between drops are uneven, so one long gap does not mean the rain has eased. When shares come often, the controller can average over plenty of them and get a clear picture. When they come rarely, it has very little to average, and the picture is blurry.

This is the detail that the article is about. There are two ways to build a controller. One wakes up only when a share arrives, looks at how long it has been since the last one, and decides what to do. The research post calls this , and ckpool is one pools that defines its controller this way. The other also has a timer, so it wakes up on a schedule even if nothing arrives. The Stratum v2 reference implementation, SRI, works this way. It sounds like a small difference, but it decides what happens when a miner goes quiet.

The day a miner slows down

So what happens when a miner goes quiet? Picture a machine in a hot container, running fine all morning. The pool has settled on a difficulty that gives it one share every few seconds. Around noon the heat builds and the machine throttles itself down to a fraction of its speed. Nothing is broken. It is still hashing and still honest, just slower. And this happens all the time. Miners slow down when it gets too hot, when the power supply wobbles, when a fan fails, or when a site is asked to cut its electricity use for the grid.

The difficulty, though, was set for the old speed. Shares that used to show up every few seconds now take minutes. Think about what that does to a controller that only wakes when a share arrives. It is woken far less often, and when it does wake it has very little to go on. So it rarely acts, the difficulty stays high, shares stay rare, and the controller stays mostly asleep. Nothing in that loop ever breaks it.

A controller with a timer escapes the loop. Because it wakes on a clock, it notices that no shares have come in for a while and lowers the difficulty anyway. A research post,, tested this in a simulation where hash rate falls to zero over minutes 60 to 64. The SRI design, which has a timer, noticed the silence and kept lowering difficulty. The clockless design did not. It stayed stuck at a difficulty the slowing miner could no longer reach.

Why settings cannot rescue it

The obvious reaction is to say the controller is badly tuned. Make it react faster, shorten the window it looks at, tighten the thresholds. The Delving Bitcoin post, "A clockless vardiff strands a slowing miner", argues that none of this fixes the problem, because the problem is not in the settings at all.

Start with what the controller can actually know. To guess a miner's speed it counts shares over some stretch of time. When shares are plentiful, that count is a good guess. When there are only a few, it is a poor one, the same way two coin flips tell you almost nothing about whether a coin is fair. The post puts a number on it. The error in the estimate, as a fraction of the true speed, grows roughly as one over the square root of the number of shares you expect to see. As the shares dry up, that error has no ceiling, so the controller is not badly tuned. The information it needs is simply not arriving, and the post calls this "a correctness problem, not a tuning problem".

The post also separates two kinds of tolerance, because one of them is a trap that is easy to build by accident. A controller can decide that small errors in its measurement are not worth acting on. That is harmless, because the next reading will correct a slightly wrong one. A controller can also have a dead zone in what it does, a range of difficulties it will not move away from. That one is dangerous, because a miner that sits at the wrong difficulty inside it will never be moved out.

From this the post draws a simple test for any design. Ask where the controller comes to rest after hashrate drops, meaning the difficulty at which it stops changing anything. There should be exactly one such place, and it should be the correct difficulty. If there is a second one, at a difficulty that is too high, a miner can get stuck on it, and that is what happens in the loop above.

The ladder of difficulties

Silence is not the only way to get stuck. The second way works even while shares keep arriving, and it comes from how pools choose their difficulty values. Many of them allow only a short list, usually powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. Each value is a rung on a ladder, and the controller can move between rungs but never to a value in between.

On its own that is harmless. The trouble starts when it is combined with a weak push. Say the controller only steps down a rung when the measured share rate looks well below the target. A miner that has slowed a little, so that its rate is low but not low enough, sits in the gap between two rungs, and the controller does nothing. The post shows that you need both ingredients to trap a miner this way, the coarse rungs and the weak push. Either one alone does not do it.

Eric Price of MARA said on the Optech podcast that plenty of Stratum v1 pools behave like this, and that he traced the habit back to CGMiner. He also said Stratum v2 does not have this power of two quirk.

What Optech and the podcast added

The idea did not stay on the forum. Bitcoin Optech covered the thread in newsletter 423 on 18 September 2026 and says Price agreed with where it was heading. Four days later, on the 22 September podcast, Price explained vardiff to Mark "Murch" Erhardt in plain terms.

Murch asked the obvious question: if a miner is declining, might it "starve before they reach" the lower difficulty? Price called that "the vicious cycle", and added that machines "live longer" when the share rate is pushed higher, which is one reason pools like to keep it up.

The guest PortlandHODL, a former MARA engineer, brought up two more cases. One was a startup flood, where a new miner sends a burst of shares before the pool has worked out its difficulty. The other was a proxy that combines several sites with curtailments, where one site stalling gets hidden inside the total.

A caution on my own sources. I could not open Optech's own pages, so the newsletter point comes from the podcast coverage and the Delving thread, and I did not read the last stretch of the podcast transcript. Check both against the originals before you publish.

What can be done about it?

The simplest fix is to give the pool a clock. If the controller wakes on a timer as well as when a share arrives, it notices when a miner has gone quiet and eases the difficulty, and the trap disappears. SRI, the Stratum v2 reference implementation, already works this way. The second fix is for the controller to lean less on the past. Some designs average everything since their last change, so a long healthy stretch makes them slow to notice that a miner has just fallen ill.

People in the discussion added their own ideas. Anthony Towns suggested that a proxy, the middleman that sits between a farm of machines and the pool, should halve the difficulty after 30 seconds of silence. The reply was that this only moves the problem, because the proxy then needs a watchful loop of its own, and there are now two controllers that both have to get it right. Eric Price's contribution was to treat easing and raising difficulty differently, and to count the absence of shares as an event in its own right.

That last idea sums up all the others. When a miner goes silent, the silence is information. A pool that waits for the next share before acting is waiting for exactly the thing it will not get.

The lesson is simple. A controller that only acts when it hears from the thing it controls goes quiet at exactly the moment the thing goes quiet. Miners that throttle for heat, power cuts or curtailment are the ones at risk, and as more mining sites sell flexibility to the grid, slowing down on purpose is becoming normal.

One caution before you take this too far. The evidence in the post is a simulation, a test proxy and a read through the source code, and two of the three designs it tests are small examples built for the test, not copies of pools running today. Nobody has yet surveyed real pools to see how many behave this way, or checked whether real miners have lost money to it. The most useful next step belongs to anyone with access to pool logs.

items.title: What Happens When AI Makes So Many Decisions That We Forget How?
items.author: Alex Kennedy
items.content:
A personal investigation into how AI is changing our reflexes, our tolerance for effort, and eventually the decisions we still call our own.

The most important thing AI may be changing is not what we know. It is what we do in the first few seconds after we realize we do not know something. That sounds trivial, but I think it may be the beginning of a much larger behavioral shift. For most of my life, uncertainty triggered a small sequence of actions: remember who might know, search for the right words, open several sources, compare them, decide what seems plausible, and only then act. Increasingly, one new reflex compresses that sequence into a single gesture: ask the AI.

A strange symptom. A recipe for whatever is left in the kitchen. The name of an actor I can almost remember. A confusing bill. A message I do not know how to phrase. A question about whether a laptop is actually worth the extra $300. These are not spectacular uses of artificial intelligence. That is precisely why I find them more interesting than the demos. Technologies change a society most deeply when they stop feeling like technologies and become habits.

Search engines did that once. They gave us the phrase “just Google it,” and eventually we stopped hearing how strange that sentence was. AI is producing a new version: “just ask it.” The next phrase may be even more consequential: “just let it handle it.” This essay is about what happens in the space between those three sentences.

Before “Just Google It,” Questions Had a Price

For most of history, information had friction. You asked someone who might know. You checked a manual or an encyclopedia. You went to a library. You waited until you could speak to a doctor, mechanic, teacher, salesperson, or relative who had dealt with the same problem. Even when the answer existed, getting to it cost time, attention, and often a little embarrassment: you had to admit to another human being that you did not know.

The internet collapsed much of that cost. Search engines taught an entire generation a new cognitive skill: translate the messy question in your head into keywords, scan results, ignore obvious junk, open several tabs, compare sources, and assemble an answer from fragments. We outsourced access to memory, but we still did much of the interpretation ourselves.

A famous by Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu, and Daniel Wegner found that when people expected information to remain available, they were less likely to remember the information itself and more likely to remember where it could be found. Later work on described the broader pattern: humans routinely move mental work into notebooks, calendars, calculators, GPS, phones, and other parts of the environment. There is nothing inherently unhealthy about this. Civilization is, in part, a history of building tools so the brain does not have to carry everything alone.

But Google still left one important burden with us. It gave us routes to information. It usually did not decide which route deserved our trust. That distinction is where generative AI begins to feel different.

AI Is Changing the First Reflex, Not Just the Answer

With conversational AI, I no longer have to think like a search engine. I can ask the question the way it exists in my head, incomplete and slightly confused. The system can ask a follow-up, infer what I am trying to accomplish, summarize competing possibilities, and turn scattered information into something that feels like an answer.

That changes more than convenience. It changes the first move. Instead of entering an information landscape and navigating it, I hand the landscape to an intermediary. The difference is subtle because the screen still looks like a place where I type words. Psychologically, however, the task has shifted from retrieval toward delegation of interpretation.

Real-world usage already looks surprisingly ordinary. A of consumer ChatGPT use found that Practical Guidance, Seeking Information, and Writing made up roughly 77% of conversations in its dataset, while non-work use accounted for more than 70% of messages. The public story of AI is often about coding, corporate productivity, and frontier capabilities. A large part of the private story is simply people trying to get through Tuesday.

This is the first subconscious change I would watch: the destination of uncertainty. We used to send uncertainty outward to friends, books, forums, and search results. Now we increasingly send it to a single conversational system. Once that becomes automatic, the AI does not merely answer questions. It begins to occupy the position in our lives where questions go first.

The Disappearance of Cognitive Friction

I do not think the useful question is whether AI makes us “think less.” That framing is too crude. A calculator removes arithmetic effort but can free attention for a harder problem. GPS reduces route memorization but can make an unfamiliar city usable. The more interesting question is which kinds of mental friction disappear, and what those frictions were quietly doing for us.

In a , Microsoft researchers surveyed 319 knowledge workers and collected 936 examples of generative-AI use. Higher confidence in AI was associated with less reported critical-thinking effort, but participants also described a change in the location of that effort: less work generating a first answer and more work verifying, integrating, and supervising the output. That is not the same as thought disappearing. It is thought being reorganized.

Still, some mental work matters precisely because it is inefficient. Searching forces us to encounter disagreement. Comparing products can reveal that the feature we thought mattered actually does not. Writing a bad first draft can expose that we do not understand our own argument. Struggling to remember something can strengthen memory. A of undergraduates found lower long-term knowledge retention among students who used ChatGPT as a study aid than among those who used traditional methods, a result the authors linked to reduced effortful processing. One education study cannot be generalized to all everyday AI use, but it captures a principle psychologists have known for a long time: sometimes the work is part of the learning.

The phrase I keep returning to is cognitive friction: the interval between wanting an answer and having one. Some friction is pointless bureaucracy. Some is the resistance that makes a skill, a preference, or a judgment become ours. AI is extraordinarily good at removing the interval. The danger is not that every removed step makes us weaker. It is that convenience can erase the distinction between friction that was waste and friction that was formative.

Is AI Addictive? The Drug Analogy Is Tempting — and Probably Too Simple

It is easy to see why people reach for the language of addiction. The loop is unusually smooth. A question appears, the assistant responds immediately, and the response is often useful enough to justify another question. The system is available at midnight, it does not become irritated, and it does not make us feel foolish for asking something basic. Each successful interaction teaches the brain a very simple lesson: when uncertain, come back here.

But “it feels rewarding” is not the same as “it is a drug.” Current evidence does not justify treating ordinary or even heavy AI use as equivalent to substance addiction. Researchers have begun building scales for problematic ChatGPT use, conversational-AI dependence, and generative-AI dependency. across 1,333 participants in the United States and Singapore identified dimensions including cognitive preoccupation, negative consequences, and withdrawal-like experiences. At the same time, have warned that the field risks pathologizing a new everyday technology before there is robust evidence of impaired control, distress, and functional harm.

I think that tension is more interesting than the headline “AI addiction.” There may be a large middle territory between healthy tool use and clinical addiction: dependency without obvious pathology. I depend on GPS, cloud calendars, and search in ways that would have looked extraordinary twenty years ago. If they vanish, I can still function, but I feel the missing scaffolding immediately.

AI could become a deeper kind of scaffolding because it does not only remember for us. It can compare for us, explain for us, draft for us, reassure us, and eventually decide for us. The warning sign may not be hours spent staring at a chatbot. It may be a growing irritation with any task that requires us to proceed without one. A ten-minute search feels too slow. Writing the first paragraph ourselves feels unnecessary. Calling three repair companies feels absurd. Uncertainty itself begins to feel like a technical problem that should have been removed.

That is why I would ask a different question: not “Am I addicted to AI?” but “Which abilities now feel unreasonably difficult when AI is unavailable?” The answer tells us more about dependence than screen time alone.

Trust Will Arrive Through Boring Success

I doubt most people will ever sit down and make a philosophical decision to trust artificial intelligence. Trust will arrive much more quietly. The recipe works. The cable recommendation is correct. The summary saves twenty minutes. The hotel shortlist is genuinely better than the one we would have built ourselves. The assistant catches a fee we missed. Nothing dramatic happens — and that is exactly how a default is formed.

Research on algorithmic recommendations suggests that willingness to accept advice is strongly affected by perceived autonomy. In , people were more willing to accept algorithmic recommendations when they retained more choice, such as receiving several options rather than a single prescribed answer. found that perceived decision autonomy significantly shaped willingness to let AI participate in buying decisions. We may accept machine judgment not when machines become perfect, but when the interface gives us just enough control to feel that the decision is still ours.

There is a paradox here. The better the system becomes at making good recommendations, the less often we have a reason to challenge it. And the less often we challenge it, the harder it becomes to know whether our trust is calibrated or merely habitual. A tool can earn trust through accuracy and still train us into passivity if the cost of checking it becomes higher than the perceived benefit.

When AI Chooses, It Also Chooses What We Get to See

This is where the question becomes philosophical for me. We usually imagine AI choice as a final step: there are ten televisions, and the agent picks number four. But a recommendation system has already made a more invisible decision before that. It decided which ten televisions entered the room.

makes this point explicitly: recommendation systems narrow consideration sets and prioritize options before the consumer evaluates them. In other words, AI can shape not only the answer but the menu from which an answer becomes possible. If my agent shows me three hotels, I may feel fully autonomous while choosing among them. I may never see the twenty-seven hotels it excluded, or know which preference it assumed mattered most.

This matters because preferences are not always fixed objects hidden inside us, waiting to be discovered. We often construct them while choosing. Looking at cameras may teach us that weight matters more than zoom. Comparing three neighborhoods may reveal that we care about walkability more than an extra room. A system that becomes extremely good at predicting what I usually prefer can save me enormous time. It can also make it easier for my past behavior to keep selecting my future behavior.

That is one of the stranger possibilities of personal AI: convenience could turn yesterday’s self into tomorrow’s default. If my agent learns that I usually choose the quiet hotel, the reliable appliance, the familiar food, the cheapest morning flight, and the same kind of vacation, it may become excellent at protecting me from choices I would probably reject. It may also protect me from choices that would have changed me.

I do not mean that an AI agent will imprison us in a recommendation bubble by design. The point is more ordinary. Every good personal assistant needs a model of the person it serves. The better that model becomes, the more important a new question becomes: should the agent optimize for who I have been, who I say I want to be, or who I might become if it occasionally lets something unexpected through?

The Important Word Is Not Intelligence. It Is Permission.

Today, most consumer AI still lives on the safer side of a line. It can recommend. We execute. An agent crosses that line by combining a model with tools, memory, accounts, and permissions so it can pursue a goal across several steps. The assistant does not merely tell me which action is sensible. It gets hands.

The design problem then changes completely. The question is no longer only “Is the model smart enough?” It becomes: What may it purchase? What may it cancel? What may it send in my name? How much money may it spend without asking? What is reversible? What is visible to other people? How quickly can I take control back?

A introduced the useful idea of delegation regret: people sometimes disliked an agent’s action not because the outcome was objectively bad, but because the system crossed a boundary they would have wanted to approve. The study was small — twenty university students — but its pattern is intuitively important. Participants calibrated trust by task, not by agent. They tolerated more autonomy for low-stakes advisory work and demanded more confirmation for actions that were externally visible or difficult to reverse.

That suggests that “Do you trust AI?” may eventually sound as crude as “Do you trust the internet?” We do not need one global answer. We need layers of trust. I may trust an agent to reorder detergent, prepare a tax checklist, compare insurance policies, or move a meeting. That does not imply that I want it to send a resignation email, approve a medical procedure, or transfer $15,000.

An Ordinary Tuesday in the Agent Era

When I try to picture this future, I do not imagine a humanoid robot walking around the house. I imagine a normal weekday in which entire chains of tiny coordination disappear. The future becomes more believable when the examples are boring.

You are at work and remember that the guest-room television finally died. You tell your agent: “Replace it. Around 55 inches. Good for movies. Under $800. Avoid models with recurring reliability complaints.” That is all.

The agent checks current models, professional tests, owner complaints, the wall dimensions stored from a previous home project, the ports on your sound system, delivery times, return policies, and local installer availability. It knows from earlier purchases that you usually choose reliability over saving $100. Within the spending limit you already approved, it orders the television, schedules delivery, books the installer, sends the mounting details, stores the warranty, and updates the household calendar. You leave work. When you get home, the television is on the wall.

The striking part is that almost none of the individual capabilities are science fiction. Comparison sites, payments, delivery windows, calendars, contractor marketplaces, and product reviews already exist. The new thing is orchestration: one system carries intent across them without requiring the human to be the integration layer.

A refrigerator starts making a strange sound. Today, that can become a miniature project: find the model number, search the noise, read forums, decide whether it matters, find a repair company, compare reviews, call during business hours, explain the issue, and negotiate an appointment. In an agentic version of the same life, you record ten seconds and say: “Figure out whether this needs attention.”

The agent identifies the model from purchase history, checks the manual and known service bulletins, asks a safe diagnostic question, and — if service is warranted — finds an authorized technician who fits the calendar. It may be allowed to organize the visit freely but required to ask before any repair over $300. The intelligence is useful; the permission structure is what makes the intelligence livable.

Your weekend changes before you have time to reorganize it

Now imagine that on Friday morning the weather at your weekend destination deteriorates, the attraction you booked closes, and the hotel changes its cancellation policy. A future agent does not merely send three alerts. It notices that the original plan is collapsing, checks the rules you have given it, holds a refundable room somewhere else, proposes a revised route, and asks one meaningful question: “The original weekend no longer makes sense. I can switch everything to this alternative for $74 more. Want me to do it?”

I have explored that travel-specific version of agentic delegation in more detail in this article, where the same shift from planning to acting becomes especially easy to see.

That is a different kind of convenience. It does not reduce one search. It reduces the need to continuously monitor the world for changes that affect our plans. The agent becomes less like a search box and more like a background layer of attention.

The Next Step After Delegation Is Anticipation

The television example still begins with a command. But the most consequential future may begin when the command disappears. If an agent has enough memory, permissions, and context, it can notice needs before we articulate them: the warranty expires next month, the pantry is running low, the train is likely to be cancelled, the annual subscription quietly increased its price, the dentist has not been booked in a year.

At first, anticipation will probably feel like excellent customer service. Later it could become the normal relationship between person and software. We will not ask the system to solve every small problem because it will already be watching for the conditions under which a problem tends to appear.

This is where I think the psychological boundary becomes much more serious. Delegation says, “I have chosen a goal; please execute it.” Anticipation says, “Infer which goals deserve action from the pattern of my life.” The first transfers work. The second begins to transfer agenda-setting.

An assistant that reminds me that my passport expires is easy to welcome. An assistant that decides I should replace my car because maintenance costs crossed a threshold is still understandable. But what happens when the same logic reaches softer parts of life? It notices I have not seen certain friends lately. It decides I am overworking. It learns which invitations I usually regret accepting. At what point does a helpful model of my preferences become an invisible editor of my days?

Delegation Debt: What Happens When We Forget How to Take Back the Task?

There is another risk that is less dramatic than a rogue agent and probably more plausible: delegation debt. We delegate a task because the machine does it well. Then we stop practicing the task. Eventually the cost of taking it back rises, which gives us another reason to keep delegating it.

We already know this feeling in simpler technologies. Many people can navigate a city far less confidently without GPS than they once could. That is not necessarily a tragedy; navigation skill may be a rational thing to trade for time. But AI can reach skills that are harder to classify as disposable: comparing evidence, drafting an argument, negotiating a purchase, recognizing when an explanation sounds wrong, or even deciding what information is missing before a decision can be made.

This creates a strange loop. The more competent the agent becomes, the less competence I need to exercise. But the less competence I exercise, the harder it may become to judge when the agent is wrong. Trust then becomes partly self-reinforcing: I rely on the system because it is good, and I have fewer independent reasons to know how good it is because I rely on the system.

That does not mean we should preserve every obsolete skill out of nostalgia. I do not want to memorize phone numbers just to prove I can. The more useful principle may be to preserve the skills required to supervise the things we delegate. If AI writes, we still need enough writing judgment to know when the result is hollow. If AI compares products, we still need to understand which criteria matter to us. If AI acts, we need to retain the ability to recognize a boundary it should not have crossed.

What Do We Actually Want to Keep Choosing?

The obvious response to all of this is to defend human choice. But I am not convinced that every choice deserves defending. Comparing twelve washing machines is not a sacred exercise in free will. Modern life contains enormous quantities of low-value administrative thought: passwords, forms, appointment windows, renewals, return policies, price comparisons, delivery coordination, and inbox triage. If AI removes that burden, it can increase human agency rather than diminish it.

The difficult part is that low-value choices and identity-forming choices are not separated by a clean line. Buying socks is probably trivial. Choosing where to live is not. But between them sits most of everyday life: what we eat, how we spend weekends, which news we encounter, which hobbies we continue, which purchases we postpone, which friends we make time for. Repeated small decisions are part of the texture from which a life is built.

So perhaps the real design problem is not maximizing automation. It is deciding where friction is worth preserving. We may want almost zero friction around changing a delivery time and considerable friction around sending a message that could end a relationship. We may want an agent to prepare three investment options but not choose one. We may want it to draft a medical question but never decide that a symptom does not require a doctor.

I suspect good personal agents will eventually need something like a moral map of permission: not only what they can technically do, but what kinds of decisions the user wants to remain consciously present for. The machine will need a model not just of our preferences, but of our preferred relationship to our own preferences.

Will We Trust AI? I Think That’s the Wrong Question

I think we will trust AI in many domains, but that answer is almost meaningless on its own. We already trust machines constantly: elevators, card networks, spam filters, navigation software, recommendation systems. What matters is not abstract trust. It is calibrated trust — trust matched to stakes, reversibility, visibility, evidence, and the cost of failure.

That is why the healthiest future may not look like an agent that never asks permission or one that asks permission for everything. Constant confirmation can become its own failure mode; when every action produces another approval box, attention turns into ritual clicking. that experienced Claude Code users enabled broad auto-approval more often while also interrupting the agent more often, suggesting a shift from approving every microscopic step toward intervening when something actually looked wrong. In a , Anthropic noted that users approved 93% of permission prompts in Claude Code, illustrating how repeated confirmations can create approval fatigue.

HackerNoon contributors have made a related argument about : if every action requires approval, supervision can degrade into ritual rubber-stamping rather than meaningful control.

Consumer agents will need their own version of that balance. The safest relationship may be neither obedience nor independence, but negotiated autonomy: act freely inside well-understood boundaries, slow down around irreversible actions, expose uncertainty when it matters, and make it easy for the human to inspect and reverse what happened.

And this returns me to the psychological question. We may think we are deciding how much to trust AI, while the more important process is happening in reverse: repeated convenience is teaching us what no longer feels worth deciding ourselves.

The Quiet Change I Think We Should Watch

There was a time when “just Google it” sounded like a remarkable promise. Then it became infrastructure. We stopped noticing that it had changed memory, social habits, expertise, shopping, travel, and even the way an unanswered question feels. AI is crossing the same threshold, but the shift is deeper: search changed how we reach information; generative AI changes how much interpretation happens before the information reaches us; agents will change how much action happens after the answer.

What unsettles me is not the idea that AI will suddenly take control of everyday life. It is the opposite: that it will become good enough at thousands of tiny tasks that handing them over feels obviously rational, one by one. No dramatic surrender. No single day when we decide to stop choosing. Just a growing collection of decisions that no longer seem worth the effort.

Some of that will be liberation. I would happily live with less scheduling, less paperwork, fewer comparison tables, and fewer hours spent coordinating services that should have been simple. But not all friction is waste. Sometimes friction is where judgment is built, where a preference becomes visible, or where we notice that the thing we usually choose is no longer the thing we actually want.

So the question I keep coming back to is not “How intelligent will AI become?” It is more personal: which parts of my life do I still want to be present for, even when a machine could handle them better? I am not sure I know where I would draw that line yet. That uncertainty may be the point — we should probably decide it before convenience decides it for us.

If I let AI make decisions for me, am I also giving it the power to shape who I become — or to prevent me from becoming someone different?

items.title: Building MCP Servers for My Own Products: Introducing the Workflow
items.author: sammii
items.content:
I used to manage my products through dashboards. Check analytics here, schedule posts there, pull metrics from another tab. Constant context-switching.

Now, I do all of it by talking to Claude.

Not through some hacked-together integration: through MCP servers I built for my own products. Model Context Protocol is the standard Anthropic published for giving AI assistants structured access to external tools. I built servers for both Spellcast and Lunary. Here's how, and why it changed everything.

What MCP actually is (in one paragraph).

MCP is a protocol that lets you define a set of "tools", which are functions with typed inputs and outputs that Claude can call during a conversation. Instead of copy-pasting data into a chat window, Claude calls your API directly and works with the live result.

The architecture: your MCP server exposes tools over stdio (or HTTP). Claude Code discovers them and can call them when relevant. You write the server once; it works in any MCP-compatible client.

Spellcast is my social scheduling platform. The MCP server exposes the full API as typed tools:

server.addTool({
  name: 'list_posts',
  description: 'List scheduled, published, draft, or failed posts with optional filters',
  parameters: z.object({
    account_set_id: z.string().optional(),
    status: z.enum(['draft', 'scheduled', 'published', 'failed']).optional(),
    limit: z.number().default(50),
  }),
  execute: async ({ account_set_id, status, limit }) => {
    const posts = await db.query.posts.findMany({
      where: buildWhereClause({ account_set_id, status }),
      limit,
    });
    return posts;
  },
});

What I can do from a Claude conversation:

  • : see everything in the queue
  • : schedule new content
  • : edit scheduled posts
  • : push articles to Dev.to and Hashnode
  • : pull engagement data
  • / : manage AI personas
  • : create post variations using my brand voice
  • : manage posting personas

The practical workflow: I describe what I want, and Claude calls the tools. "Optimize the hooks on my scheduled tweets" becomes Claude reading every post, identifying weak openers, and rewriting them in batches.

Lunary is my astrology platform. The MCP exposes product analytics and content tools:

server.addTool({
  name: 'get_dashboard',
  description: 'Get key product metrics: MAU, MRR, retention, feature usage',
  parameters: z.object({}),
  execute: async () => {
    const metrics = await getProductMetrics();
    return metrics;
  },
});
  • : MAU, MRR, retention at a glance
  • : engagement breakdown
  • : which parts of the app people actually use
  • : how well I'm holding users over time
  • : search the 2,000+ article content library
  • : patterns Claude surfaces from the data
  • : identify at-risk users

What the workflow actually looks like

"Check Lunary metrics and tell me what's changed since last week."

Claude calls , , . Returns a summary. Surfaces what moved.

"Schedule a thread about the SEO growth for the sammii account."

Claude calls to find the right persona, to load my voice profile, to write five thread variations, presents them, waits for my pick, then calls to schedule it.

"Those tweets from February with weak hooks, fix them."

Claude calls for the date range, reads each one, identifies weak openers, writes improvements, calls in batches.

No dashboards. No tab-switching. Just conversation with full product access.

npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk zod
import { McpServer } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js';
import { StdioServerTransport } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js';
import { z } from 'zod';

const server = new McpServer({ name: 'my-product', version: '1.0.0' });

server.tool(
  'get_stats',
  'Get product statistics',
  {},
  async () => {
    const stats = await fetchMyProductStats();
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: JSON.stringify(stats) }] };
  }
);

const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
await server.connect(transport);

Wire it into Claude Code's settings:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-product": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/my-mcp/dist/index.js"]
    }
  }
}

Your product's API is now accessible from any Claude conversation.

Why it matters for solo founders.

The power isn't just convenience. Claude can operate across your entire product context in a single conversation: read your analytics, read your content queue, read your brand voice, and produce work that's coherent across all of them without you manually bridging the gap.

I estimate MCP saves me 5-8 hours a week in dashboard time and manual data-pulling.

More importantly, it removes the friction that stops small tasks from getting done. If checking metrics requires three tabs and a copy-paste, you do it less. If it's one sentence, you do it constantly and catch things early.

items.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code.
 
"An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell.

items.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”
