items.title: Google Will Launch Android App Verification Requirement Globally In January 2027
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon.
 
The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won't be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.
 
In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it's not wasting any time with the January start. It says that verification will reach all devices within "several months." So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with "millions" of non-Play apps already registered. The company says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

items.title: International Men’s Day: Anthropic IPOs, Trump Meets Putin and Xi, and GTA 6 Is Released
items.author: Hyperbole
items.content:
Three of the world’s most powerful men meet to discuss nuclear weapons. An artificial intelligence company raises more money in a single IPO than most countries spend on technology. And millions of men finally get to steal fictional cars in Vice City.

Happy International Men’s Day.

  • Trump, Xi, and Putin meet
  • “$80+ to play”
  • Anthropic + world leaders: “AI chips discussed”
  • “Men doing stupid shit”

And in the center: November 19, 2026.

Someone in our HackerNoon Slack channel pointed out the final coincidence: it’s International Men’s Day.

The joke is funny enough on its own. But the more you investigate the actual news, the stranger the connections become.

Elon Musk thinks AI might eventually generate games like GTA without traditional developers. Anthropic’s CEO believes advanced AI chips should be kept away from China. Trump thinks whoever wins the race to superintelligence wins everything. Meanwhile, the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers are discussing how not to destroy civilization.

And Rockstar Games has just released a video game about committing crimes.

Let’s examine this particularly remarkable day in the history of men.

1. Anthropic Goes Public: $83 to Play

The offering comprised 980 million shares, representing approximately $81.34 billion in gross proceeds before expenses and excluding any additional shares sold through the underwriters’ option.

Not all of that money goes to Anthropic. Approximately 23.6 million shares were being sold by existing stockholders.

Nevertheless, it was an extraordinary amount of money.

When Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on November 19, shares opened at $111.50.

That’s approximately 34% above the IPO price.

The $83 price also happens to be almost identical to the price of GTA VI.

For approximately $80, Rockstar gives you a fictional world where you can do almost anything.

For $83, Anthropic gives eligible IPO investors a tiny ownership stake in a company trying to build artificial intelligence that might eventually do almost anything.

Dario Amodei’s Very Expensive Experiment

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has spent years arguing that increasingly powerful artificial intelligence could fundamentally transform society.

Now public investors get to bet on that argument.

“I don’t think we really believed it until it actually happened.”

His sister, Anthropic cofounder and president Daniela Amodei, characterized the IPO as another milestone rather than the destination:

“it’s like one stop on the journey, right?”

The company has also warned investors that its commitments to AI safety may sometimes conflict with maximizing profits.

That creates an interesting question.

What happens when shareholders want Anthropic to make more money, but Anthropic’s leadership believes making more money would create unacceptable risks?

Senator Elizabeth Warren has already raised concerns about exposing investors and retirement savings to the risks surrounding advanced AI.

In a statement ahead of the offering, she argued:

“The SEC must protect investors and Congress must act quickly to put in place safeguards on advanced AI development.”

The broader contradiction is difficult to ignore.

Anthropic was founded partly because its creators believed advanced AI required extraordinary caution.

Now it is participating in one of the largest financial spectacles in stock-market history.

Apparently, protecting humanity is extremely capital-intensive.

2. Trump, Xi, and Putin Meet: Three Men Discuss Whether Humanity Should Continue Existing

While Anthropic was making financial history in New York, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin were making diplomatic history in Shenzhen, China.

The three leaders held an unprecedented trilateral summit on November 19 during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering.

“We are really making history.”

Xi described the gathering as a historic opportunity for cooperation.

Putin emphasized that the three countries shared interests in resolving regional conflicts, including Ukraine.

There is something extraordinary about three men collectively representing such enormous military and economic power sitting around a table to discuss whether they can trust one another.

Especially when you read what they actually said.

Trump Explains Nuclear Weapons

During the summit, Trump offered a remarkably straightforward explanation of why nuclear disarmament is difficult.

“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them.”

“It’s very hard to give them up as the leader of a country.”

Both observations are broadly correct.

They are also the sort of statements that sound like a man explaining why he still has a garage full of things he purchased fifteen years ago.

Except the garage contains nuclear warheads.

Trump also praised Shenzhen, telling the gathering:

“They have a major city, one of the biggest cities anywhere in the world, and it’s flawless.”

The president of the United States was discussing global security while also delivering what sounded like a five-star hotel review.

Trump Calls Putin His Friend

Before the trilateral meeting, Trump greeted Putin warmly.

“Who is he? He is my friend.”

He also praised their longstanding relationship.

That friendship is politically consequential, given Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine and the enormous disagreements between Washington and Moscow.

Trump’s remarks illustrate the central tension of the summit: personal relationships between leaders are being presented as a potential route toward resolving conflicts involving millions of people.

Whether those relationships produce meaningful agreements remains another question.

What Did the Three Men Actually Agree On?

The leaders endorsed a declaration emphasizing the importance of reducing nuclear risks.

One of its central principles was that:

“a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”

That’s a worthwhile statement.

It is also a principle the major nuclear powers have endorsed before.

The declaration did not establish a specific schedule for eliminating nuclear weapons, end the war in Ukraine, or resolve the major strategic disagreements among the three countries.

The world’s most powerful men agreed that peace is good.

Humanity will now wait to see what they do about it.

3. The Anthropic–Trump–Xi Connection: Whoever Controls the AI Chips Controls the Future

The overlap between Anthropic’s IPO and the international summit is arguably the most important part of the meme.

Advanced artificial intelligence requires enormous computing resources.

Those resources depend heavily on sophisticated semiconductors, including Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

And access to those chips has become a central dispute between the United States and China.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been particularly outspoken about this issue.

“Export controls serve a vital purpose: keeping democratic nations at the forefront of AI development.”

His argument is that restricting access to advanced computing hardware can help preserve America’s technological advantage.

China, unsurprisingly, sees restrictions on access to advanced technology rather differently.

Trump Has a Three-Letter Theory of the Future

During his visit to China, Trump discussed the competition to develop superintelligence.

His summary was characteristically direct:

“And whoever wins SI wins.”

SI refers to superintelligence: artificial intelligence that exceeds human capabilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks.

Trump’s statement captures the geopolitical stakes in six words.

It also raises an obvious question.

The economy? Military superiority? Scientific progress? Control over the future?

At APEC, Trump also rejected international restrictions that could constrain American AI development.

As ⁠ABC News reported, Trump opposed what he called globalist regulation of advanced AI.

Meanwhile, Xi emphasized international cooperation and human oversight.

The Chinese government’s account of his position called for countries to:

“ensure that AI is always under human control”

These competing positions reveal a remarkable situation.

The United States wants to maintain its lead in artificial intelligence.

China wants greater access to advanced computing and a meaningful role in setting global rules.

Anthropic wants to develop increasingly capable AI while maintaining its safety commitments.

Nvidia wants to sell computing hardware.

And investors want all of these companies to make money.

These objectives are not necessarily compatible.

Yet they are increasingly shaping the same global economy.

4. GTA VI Arrives: $79.99 to Play

While world leaders were discussing nuclear weapons and investors were buying shares in Anthropic, Rockstar Games finally released Grand Theft Auto VI.

The game is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

Its standard edition costs $79.99 in the United States.

That is $3.01 less than Anthropic’s IPO price.

Unlike an Anthropic share, however, the game comes with an entire fictional criminal economy.

Players return to Vice City and the fictional state of Leonida, following the story of Jason and Lucia.

It has been more than thirteen years since Grand Theft Auto V arrived in September 2013.

Rockstar delayed GTA VI several times before settling on November 19, 2026.

“these extra months will allow us to finish the game with the level of polish you have come to expect and deserve.”

Apparently, building a realistic simulation of American criminality takes longer than building some forms of artificial intelligence.

GTA VI Is Also a Financial Event

Rockstar’s parent company, Take-Two Interactive, is publicly traded.

Its CEO, Strauss Zelnick, has repeatedly emphasized the enormous commercial significance of GTA VI.

Ahead of the release, he predicted:

“a lot of people will be calling in sick on November 19”

That is a remarkable prediction from the CEO of a publicly traded company.

Imagine Anthropic’s CEO announcing that the company’s next AI model would cause millions of employees to stop showing up for work.

Actually, that’s not too far from what some people in the AI industry have been predicting.

Take-Two previously forecast approximately $8 billion to $8.2 billion in net bookings for fiscal 2027.

Those figures cover the company’s broader business, not just GTA VI.

Nevertheless, they demonstrate the scale of the expectations surrounding the launch.

5. Elon Musk Thinks AI Could Make GTA VI Obsolete

The connections become even stranger when Elon Musk enters the story.

Musk has repeatedly argued that generative artificial intelligence will eventually transform video game development.

The central idea is simple.

Instead of spending years and billions of dollars building a game, developers might eventually describe the world they want and let AI generate it.

In January 2026, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch suggested:

“There’s definitely a non-zero chance we get ‘generate your own GTA 6 in a few minutes’ before GTA 6.”

Musk’s response was brief:

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney also entertained the possibility of AI-generated games.

The broader discussion concerned whether systems capable of generating images, video, and software could eventually generate entire interactive worlds.

That possibility would fundamentally change the economics of the video game industry.

Rockstar has spent more than a decade building GTA VI.

An AI system that could generate comparable experiences in minutes would represent an extraordinary technological achievement.

But generating a playable environment is not the same as creating a coherent, polished game with compelling characters, sophisticated systems, and a consistent artistic vision.

GTA VI is a particularly useful test case because its value depends on more than the number of buildings, vehicles, or characters an AI could generate.

It depends on how all those pieces work together.

Take-Two’s CEO Has Questions for Musk

Zelnick has also challenged sweeping claims about artificial intelligence replacing human workers.

Responding to Musk’s predictions about automation, Zelnick reportedly asked:

“If AI was going to take anyone’s job, wouldn’t it take his job?”

“Maybe Elon Musk is indeed a simulation, it’s possible.”

The exchange illustrates a disagreement that extends well beyond video games.

Musk believes increasingly capable AI could dramatically reduce the need for human labor.

Zelnick runs a company whose most important product depends on thousands of people coordinating their creative and technical work over many years.

Both men have enormous financial interests in their respective visions of the future.

And both are discussing a technology that could transform the businesses they operate.

On International Men’s Day, the argument is particularly appropriate.

One billionaire thinks AI might eventually generate the work of another billionaire’s employees.

The other billionaire wonders why the first billionaire still needs to work.

There is a deeper connection between Anthropic and GTA VI.

Both companies are building systems that simulate aspects of the world.

Rockstar builds a fictional environment with characters, vehicles, economies, police departments, and social systems.

Anthropic develops AI systems designed to understand and interact with the real world through language, software, and other tools.

The distinction is enormous.

GTA VI’s characters exist inside a fictional world.

Claude’s outputs can influence decisions outside the computer.

But both businesses depend on the ability to represent increasingly complex aspects of human behavior.

The comparison becomes more interesting when considering the economics.

Rockstar spends years developing a world that millions of people will pay to enter.

Anthropic spends billions developing intelligence that businesses hope will make work more efficient.

Rockstar wants people to spend more time inside its product.

Anthropic’s customers often want to spend less time completing tasks.

One sells an escape from reality.

The other sells a tool for changing reality.

And on November 19, 2026, both are asking consumers and investors to pay approximately $80 for a piece of the future.

7. The Most Expensive Game Is the One the World Leaders Are Playing

The final overlap in the Venn diagram reads:

It is attached to GTA VI and the Trump–Xi–Putin summit.

Grand Theft Auto is a video game built around criminal activity, reckless driving, violence, and increasingly elaborate ways to behave badly.

International diplomacy, meanwhile, involves leaders making decisions with consequences for millions or billions of people.

The difference is that GTA VI has a reset button.

There is also a revealing contrast in how the two events are evaluated.

Rockstar’s success will be measured through sales, reviews, player engagement, and the quality of its game.

The summit’s success will be measured through changes in international relations, nuclear risks, military conflicts, and economic cooperation.

Rockstar can release a patch when something goes wrong.

World leaders do not have that luxury.

Perhaps the most absurd part of the day is that the fictional criminal world might offer a more predictable set of rules than the real geopolitical one.

8. International Men’s Day Was Supposed to Be About Something Else

November 19 is International Men’s Day.

The observance was established to recognize positive male role models, celebrate men’s contributions to families and communities, and raise awareness of issues affecting men’s health and well-being.

Its stated objectives include recognizing:

“everyday, working-class men who are living decent, honest lives.”

Those men are largely absent from the Venn diagram.

There are no circles for fathers taking their children to school.

No circles for men caring for aging parents.

No circles for teachers, nurses, construction workers, or friends helping one another through difficult times.

Instead, the world’s attention is focused on billionaires, presidents, nuclear weapons, artificial intelligence, and a video game about stealing cars.

There is something appropriate about that.

International Men’s Day is partly about recognizing the positive things men contribute to society.

The day’s biggest headlines offer an unusually vivid illustration of how much power men still exercise over its future.

Some of that power produces extraordinary technological achievements.

Some produces entertainment enjoyed by millions.

And some creates risks that everyone else must live with.

The International Men’s Day organizers have emphasized that improving men’s lives benefits society more broadly.

That is a more useful principle than treating masculinity as a competition to accumulate the most money, military power, or technological influence.

There are also important women in these stories.

Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei helped lead the company to its public-market debut.

GTA VI features Lucia Caminos as one of its two protagonists.

And the consequences of decisions made by the three presidents in Shenzhen will affect women and men alike.

The Venn diagram is funny because it compresses three enormous stories into one ridiculous coincidence.

But the stories are connected by something more consequential than their shared date.

They are all about who gets to control the future.

Anthropic wants to build increasingly powerful artificial intelligence.

Trump, Xi, and Putin want to shape the international rules under which that technology develops.

Rockstar wants to create a fictional world so compelling that millions of people will voluntarily disappear into it.

And ordinary people are left trying to figure out what all of this means for their lives.

Happy International Men’s Day.

And if he doesn’t answer, don’t rule out Vice City.

items.title: Jensen Huang Chinese Revenue, Affairs, Resignation, and Case for CEO Reinstatement Timeline
items.author: Cyber Espionage
items.content:
The first NVIDIA earnings call after Jensen Huang’s departure opened with the answer to a question Silicon Valley had spent the weekend asking. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” chair Harvey Jones said. Earlier that day, Huang had said he would be “honored” to return if the board decided it was in the best interest of shareholders and employees. Then interim CEO Colette Kress got to the numbers. NVIDIA had just booked $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, including $11.05 billion from direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong. NVIDIA’s decision on reinstatement · Jensen Huang’s comeback statement · NVIDIA’s geographic revenue disclosure

A third number came out on the call. NVIDIA sold $2.4 billion of licensed Hopper data-center products to China in the quarter. Kress said those shipments had stopped and the company’s next-quarter guidance excluded them. The economics get harder to trace when a Chinese business rents computing power abroad or when NVIDIA hardware reaches an end user through intermediaries. Licensed Hopper sales and the shipment halt · NVIDIA’s definition of indirect customers

How much revenue does NVIDIA get from China?

NVIDIA used to assign revenue geographically by the address on the bill. In Q3 FY2026 it switched to the headquarters of the direct customer and recast earlier figures. A company can be invoiced in Singapore, be headquartered elsewhere, take delivery in Malaysia, and rent computing capacity to a business in China. Each is a different fact about the transaction. NVIDIA’s newer tables answer the headquarters question. The older ones answer the billing question. FY2025 billing geography · FY2026 geographic reporting change

On a comparable headquarters basis, China and Hong Kong revenue fell in FY2026, then rose year over year in the first nine months of FY2027. The region’s share of total revenue still fell over those nine months because NVIDIA’s overall business grew faster. The geography line covers multiple product categories, while Kress’s $2.4 billion figure describes licensed Hopper data-center products specifically. Adding the latter to the former would mix two views of overlapping sales. NVIDIA’s annual geographic comparisons · NVIDIA’s nine-month revenue comparisons · Kress on licensed Hopper sales

Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the money beyond the China line

Singapore’s $23.684 billion was a billing figure. Singapore accounted for about 18% of FY2025 revenue on the old basis, up from $6.831 billion the year before. NVIDIA said shipments to Singapore amounted to less than 2% of FY2025 company revenue and explained that customers used the country to centralize invoicing. The filing gives no destination breakdown for the difference. The new headquarters tables group Singapore into a broader geography presentation. They provide no standalone Singapore line and no end-user reconciliation. The same issue runs in the opposite direction in Taiwan. NVIDIA estimated that 76% of FY2026 Data Center revenue from Taiwan-headquartered customers was attributable to U.S. and European end customers. Singapore revenue and shipment footnote · Taiwan end-customer estimate and new geography table

The larger numbers measure different things. The $4.8 billion figure carried in the original timeline describes equipment reportedly bought by a Megaspeed-linked Malaysian company over a specified period. The Information’s figure, as reported by Reuters, was an estimate of chips allegedly shipped to Chinese firms through a broader network. Those figures can cover overlapping hardware, different windows, and different points in the supply chain. A customs value can include server components and reseller markups. A cloud rental is revenue to the provider, even when Chinese demand helped justify the provider’s original NVIDIA hardware purchase. NVIDIA’s filings provide no defensible dollar total for that indirect exposure. HackerNoon’s equipment purchase timeline · Reuters on the reported $7.5 billion shipment estimate · NVIDIA’s direct and indirect customer definitions

Indonesia had an enforcement lead of its own. The Straits Times reported that Indonesian police inspected a Megaspeed subsidiary earlier in 2026 and found empty server racks. The report attributed suspicions about where hardware went to an unnamed official. Malaysia separately said it was checking the status of advanced chips imported by Speedmatrix. Reuters reported that Megaspeed also had subsidiaries in Thailand, Australia, and the United States. A corporate presence gives investigators a place to look. A sale, re-export, or cloud rental still needs a transaction record. Indonesia’s reported Megaspeed inspection · Malaysia’s Speedmatrix statement · Reuters on Megaspeed’s overseas subsidiaries

The new U.S. rule goes after access as well as shipments. The rule effective November 19 adds license requirements for covered advanced chips in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. It also addresses certain overseas data centers providing significant computing capacity to entities headquartered or ultimately parented in covered jurisdictions. Inclusion on the list reflects the scope of the regulation. It supplies no historical revenue figure for any country. November 19 advanced-chip and remote-access rule

November 2015 — 7Road International incorporates in Singapore

The entity that became Megaspeed starts as 7Road International, associated with the Chinese gaming company 7Road. This is the start of the corporate paper trail. The people and facilities later associated with the cloud business enter the picture years later. 7Road International’s Singapore incorporation

March 2023 — Megaspeed takes its name and Alice Huang joins

December 7, 2023 — The Huangs are photographed at a dinner in Singapore

Early 2024 — Another reported encounter and the Malaysian subsidiary

TechCrunch reported an early-2024 meeting at an NVIDIA event, and dated photos surfaced from Computex that June. The New York Times traced the establishment of Speedmatrix to early 2024, giving Megaspeed a Malaysian entity through which it could buy and install equipment. Reported early NVIDIA event · Speedmatrix’s formation in Malaysia

June 7, 2024 — A bar in Taipei

Parker Schmitt, a tech executive who was there, recalled Alice Huang telling the group, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here.” He came to the bar and joined them for a drink. Photos put the two in the same place during Computex. The timing of any romance or alleged intelligence recruitment remains unresolved. The Taipei bar account and Computex photographs

Commerce later said proactive monitoring detected suspicious activity and that the department opened an export-control investigation in 2024. The public statement gives the year. It leaves the opening date unspecified, so the probe cannot be placed precisely before or after the Taipei encounter. U.S. Commerce and Justice investigation chronology

August 28, 2024 — Huang sells the Blackwell ramp

In a Bloomberg interview after earnings, Huang talked about demand for the forthcoming Blackwell platform. The interview belongs in the public business timeline because Blackwell was about to become crucial to the overseas data-center buildout. His public pitch centered on product demand. Jensen Huang’s Bloomberg interview on Blackwell demand

2025 | Export limits, a second Taipei encounter, and a no-sell list

February 2025 — Singapore starts its own server investigation

Singapore police and customs open an inquiry involving Megaspeed, other companies, and individuals over possible false declarations in purchases of servers. Singapore says it initiated this probe independently and that it concerned potential domestic offenses. U.S. Commerce was already looking into possible export-control violations under a different legal framework. Singapore Police and Customs investigation · U.S. Megaspeed investigation

February 26, 2025 — NVIDIA discloses the Singapore billing gap

NVIDIA’s annual filing reports $17.108 billion billed to customers in China and Hong Kong and $23.684 billion billed to customers in Singapore for FY2025. It also explains how little hardware ships to Singapore relative to the size of the billing line. Later reports often cite the 18% figure without its most important noun, . NVIDIA’s FY2025 geographic revenue and shipments

April 9–15, 2025 — Washington requires H20 export licenses

NVIDIA says the U.S. informed it on April 9 of a new license requirement for H20 sales to China and certain other destinations, then said on April 14 the requirement would remain in effect indefinitely. NVIDIA disclosed the change on April 15 and estimated charges of up to $5.5 billion. H20 was a product built for a market already subject to U.S. restrictions. NVIDIA’s H20 export-control disclosure

U.S. investigators request records for both direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed, according to the Justice Department’s later account. The distinction reached beyond NVIDIA’s own invoices. Intermediaries and system integrators could be involved even when NVIDIA did not invoice the company receiving the servers. Commerce’s records request for Megaspeed sales

May 17, 2025 — Huang says there is no evidence of AI chip diversion

The original timeline dates this Bloomberg exchange to May 17. Huang said there was “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” The record request announced later establishes that investigators were looking at Megaspeed that month. The public chronology leaves the day of the request and what Huang personally knew at the interview unresolved. Huang’s 2025 remarks on chip diversion · The public dates of the U.S. investigation

May 21, 2025 — Huang calls the export controls a failure

Speaking at Computex, he called the restrictions “a failure,” arguing they gave Chinese companies a reason to develop alternatives to U.S. chips. That was Huang’s public industrial-policy argument. NVIDIA would keep making versions of it when Washington considered which products to license. Huang’s Computex remarks on U.S. chip controls

May 22, 2025 — Alice Huang and Jensen Huang attend a private dinner

Taipei video reviewed by Reuters shows the two at a private dinner. Contemporary footage and subsequent accounts place Alice Huang at the event about a year after the bar encounter. The two sightings provide public dates for their association. The first public admission of infidelity would come in November 2026. Reuters on the Taipei dinner footage · HackerNoon’s Computex dinner timeline

May 28, 2025 — NVIDIA puts a price on the H20 restriction

NVIDIA records a charge related to H20 inventory and purchase obligations. It says it sold in H20 products in fiscal Q1 before the new requirement and was unable to ship another during that quarter. The sales, the unshipped orders, and the accounting charge tell three different parts of the same story. NVIDIA’s H20 sales and inventory charge

June 2025 — NVIDIA puts Megaspeed on its no-sell list

Commerce and Justice later say NVIDIA put Megaspeed on its internal “no sell” list in June. That action matters when reading the company’s later public descriptions of Megaspeed as an ordinary cloud business. An internal sales restriction and a federal Entity List designation have different scopes. The agencies’ statement leaves the treatment of individual affiliate and reseller transactions unspecified. U.S. confirmation of NVIDIA’s Megaspeed no-sell decision

June 24, 2025 — U.S. and Singapore investigators interview Alice Huang

July 7, 2025 — Singapore asks for help getting records

Singapore police and prosecutors tell U.S. authorities that server supplier Supermicro has provided limited cooperation, according to Singapore’s later account. Singapore says it made repeated requests for assistance from September onward. Those requests show how much of the investigation depended on evidence held outside the country where Megaspeed was incorporated. Singapore’s requests for U.S. investigative assistance

July 14, 2025 — NVIDIA announces a route back for H20

NVIDIA says the U.S. government has assured it that licenses would be granted and that it hopes to start H20 deliveries again. Huang was in China after meeting U.S. officials in Washington. An assurance and a license can precede a sale by months. The company’s subsequent filings show how much business actually cleared. NVIDIA’s July H20 China announcement

July 2025 — Malaysia adds its own permit requirement

Malaysia says exports, transit, and transshipment of covered U.S.-origin high-performance AI chips require a strategic trade permit. That placed a domestic enforcement requirement on activity out of Malaysia while U.S. authorities were investigating the disposition of NVIDIA hardware. Malaysia’s July 2025 advanced-chip permit notice

August 2025 — The proposed 15% arrangement

NVIDIA says U.S. officials expressed an expectation that the government would receive 15% of revenue from licensed H20 sales to China. Its August quarterly filing says the government had yet to publish a regulation codifying the expectation. That number belongs to the policy negotiations. It should stay off the revenue table. NVIDIA’s filing on the proposed 15% H20 arrangement

August 30, 2025 — Megaspeed’s stated date for Alice Huang’s departure

Megaspeed supplied this date publicly in November 2026, saying she had no current role with the company. Earlier reporting and official statements described her as a controller or CEO during earlier periods. The departure date is the company’s account and was disclosed well after the fact. Megaspeed’s statement on Alice Huang’s departure

September 26, 2025 — Huang calls China’s chip industry “nanoseconds behind”

October 9, 2025 — The New York Times publishes its first Megaspeed investigation

October 14, 2025 — Huang says market share went from 95% to zero

November 5, 2025 — “China is going to win the AI race”

Huang made the remark at the Financial Times’ Future of AI Summit and later qualified it, stressing that the U.S. lead depended on moving quickly. His argument linked the fight for AI market share to how easily rivals could build and power data centers. Huang’s remarks at the Financial Times AI summit

November 2025 — Singapore disappears as a standalone line

NVIDIA switches its geographic revenue presentation to direct-customer headquarters in Q3 FY2026 and recasts previous periods. FY2025 China and Hong Kong revenue becomes on that basis, up from on the old billing basis for the same fiscal year. The difference reflects a change in geographic attribution for the same recorded sales. The filings provide no customer-by-customer bridge between the two figures. NVIDIA’s explanation of its geographic accounting change

December 2025 — Trump opens a conditional path for H200 sales

Trump announces that H200 sales to approved Chinese customers would be allowed under an agreement with NVIDIA. A Commerce rule in January put qualifying applications on a case-by-case footing. The policy applied to a defined set of products and customers, subject to security conditions. The H200 export announcement · Commerce’s January licensing rule

December 22, 2025 — Bloomberg puts a multibillion-dollar figure on Megaspeed

Bloomberg reports that Malaysian and Indonesian customs records show at least in NVIDIA hardware imports by Megaspeed. NVIDIA describes Megaspeed as offering “a cloud service permitted under the export control rules.” Hardware moving across a border and a customer renting compute from hardware installed abroad present different regulatory questions. Both matter to the ongoing inquiry. Bloomberg’s Megaspeed customs records and NVIDIA response

January–October 2026 | H200 licenses, intelligence reports, and a public denial

January 15, 2026 — Case-by-case H200 reviews take effect

February 2026 — Singapore warns Alice Huang and bars her re-entry

Singapore later says prosecutors and police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang committed offenses involving the suspected inaccurate server declarations. Police concluded that she had knowingly given inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed, issued her a warning, and barred her from re-entering the country. The ministry expressly said its investigation concerned potential domestic offenses and did not investigate her for espionage. Singapore’s findings on Alice Huang

February 25, 2026 — NVIDIA discloses $19.677 billion in annual China and Hong Kong revenue

On the new geography basis, China and Hong Kong account for 9.1% of FY2026 company revenue, down from 19.2% on the recast prior-year basis. That fall takes place while worldwide sales rise from $130.497 billion to $215.938 billion. NVIDIA FY2026 annual results and recast China revenue

March 17, 2026 — Huang says Chinese customers have placed H200 orders

March 19, 2026 — U.S. prosecutors bring a separate server diversion case

Federal prosecutors in New York charge three people with conspiring to divert U.S. AI technology to China through a Southeast Asian intermediary. The allegations concerned servers with advanced NVIDIA chips and a separate set of defendants. The case brings concrete allegations about how physical diversion can occur, with responsibility to be determined in court. Justice Department’s March AI server diversion charges

Elizabeth Warren and Jim Banks ask Commerce about NVIDIA’s knowledge of chip diversion and whether Huang’s public statements misled officials. They point back to his May 2025 remarks and to the new criminal charges involving advanced servers. Their letter asks for an investigation and answers from Commerce. Warren and Banks’ March letter on chip diversion

Spring 2026 — A classified memo reportedly reaches senior U.S. officials

The New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw preparation of a classified memo about the relationship and the intelligence concerns. As Reuters summarized the reporting, the memo warned senior Trump administration officials about Jensen Huang’s proximity to Alice Huang. The underlying intelligence and a public account of any information actually transferred were still unavailable. Reporting on the classified memo · The New York Times’ initial intelligence report

April 15, 2026 — Huang tells Dwarkesh Patel why he wants China on the NVIDIA stack

“The day that DeepSeek comes out on Huawei first, that is a horrible outcome for our nation,” Huang said. His argument was that developers who build around a rival’s hardware make that hardware more valuable over time. The podcast transcript is dated , several months earlier than the August placement in the original HackerNoon timeline. Dwarkesh Patel’s Jensen Huang interview and transcript

April 26, 2026 — China and Hong Kong revenue finishes the quarter at $4.55 billion

NVIDIA will report from direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong and globally. The China line was in the equivalent quarter a year earlier. This is the low point among the first three FY2027 quarters disclosed by November. NVIDIA’s Q1 FY2027 geographic revenue

May 13, 2026 — A short seller scrutinizes Megaspeed as Huang joins the China delegation

Culper Research releases a report questioning NVIDIA’s China exposure and describing the Jensen Huang–Alice Huang relationship as “uncomfortably close.” Culper held a short position and stood to benefit if NVIDIA shares fell. Separately, Reuters reported that Trump added Jensen Huang to the U.S. delegation traveling to Beijing. The short seller’s estimates and the diplomatic trip belong to the same date, with distinct sources. Culper’s NVIDIA report and position disclosure · Reuters on Huang’s addition to the Beijing delegation

June 1, 2026 — Senators press the board on export oversight

A letter to NVIDIA cites Huang’s public remarks about diversion and China market share, a recent indictment, and the Culper estimate. The authors ask whether the board’s controls give it meaningful oversight of where advanced hardware goes. The short seller’s estimate remains an allegation even when lawmakers cite it. June congressional letter on NVIDIA export compliance

July 26, 2026 — China and Hong Kong revenue rises to $7.88 billion

NVIDIA closes its second fiscal quarter with from China and Hong Kong direct customers, up from in the prior-year quarter. Company revenue reaches . That puts the geography at 8.2% of sales on the headquarters basis. NVIDIA’s Q2 FY2027 China and Hong Kong data

September 14, 2026 — Trump calls into Huang’s All-In Summit appearance

Huang takes Trump’s call during a live recording. Reuters reported that the two discussed U.S. AI leadership and argued against slowing development. The exchange shows how publicly the two were aligned on accelerating AI development weeks before the intelligence story broke. Reuters on the All-In Summit call

October 8, 2026 — Trump presents Huang with the National Medal of Science

October 25, 2026 — NVIDIA closes a record quarter

The third quarter ends four days before the Times publishes the intelligence story. NVIDIA later reports that China and Hong Kong reached against a year earlier. The quarter captures the operating period before the resignation, even though Kress would present the results afterward. NVIDIA’s October-quarter geographic results

October 29, 2026 — The Times reports that U.S. officials suspected an intelligence operation

Huang describes NVIDIA’s dealings with Megaspeed as “normal and not unusual” and says the company checked whether the firm diverted chips. Bloomberg dates the published story October 30 in UTC and describes the interview as taking place Thursday, October 29. The account would sit alongside a different kind of statement from Huang ten days later. Huang’s Bloomberg interview about Megaspeed

October 31, 2026 — Singapore challenges an account of its investigation

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs disputes the way The Wall Street Journal characterized what it had said about Alice Huang and intelligence suspicions. It confirms that its Megaspeed investigation remains open. The ministry gives a fuller public account on November 12. Singapore’s response to The Wall Street Journal

November 4–13, 2026 | The admission, the other reports, and the resignation

November 4 — Three House chairs seek a closed-door briefing

Rick Crawford, Brian Mast, and John Moolenaar request information about NVIDIA’s security procedures and Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang. Their letter requests a November 18 briefing or an alternative date. That initial request was eventually superseded by the December interview schedule. The November 4 letter to Jensen Huang · The later House interview schedule

November 6 — The Financial Times reports that officials described a romantic relationship

November 8 — Jensen Huang tells NVIDIA employees he was unfaithful

November 8 — The board opens an independent investigation and backs Huang

The directors create an independent committee assisted by outside counsel. Their statement says the board has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised” and expresses confidence in Huang and his leadership team. This was the board’s stated assessment at the opening of the inquiry. NVIDIA board’s November 8 statement

November 9 — China disputes the espionage allegations and shareholders sue

November 10 — The board hires Joon H. Kim to investigate

NVIDIA’s independent directors retain Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, and Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. On the same day, The Information reports the broader alleged shipment estimate, as summarized by Reuters. The internal inquiry and the shipment estimate raise questions about what NVIDIA knew, when it knew it, and how its public statements were vetted. Independent directors’ announcement of Joon H. Kim · Reuters on the alleged shipment estimate

November 11 — The Times reports a relationship with Kimberly Powell

The Times cites five people who had worked at NVIDIA in reporting that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare and a direct report. “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” Huang reportedly told a Times reporter before ending the call. Powell did not respond to the paper’s request for comment, according to Axios. The relationship’s start and end dates remain uncertain. The reporting line makes the board’s question immediate. A CEO can influence a direct report’s assignments, evaluation, pay, and future in the organization. The New York Times’ November 11 account of the Powell allegation · Huang’s reported response to the Times · Axios on the November 11 report

November 11 — The board accepts the resignation

The SEC filing identifies November 11 as the effective date of Huang’s departure as president, CEO, and director. The board appoints Colette Kress interim CEO and keeps her in the CFO job. The director seat mattered independently of the executive role. Huang had spent 33 years leading the company he cofounded, and the filing records the end of his formal authority in all three positions. NVIDIA’s November 11 SEC resignation and succession record · NVIDIA’s CEO transition release

November 12 — NVIDIA makes the departure public

The company announces the transition and names longtime director Harvey C. Jones its first board chair. It says the search for a permanent CEO will look at internal and external candidates. Kress says she will build on “the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.” That public handover is why many accounts use November 12 for the resignation. NVIDIA CEO transition announcement · November 11 effective date in the SEC filing

November 12 — Reuters reports an allegation involving a second NVIDIA employee

Two people familiar with the matter tell Reuters Huang had an intimate relationship with another employee. Reuters withholds her name and says attempts to reach her were unsuccessful. NVIDIA declined to comment. Jensen Huang, Powell, and a board representative did not reply to requests for comment. The public report provides no beginning or end date and came after NVIDIA announced the departure. It is the third reported relationship in this chronology, following the Alice Huang and Powell accounts. Reuters report on the unnamed NVIDIA employee

November 12 — Singapore publishes its findings and the U.S. describes an open inquiry

Singapore publicizes its February warning and re-entry ban and says the Megaspeed investigation is ongoing. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche says the Justice Department had yet to reach a conclusion about Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence role and that the FBI was investigating. Those accounts cover different questions. Singapore describes its domestic server investigation, while U.S. officials describe continuing work on the intelligence allegation. Singapore’s November 12 findings · Reuters on Blanche and the FBI inquiry

November 13–19, 2026 | The campaign to bring Huang back

November 13–14 — Stand with Jensen makes three demands

The open letter asks the directors to reinstate Huang pending an independent investigation, give him a fair opportunity to respond, and explain the decision to employees and shareholders. Elon Musk says he is signing. Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan writes that “Jensen deserves due process.” Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney says he signed and had already seen someone else enter his name. That makes the distinction between endorsements made by identifiable people and the site’s self-reported tally particularly important. Stand with Jensen open letter · Musk, Tan, and Sweeney’s public posts

November 13–14 — Two investors ask the board to keep the door open

Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker write to the directors urging them to avoid rushing a permanent appointment and to keep Huang in consideration while facts emerge, The Information reports. Their firms held about 10.6 million NVIDIA shares combined as of June 30, according to that report. Under their proposal, the board could continue its search and revisit Huang after the investigation. The Information on the Altimeter and Atreides letter

November 15 — Megaspeed says Alice Huang left and hires outside counsel

November 15 — The Wall Street Journal traces the offshore cloud business

The Journal reports that under Huang, NVIDIA cultivated overseas cloud partners whose hardware could serve China-based customers remotely. That way of supplying computing power helps explain the gap between tracking where the GPU shipped and knowing who ran workloads on it. Reports of remote access and reports of a physical diversion call for different evidence. The Wall Street Journal on NVIDIA’s offshore data-center strategy

November 16 — Trump backs the possibility of a return

Trump says he “would certainly not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO. Reuters reports more than people had signed the petition at its later count, with about identifying themselves as NVIDIA employees. The affiliations were self-reported. In Taipei, the campaign gets a high-rise endorsement when Taipei 101 lights up with “Taiwan Loves Jensen.” Reuters also reports that people familiar with the board’s thinking say directors are already disinclined to bring him back. Trump’s comments on reinstatement · Reuters on the petition count, Taipei 101, and board discussions

November 16–17 — Federal agencies publish the Megaspeed investigation chronology

A joint statement dated November 16 appears on DOJ’s site on November 17. It records the 2024 Commerce investigation, the May 2025 records request to NVIDIA, the company’s June no-sell decision, and the June on-site check. It confirms that DOJ took the lead on the criminal investigation. Several of those details predate the public uproar by more than a year. Signed Commerce and Justice statement · DOJ publication of the Megaspeed chronology

November 17 — Huang makes his pitch to return

Huang describes an “outpouring of calls” for his return from employees, investors, partners, and customers. He puts the decision with the directors, acknowledges that he created problems for the board, and commits to cooperating with its inquiry. The statement appeals to the company’s interests and to America’s interest in the success of its AI industry. It is his first public statement since leaving the job. Jensen Huang’s November 17 statement in full

November 17 — Congress sets dates for Huang and NVIDIA’s general counsel

The three House chairs announce that Huang and NVIDIA general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to voluntary, transcribed interviews. Huang is scheduled for and Teter for . The November 18 date was the initial request. Neither December interview had occurred by this update. House announcement of the Huang and Teter interviews

November 17 — The board publicly rules out reinstatement

November 17 — Kress delivers record results and says Hopper shipments to China have stopped

NVIDIA announces in fiscal Q3 sales, from Data Center, and a fiscal Q4 revenue outlook of , plus or minus 3%. The outlook assumes zero Data Center compute revenue from China. On the call, Kress reports in licensed China Hopper sales in Q3 and says, “we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data centre products to China,” in Reuters’ transcription. NVIDIA gives no date for a possible resumption. NVIDIA’s quarterly results and China outlook · Kress’s comments on China Hopper shipments

November 17 — Jeff Bezos makes the case for institutional knowledge

At a Semafor event, the Amazon founder says, “If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated.” It is a conditional endorsement of continuity. His point is that the work of running NVIDIA demands knowledge of how the company fits together, and that an internal successor might bring that knowledge too. Jeff Bezos on the NVIDIA CEO search

The report describes an introduction and cites corporate records linking a Malaysian Megaspeed subsidiary to an Alibaba-owned entity in Singapore. That is a more specific allegation than a general claim that Chinese companies used offshore servers. NVIDIA says it works to comply with evolving cloud-service rules. The report does not establish the dollar amount NVIDIA ultimately earned from the arrangement. The Information’s Alibaba, NVIDIA, and Alice Huang reporting

November 17 — The Wall Street Journal reports SEC scrutiny

Reuters relays the Journal’s reporting that the SEC is investigating NVIDIA following Huang’s departure. The reported securities inquiry raises disclosure questions alongside the export-control investigation and the board’s internal review. The disclosure and export cases have different authorities and different questions to resolve. Reuters on the reported SEC investigation

WIRED reports that Kress told employees they could expect pay raises and more equity in December, ahead of the normal schedule. Compensation was the most common topic in advance questions, followed by requests for board transparency. Bloomberg reported that management also made clear Huang would not return. The company’s response to employee uncertainty included both a succession decision and a concrete retention measure. WIRED’s account of NVIDIA’s first post-Huang all-hands · Bloomberg’s reporting on the town hall

Chair Brett Guthrie writes to Kress and Commerce officials over the Megaspeed reporting, export compliance, and allegations that an NVIDIA official may have tried to intervene in a federal inquiry. The committee asks about “the robustness and efficacy of the company’s security controls.” This request adds a distinct set of questions to the December interviews already on the calendar. House Energy and Commerce briefing requests

November 19 — The remote-access rule takes effect and Chinese tech firms assess the impact

The published rule takes effect. AP reports that Alibaba warned the rule could affect global data-center expansion and that Tencent expected tighter access to delay some model training. “Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with,” Tencent president Martin Lau said on the company’s earnings call. That is evidence of how companies say the rule may affect them. It does not price the affected demand into NVIDIA’s revenue. November 19 Federal Register publication · Alibaba and Tencent on overseas compute restrictions

The case for reinstatement

The strongest argument for bringing Huang back is continuity across work that usually belongs to several different executives. For 33 years he was the public face of NVIDIA, set its product direction, and negotiated with suppliers, hyperscalers, developers, and governments. Shareholders who favor a return are arguing that some of those relationships are unusually personal and that losing them suddenly could affect execution. Bezos’s advice also sharpens the alternative within that argument. Deep knowledge of NVIDIA matters whether it comes from Huang or an internal successor. NVIDIA’s account of the founder’s tenure and succession search · Jeff Bezos on internal candidates

The case for moving on rests on the direct-report allegation, the possible conflict with a customer, and the volume of oversight work already underway. The board has to run a workplace in which employees can raise concerns about top management and cooperate with investigators. It also has to set and enforce export rules for distributors, cloud partners, and resellers whose activities can trigger scrutiny across multiple governments. An eventual finding on the intelligence allegation would answer one question. Board oversight, employment policies, and the controls around advanced-chip sales have their own tests. Reporting on the relationship with a direct report · NVIDIA’s new trade and security oversight committee · Congressional requests on security controls

Kress’s first call gave the board time. Sales grew 103% year over year, the company issued guidance excluding China data-center compute revenue, and it had a sitting CFO willing to run the company through a search. The quarter ended before Huang’s resignation, so the results also reflect a business he led. The next test of execution will come in decisions made under Kress, including whether NVIDIA can retain people, deliver its roadmap, and manage its overseas cloud relationships under the new rules. NVIDIA’s Q3 FY2027 financial release · Kress’s first post-Huang all-hands · New U.S. cloud-access rule

December 1–2 and the questions still open

items.title: Palo Alto Networks Signs $4.5 Billion Deal For Applied Compute
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to acquire AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion as it expands beyond traditional cybersecurity into securing enterprise AI systems, including the training and deployment of open-weight models. The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027. Reuters reports: Palo Alto Networks has been repositioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider, with recent deals, including its $3.35 billion acquisition of cloud management and monitoring firm Chronosphere and an agreement with Israeli startup Koi. The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks and gives attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities.
 
"AI tools are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than companies can patch them, and that is pushing customers to consolidate onto fewer platforms," said Catharine Trebnick, senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities. With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto aims to offer a technology platform that helps customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI.

items.title: Anthropic Tops $2 Trillion Market Cap After IPO Debut
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest initial public offering in history. Shares opened at $111.50, a 34% premium that briefly pushed the Claude developer's market capitalization above $2 trillion, making it one of the world's most valuable companies. CNBC reports: The 5-year-old company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which have fueled its meteoric rise this year. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up a staggering 1,200% from the same period last year.
 
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI, now its chief rival. Anthropic has faced a sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, including by President Donald Trump and other senior government officials. [The Pentagon formally designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk in March following a dispute over military use of its AI models.]

items.title: My Wallet Introduces 1:1 Cross-Chain Stablecoin Swaps After Being Listed First on WalletConnect
items.author: Chainwire
items.content:
Dubai, United Arab Emirates, November 19th, 2026/Chainwire/--, a self-custodial, open-source crypto wallet serving more than 10 million users, has launched 1:1 swaps for USDT, USDC, USDe and USDS across supported blockchains. On eligible routes, users can switch both stablecoins and networks within a single in-app flow, with the amount they will receive fixed before confirmation.

The launch follows My Wallet’s listing at the top of . The wallet is also WalletConnect Certified and connects users to more than 80,000 compatible apps.

Simplifying Stablecoin Transfers Across Blockchains

According to research published in October 2026 by , organic stablecoin transfer volume exceeded $400 million per hour during Q3 2026. Yet stablecoins operate across multiple blockchains and token issuers, creating friction when users need a specific token on a specific network. Even when funds arrive on the right network, users may still hold the wrong stablecoin for a payment, trade or application.

addresses this through its in-app swap aggregator, powered by LayerZero, NEAR Intents, and other bridges resulting in the best rate. On eligible stablecoin routes, the aggregator offers a fixed 1:1 token rate, with no exchange-rate spread, slippage or My Wallet swap commission. My Wallet is the first among major crypto wallets to offer between different stablecoins across blockchains in a single in-app flow.

How the 1:1 Stablecoin Swaps Work

The fixed can apply whether users switch to a different stablecoin or move the same token to another blockchain. On a supported cross-chain USDT-to-USDC route, for example, a user sending 10,000 USDT receives exactly 10,000 USDC. The same rate applies when the token stays the same: a supported transfer of 10,000 USDT from Ethereum to TRON delivers exactly 10,000 USDT on TRON.

The 1:1 option is available for swaps above $30 on supported routes. There is no exchange-rate spread, slippage or My Wallet swap commission. Applicable blockchain network fees are paid separately, and the exact destination token amount is shown before confirmation. Other routes may have different rates and fees.

“Stablecoins are supposed to make moving money simpler, but users still have to think about which token they hold and which blockchain it’s on,” said Alexander Zinchuk, founder of My Wallet. “We’re removing that friction. If you hold USDT and need USDC on another network, you should be able to make that change in one step, know exactly how many tokens you’ll receive, and not pay an additional swap commission to your wallet.”

Native Bitcoin and Gasless EVM Transfers

The stablecoin launch follows the introduction of in My Wallet. Users can hold, send, receive and swap BTC alongside assets on Ethereum, Solana, TON and other networks, as well as buy Bitcoin with a bank card or sell it for fiat through MoonPay.

My Wallet now supports gasless transfers on Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Arbitrum and Optimism, adding to the existing support on Solana and TON. For these EVM transfers, the network fee is deducted from the tokens being sent, so users do not need to acquire a separate native token for gas. Supported assets are USDC on all five EVM networks, USDT on Ethereum and BNB Chain, bridged USDT on Base and Optimism, and USDT0 on Arbitrum. There is no minimum transfer amount or daily limit on the number of transactions.

Together, these innovative features advance My Wallet’s broader “All You Need to Enjoy Crypto” vision, combining asset management, seamless trading, and ease of use into one self-custodial app.

The new features are already available in . Swap availability is subject to the selected assets, networks and routes.

is a self-custodial, open-source multichain wallet for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Hyperliquid, TON, TRON, BNB, Base, Robinhood, Monad, Arbitrum, Polygon, and more. Founded in 2022, My Wallet serves over 10 million users across mobile, desktop, web and its Telegram Mini App. The wallet has been audited by CertiK and ranks among the .

Staking inside My Wallet is powered by Stakee, its own staking protocol, ranked among the top-2 TON DeFi protocols by TVL on .

items.title: Gamers Skip Work to Play GTA VI After 13-Year Wait
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
After a 13-year wait, Rockstar games' Grand Theft Auto VI has officially (and finally) launched today to near-universal acclaim, earning a 99/100 score on Metacritic and generating an estimated $1.84 billion from 19 million copies sold. The highly anticipated release has prompted gamers to take time off work, attracted nearly 2 million concurrent Twitch viewers, and sparked celebrations around the world. "Video game critics have lauded it, describing it as a 'masterpiece' and 'the single most impressive video game' they've ever played," reports NBC News.
 
An expert told Reuters that there could be a "work blackout across the board." Another expert suggested that $1 billion in U.S. productivity could be lost as people take time off to play the game, which is estimated to take about 50 hours to complete.
 
Here's a roundup of GTA VI reviews:

 IGN (10/10) calls it "the single most impressive video game I have ever played." GameSpot (10/10) praises its extraordinary attention to detail, calling it a culmination of Rockstar's open-world achievements. Push Square (10/10) describes it as Rockstar's deepest and most accomplished open world since Red Dead Redemption 2, though it notes the 30fps cap and occasional pacing issues. Eurogamer (5/5) praises its ambitious world and the emotional depth of Jason and Lucia's relationship. Digital Foundry highlights its groundbreaking visual realism, ray tracing, and simulation detail, while acknowledging compromises from the 30fps target. Bloomberg calls it an all-time classic, praising the unpredictable interactions and remarkable freedom of exploration.
