items.title: Data Extraction for AI Agents: 10 MCP Prompts for PDFs, Scans and Forms
items.author: Nutrient
items.content:
Your agent can read an invoice. What it can't do is show you where each number came from, or do the same thing reliably across 10,000 invoices.

Ask Claude Code or Codex to pull the total from a scanned PDF and you usually get one of three things: a guess, a value from the wrong table row, or a confident answer with no way to check where it came from. That's fine for a demo. It isn't fine when the number goes into an accounting system.

This post gives you 10 copy-paste prompts that let an agent read documents properly: pull fields from invoices, tables from statements and text from scans, each value with its source. The agent connects to a over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Every prompt below was run with the live server connected, and the outputs shown are real.

Where agents fall short on document data

I tested this on a tilted, noisy scan of a supplier invoice: an image with no text layer at all. Claude read it on its own and got the invoice date and the total right. When I asked where those values were, the best it could do was "top right, about 13% down the page" for the date, and "right side, about 55% down" for the total.

The extraction API returned the same values with evidence:

Bounding box (x, y, w × h, px)

One caveat: a citation points to the source region, not always the exact word. The date's box is tight and covers the label and the value. The total's box covers the whole totals block, from subtotal to total. A review screen highlights that block, which is still far quicker to check than "about 55% down".

A PDF doesn't store "a table" or "a paragraph". It stores characters at coordinates. Everything a human sees has to be reconstructed: reading order, columns, table cells, which number belongs to which label. Scans are worse, because there's no text at all until OCR runs.

When a general-purpose model reads a PDF directly, four things tend to go wrong:

  • Tables collapse. Cells merge, rows shift, and a debit ends up in the credit column.
  • Reading order breaks. Two-column layouts get read straight across the page.
  • Scans are harder. Tilted or noisy pages produce more misreads, and nothing tells you which values to check.
  • There's no evidence. You get a value, but not the page and position it came from.

The fix is to give the agent a tool that does the parsing and returns structured output with a source location for every value. The agent keeps doing what it's good at: deciding what to ask for and what to do with the answer.

The server is hosted, so there's nothing to install and no API key in a config file. You sign in once with OAuth.

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user nutrient https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp

Then start a new session, run /mcp, choose nutrient, and select Authenticate.

codex mcp add nutrient --url https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp && codex mcp login nutrient

: Settings → Connectors → add a custom connector with https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp.

Each prompt is written the way you'd type it to your agent. Swap in your own file names.

: any time a number from a document goes into another system.

Extract vendor, invoice number, date, line items and total from invoice.pdf.

: every field correct. Shortened, showing 2 of the 6 line items:

  "vendor": "Halvorsen Tool & Supply Co.",

  "invoice_number": "HTS-26-1187",

  "invoice_date": "2026-10-14",

    { "sku": "HB-2210", "description": "Galvanized steel bracket, 4 in (box of 50) T", "quantity": 12, "unit_price": 84.5, "amount": 1014 },

    { "sku": "AB-1620", "description": "Anchor bolt M16 x 200 mm T", "quantity": 300, "unit_price": 1.95, "amount": 585 }

All 6 line items came back, including a −$169.00 credit for returned brackets. The total matches the invoice: $1,835.00 subtotal + $48.00 shipping + $114.91 tax = $1,997.91.

Every value comes with its page, a bounding box and a groundedness score. Here's the citation for the total, as returned:

"total": {
  "pageNumber": 1,
  "bbox": { "x": 874, "y": 1060.75, "width": 667, "height": 158.25 },
  "match": "id_match",
  "citation": { "status": "cited", "confidence": { "groundedness": 0.9997 } }
}

You don't need to ask for locations; they come back anyway. My first version of this prompt ended with "Show the page and source location for each value." The server turned that into extra fields filled with descriptions like "Upper right, beside 'Invoice date'", which added nothing and caused review flags (see prompt 2).

. The field names are generated for each document: vendor and total here, not a fixed schema. And the output keeps what’s printed: line-item descriptions kept the invoice’s tax marker, as in “Anchor bolt M16 x 200 mm T”.

before you import anything automatically.

For every value you extracted, flag anything with low confidence so I can review it before import.

: one value flagged for review: the unit price on the −$169.00 credit line, with a groundedness score of 0.18. The value was correct. Every other field scored between 0.97 and 0.9997 and was marked ready to import.

That's the behavior you want from a review step: it leans towards asking a person. An earlier run, using my first version of prompt 1, came back with 14 flags, mostly on the extra "source location" fields that prompt created. It's a good reason to keep extraction prompts to the fields you need.

3. PDF to Markdown for RAG

: before chunking documents for retrieval.

Parse report.pdf to Markdown, keeping tables and reading order, and save it as report.md.

: clean headings, the abstract and introduction in order, and the results table intact (as an HTML table, which keeps merged cells). A chart even came back as a table. The test file was a three-page, two-column research paper, and reading order wasn't perfect:

  • A table and a methodology paragraph landed after the Results section.
  • Two headings merged into one line: "V. Discussion VII. Conclusion".
  • One table's cells shifted by a column.

Check the Markdown of a multi-column document before you index it. Single-column documents are much easier.

4. Read a scanned document

: contracts, faxes, anything that arrived as an image.

This is a scanned contract. Parse it with OCR and list the parties, the effective date and who signed.

: the test file was a 3-page image-only scan, slightly tilted and noisy. Parsing took about 13 seconds and cost $0.054 ($0.018 a page). The answer:

  • Parties: Nexus Digital Solutions, LLC (Service Provider) and Bridgewater Logistics Partners, Inc. (Client)

  • Effective date: February 14, 2024

  • Signed by: Elena V. Marchetti, Chief Executive Officer, and Derek L. Fontaine, Chief Operating Officer, both dated February 14, 2024

    All correct. The noise left stray characters in the parsed text, such as "oo", "ve" and "fe" between two sections, and "Derek L. Fontaine t t" on the signature page. That's normal for scans. The agent's answer stayed clean, and the citations tell you which region to check if something looks off.

: statements, price lists, reports.

Pull every table from statement.pdf into JSON, then save each table as its own CSV file.

: both tables, the account summary and all 7 transactions, saved as two CSV files. Shortened:

Date,Description,Debit,Credit,Balance
06/03/2026,Rent — Oakview Apartments,"1,850.00",,"2,360.35"
…
06/28/2026,Payroll — Brightline Logistics Inc.,,"2,891.44","7,692.81"

Empty debit and credit cells came back empty, not as zero, which matters if you sum the columns later. The closing balance matched the statement: $7,692.81.

6. Sort a pile of documents

: an inbox or upload folder with mixed file types.

Classify every file in ./inbox as invoice, receipt, contract or ID document, and move each file into a folder named after its type.

: 4 of 4 correct.

The server classifies; the agent moves the files. Run this one in Claude Code or Codex rather than a chat app.

7. Same fields from many files

: monthly invoice runs, batches of forms.

Extract the same fields from all invoices in ./invoices in one batch, and build one spreadsheet with a row per invoice.

: three invoices from three different suppliers, each with a different layout. The server generated one 20-field schema and applied it to all three. A few columns from the spreadsheet:

All three totals are correct. On the Tidewell invoice, it took the balance due after a $1,500 retainer, not the $6,152.50 in fees.

: run files of one kind together, and say how you want values formatted. Without that, our batch came back with "USD" on two invoices and "$" on the third, and three different date formats. Adding "Use ISO 4217 codes for currency and YYYY-MM-DD for dates" fixed all three. Two things to check after a run like this. A "$" with no country is the model's best guess: here it said USD, citing the supplier's Oregon address. And a field that doesn't fit the format can come back empty: one invoice listed three ship dates, and with the date rule that field came back blank.

8. Preview the fields before you pay

: a new document type you haven't processed before.

Show me which fields you'd extract from claim.pdf before running the extraction.

: 19 proposed fields for a property damage claim form, including claimant_name, policy_number, date_of_loss, type_of_loss and account_number. Each field comes with a rule. Every rule starts with "If no value is observed, return null rather than inventing a value", and then adds specifics. For example, the rule for police_or_fire_report_number is "including an explicit N/A; null if blank". The response said: "Nothing was extracted, billed or stored."

The list isn't fixed. An earlier run on a similar form proposed 21 fields. Edit the list until it has what you need, then use the same list for every file of that type.

before sending a document to a vendor, a model, or a colleague who doesn't need the personal data.

Redact names, email addresses, phone numbers and bank account numbers in claim.pdf, then save a redacted copy.

: the claimant's name, email, phone number and account number were removed, both in the form fields and in the free-text description. It also caught the name of a neighbour mentioned in the description. The text is gone from the file, not just covered by a black box. The policy number, address and routing number stayed, because the prompt didn't ask for them.

. The bank name was removed even though the prompt didn't ask for it. And thetyped signature "R. M. Okafor" was removed in one run and left in another. If something must go, name it in the prompt ("…and signatures"), and open the redacted copy before you send it.

10. Estimate the cost before a batch

before you process a folder of documents.

Count the pages in ./invoices and estimate what extracting them will cost at $0.015 per page.

: 3 invoices, 1 page each, so about $0.045. The agent counted the pages itself, locally, without sending anything to the server, so the estimate is free. The rate comes from your prompt. Extraction currently costs $0.015 per page, and parsing $0.009 or $0.018 depending on the mode. To see what you've actually used, check the .

Start with prompt 1 on one real document from your own work, and open the cited regions to check them. Once you trust the output for that document type, move to batches.

The parsing mode decides most of the cost:

  • Extraction (prompts 1, 5 and 7) ran in understand mode, at $0.015 per page.

  • Parsing a document to Markdown (prompts 3 and 4) defaults to agentic mode, at $0.018 per page.

  • On the clean three-page research paper, I reran the parse in understand mode at $0.009 per page. The Markdown was nearly identical, at half the price, in 1.2 seconds.

  • Agentic mode is for messy scans and complex layouts. For clean digital PDFs, ask for understand mode and compare both on a sample before you process thousands of pages.

Finally, keep a person in the loop for anything that moves money or makes a decision. The citations and confidence scores are there so the review takes seconds, not so you can skip it.

items.title: Your Crypto Exchange's Default Settings Could Change Your Tax Bill
items.author: Elena Mocchi
items.content:
Sell one bitcoin from a balance of two on an exchange, and the confirmation shows a price and a quantity. It does not show which Bitcoin you sold.

That detail decides the tax bill. Take an illustrative investor who bought 1 BTC at $20,000 and another at $90,000, both more than a year ago, then sold 1 BTC at $110,000. If the older coin counts as sold, the gain is $90,000. If the newer one does, it is $20,000. Same trade, same day, a $70,000 difference in reported gain.

For two years the IRS has let U.S. investors settle that question in their own records. That arrangement ends on December 31, 2026. From the first sale of 2027, the choice has to go through the platform holding the coins, which raises a plain question: what can a customer actually tell the platform?

To find out, I read the public tax pages of 15 U.S. crypto platforms between October 27 and 29, 2026. Six of them do not state which coins they sell first.

Why a Default Nobody Reads Is About to Matter

The rule sits in Treasury Regulation 1.1012-1(j). When a broker holds your coins, and you do not identify specific units by the date and time of the sale, the earliest-acquired units in that account are treated as sold first. That is first-in, first-out, or FIFO, and it runs account by account. Coins at one exchange are not pooled with coins at another.

The IRS granted temporary relief in Notice 2025-7 and extended it in Notice 2026-20. Through December 31, 2026, an investor can identify units on their own books, no later than the date and time of each sale, or record a standing order there before selling. For 2026 sales, the units identified that way control for federal income tax purposes, even if the broker's report shows something else.

After that date, the notice says, taxpayers "may not rely" on the relief. Unless new guidance arrives, the identification has to reach the broker, either as a standing order or as a lot choice on the trade.

A quieter line in the same regulation matters too. When a broker offers only one way to identify units, that method "is treated as a standing order or instruction." The notice switches this off during the relief period for investors using it. From 2027 it applies, so on a single-method platform, the platform's method effectively becomes the customer's own instruction.

I used each platform's own help center, tax pages and terms, read against the IRS rules, and no third-party summaries.

  • Kraken, Gemini, Robinhood, Fidelity Crypto, River and Cash App (in its gain and loss CSV).
  • HIFO, highest cost first (3): Strike, Uphold (on a page written for tax year 2025), and PayPal, which names HIFO for its own gain and loss statement.
  • Coinbase for retail accounts, Crypto.com, Binance.US, Webull Pay, eToro US and Bitstamp.

"Not disclosed" means I found no statement on the platform's public pages. It does not mean the platform has no policy. Coinbase, for instance, names FIFO for its institutional Prime accounts but not for retail customers, and Webull's FIFO language covers securities.

Changing the method is a separate question:

  • Coinbase, Kraken, Gemini and River.
  • Lot picking on each sale (3): Robinhood, Fidelity Crypto and eToro US.
  • HIFO only, no change (1): Strike.
  • Uphold, PayPal and Venmo, Cash App, Crypto.com, Binance.US, Webull Pay and Bitstamp.

Those settings have their own fine print. Kraken's has to be changed from a desktop device and applies only going forward. Coinbase says the method must be chosen before the trade settles, and a new choice covers open and future trades only.

One Transferred Coin, Four Different Answers

2026 is the first year brokers must report cost basis on Form 1099-DA, and only for "covered" assets: coins bought on that platform on or after January 1, 2026, and kept there. Anything moved in from a wallet or another exchange is noncovered. For people who self-custody, that can be most of what they own.

What happens to those coins depends on where they land:

  • Coinbase leaves basis blank on the form with the noncovered box checked, and its Retail Tax Center estimates the gain using a $0 basis.
  • Kraken reports no basis and tells customers that a missing figure "does not mean your basis is $0."
  • Strike assumes you acquired the coins at the price and date they arrived.
  • Robinhood closes lots with an unknown or zero basis first, before applying FIFO.

None of those is your actual cost. The same coin can show up as a blank, a $0 estimate or the price on the day it arrived, depending only on where you sent it.

Robinhood's ordering is no quirk. Treasury Regulation 1.6045-1 tells a broker with no customer instruction and no adequate transfer records to report units it did not acquire for the customer first, and only then work from the earliest date. Your own default is plain FIFO. So the form can list different units from the ones you must treat as sold, and a worked example in Regulation 1.1012-1 shows exactly that.

The form can be right and your return can still need different numbers, with the adjustment shown on Form 8949. That matters because the IRS gets a copy of the form. As attorney and CPA David Klasing explained in a HackerNoon interview on John Doe summonses, the agency has used those orders to spot mismatches between crypto activity and reported taxes. Form 1099-DA puts that data on a standard form for every customer.

What to Do Before the Window Closes

Find your method and date it. Look up your platform's default, save the page and note the day you checked. If nothing is published, ask support and keep the written answer.

Identify lots before each 2026 sale, not after. The relief requires the identification no later than the date and time of the sale, so a spreadsheet filled in during January will not rescue December trades. Use something that pins down basis and holding period, such as the purchase date, time and price.

Decide your 2027 setup before your first January sale. If your platform has a setting, pick the method and screenshot it. If it offers lot picking, plan to choose on every order. HIFO is not automatically the better pick: the highest-cost lot may be short-term, and using it first leaves your low-basis coins for a later year. Run both numbers on your own lots.

An earlier HackerNoon piece on crypto tax myths pointed out that most reputable exchanges let you download your transactions into a spreadsheet. Do that for every account, including the ones you rarely open, and keep withdrawals and deposits so both sides of each transfer can be matched.

Add missing basis before forms are generated. The windows are short. Strike asks customers to finish their details before it generates forms in mid-February. Robinhood's cutoff for 2025 sales was January 14, 2026, with a warning that updates after January 7 could delay forms. Assume the next window will be just as tight.

What Investors Should Watch

One date to remember: It is the last day a lot choice on your own books can count, and Strike warns that its tax year follows UTC, so there the year ends at 7:00 p.m. ET. The next marker follows quickly. Forms are due to customers by February 16, 2027, because February 15 is Washington's Birthday, and those will be the first to carry basis.

The IRS has extended this relief once. Planning on a second extension is a gamble.

Platforms are also still catching up. Several help pages show the old $600 threshold for Form 1099-MISC, although the figure for 2026 is $2,000. So treat any table, this one included, as a snapshot. The full version, with the quote and source link for each platform, is in the study, and the data is archived on Zenodo under a CC BY 4.0 license.

Disclosure: This is general information, not tax advice, DYOR! The author is a Florida CPA who runs a crypto accounting practice.

items.title: Microsoft Testing Remote Lock For Lost Or Stolen Windows Devices
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels.
 
Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. "Nothing is erased: the device stays enrolled and managed, BitLocker stays on and user data stays in place. The lock holds across restarts and while offline, and only an admin can lift it remotely, so the user picks up where they left off."

items.title: I Sent 12 AI Shoppers Through a Broken Checkout, but Only One Bought Anything
items.author: Aditya Reddy
items.content:
The store was charging for one telescope

Three telescopes, $101.96 each, plus $26.97 shipping. The cart wanted $128.93.

I was running release 2.1.3 of the OpenTelemetry Demo. Its frontend added each product's price once, regardless of quantity. The right total was $332.85. There's an upstream report of this in issue 1526. I kept 3.1.0 as a separate clean reference.

A checkout script could still place the order. I wanted to see if a browser agent would check the cart total before paying.

Give the shopper permission to leave

I built Walkout with a purchase goal and a short persona card for each shopper. Playwright returns a browser observation, the model chooses an action, and the runner carries it out. Then it sends back the next observation with the earlier steps.

Muse Spark 1.3 runs that loop. It can click, select, type, press a key, scroll, or give up. The shop has to show an order confirmation before I count a purchase, even if the model says it's done.

For the recording, I told the shoppers to buy three telescopes and check the quantity, price, shipping, and total. If the arithmetic didn’t agree, they were supposed to leave. The counts below show how the agents did on that task.

The profiles needed different browser conditions or I would just have twelve copies of the same test. Rosa gets a budget phone profile with slower CPU and network settings. Margaret has enlarged text, Lucía an es-MX locale. Dev uses keys. Amara gets the accessibility tree.

Dev sees a plain screenshot and can use keyboard actions. Giving him numbered targets he could click would let him get around a focus problem without ever seeing it. Amara's tree references give her a different view of the page again.

I can repeat those configurations. They don't reproduce every phone or a person's full screen reader session, and the recordings let me see exactly which inputs each simulated shopper had.

One shopper bought before the patch. Eleven left, and ten cited the quantity calculation. I saved each shopper’s explanation next to the browser steps that led to it.

Lucía explained in Spanish that the total charged for one telescope plus shipping. In her replay I can see what the browser showed her before she gave up.

My runner had its own bugs

An early smoke run got stuck scrolling between the total and the checkout form for twelve steps. The shopper had already read the cart. I wasn't returning its notes with the history, though, so that useful observation kept dropping out of the next decision. Passing the notes back fixed the loop.

The native quantity dropdown caused another problem. Its open menu didn't appear in the headless screenshot. Repeated taps weren't going to make that screenshot any more informative. I added a select action so the shopper could choose the quantity.

Those were my bugs. Having the saved steps helped me find them before blaming the storefront.

What the $8.34 actually paid for

The October 28 model ledger has 1,862 calls. They added up to $8.33742325, or $8.34. I tracked model calls, so the figure leaves out server costs and my time.

The November 4 takes and work added $6.11. By the end of that recording I’d spent $14.45 on model calls across the project.

The repair was two multiplications

Spark reads the saved reasons for leaving and picks source files. Muse Wonder 1.0 proposes replacements, and another Wonder call reviews them.

The change was in . It multiplied by quantity in the whole-unit sum and in the nanos sum. The existing carry from nanos into units stayed in place.

Another call to the same model approved the patch. Release 2.1.3’s frontend had no test command. Its image build runs type checking and lint, and Walkout won’t serve a patch if that build fails. A successful build still couldn’t tell me what three telescopes cost.

I emptied the cart and tried again

The rebuilt frontend replaced the release image on the same port. I emptied the cart, added three telescopes and checked the total before ordering. Then I sent the same twelve profiles through it again.

Nine bought this time. Rosa couldn't open the full cart on her phone profile. Dev couldn't reach the quantity or Add To Cart controls with the keyboard. Lucía checked the peso arithmetic and found a one-cent difference.

I left Rosa, Dev and Lucía red on the board so I could find the purchase attempts that still needed work. The profiles stayed the same across the two rounds. Their model-chosen actions can vary from one run to the next.

Try the checkout checks without model calls

items.title: Building a Browser-Based Image Editor With Web Workers and OffscreenCanvas
items.author: sammii
items.content:
Photoshop can do everything ScapeStudio does. That is not the point. Preparing photographs for fine art prints and T-shirt production is a specific pipeline: greyscale, curves, threshold knockout with feathered edges, export at 300 DPI across fixed paper and garment sizes. In Photoshop, that is opening each file, running an action, exporting, renaming, repeating. Twenty photographs is an afternoon.

ScapeStudio does those four steps, nothing else, and the entire pixel pipeline runs in a Web Worker. Dragging a curves handle has to re-render the preview in under 16ms or the feel is gone. Main-thread processing on a 24-megapixel shot cannot hit that. A worker with an OffscreenCanvas can.

Why the main thread loses

Canvas 2D is not slow in itself. Every pixel operation on the main thread competes with layout, paint, input handling, and React reconciliation. Luminance conversion on an 8000x6000 image is 48 million pixels, 192 million byte operations. On a warm JIT, around 150ms. For the duration of that loop, the UI is frozen, scrolling halts, and the curves handle stops tracking.

Most web editors work around this by downsampling aggressively and processing the thumbnail, only running the full pipeline on export. That gets interactive curves, but what you see is not what you get. Shadow clipping and highlight roll-off are invisible in a 400-pixel preview.

ScapeStudio processes a 2000-pixel preview in a worker on every parameter change, and runs the full-resolution pipeline only at export. The worker does not block the main thread, so the curves handle drags smoothly while the pipeline works.

The message shape between the main thread and the processing worker is deliberately tight:

export interface ProcessMessage {
  type: "process";
  imageBitmap: ImageBitmap;
  curveLUT: Uint8Array;
  threshold: number;
  feather: number;
  previewMaxSize: number;
}

export interface ProcessResult {
  type: "result";
  printBitmap: ImageBitmap;
  tshirtBitmap: ImageBitmap;
  histogram: Uint32Array;
}

Two details are load-bearing. The image moves as an , not raw : is a transferable reference to decoded pixel memory, so hands the GPU-side resource across thread boundaries without copying. The curves state is pre-baked into a 256-entry lookup table on the main thread before sending. The worker never sees the user's control points; it just indexes the LUT.

This is the serialisation gotcha that kills naive worker pipelines. Send four control point objects and expect the worker to rebuild the spline every frame, and you pay spline evaluation per frame. Send a of 256 bytes, the worker runs one array lookup per pixel, and the spline maths happens once per parameter change, on the main thread, where it is cheap.

OffscreenCanvas is the whole trick

A normal is a DOM node. Its 2D context reaches into layout, compositor, and the DOM in ways that only exist on the main thread. You cannot instantiate one in a worker. For years, image processing in workers meant shuttling raw buffers through , which either copies (slow) or transfers (you lose the buffer on the sender side).

exists in the Web Worker global scope. Its behaves like the DOM canvas context and can produce via . The pipeline is built around that:

const canvas = new OffscreenCanvas(width, height);
const canvasCtx = canvas.getContext("2d")!;
canvasCtx.drawImage(imageBitmap, 0, 0, width, height);

const imageData = canvasCtx.getImageData(0, 0, width, height);

applyGrayscale(imageData.data);
applyCurveLUT(imageData.data, curveLUT);

const printBitmap = await createImageBitmap(imageData);

Everything after operates on a single that never leaves the worker. returns a transferable bitmap handed back to the main thread by reference. The only bytes that actually cross the worker boundary are the 256-byte LUT in, and a pointer-sized bitmap handle out.

uses luminosity weighting, not an RGB average:

function applyGrayscale(data: Uint8ClampedArray): void {
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i += 4) {
    const lum = 0.299 * data[i] + 0.587 * data[i + 1] + 0.114 * data[i + 2];
    data[i] = lum;
    data[i + 1] = lum;
    data[i + 2] = lum;
  }
}

Coefficients from Rec. 601 match how the eye perceives brightness. Naive loses shadow detail in greens and blows out blues. For fine art prints, weighted luminance is non-negotiable.

is a pre-baked 256-entry LUT applied to the luminance channel:

function applyCurveLUT(data: Uint8ClampedArray, lut: Uint8Array): void {
  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i += 4) {
    const v = lut[data[i]];
    data[i] = v;
    data[i + 1] = v;
    data[i + 2] = v;
  }
}

One array lookup per pixel. No branches, no arithmetic. Fastest possible tonal transformation.

Threshold with feathering modifies the alpha channel based on luminance:

function applyThreshold(
  data: Uint8ClampedArray,
  threshold: number,
  feather: number
): void {
  const lower = Math.max(0, threshold - feather);

  for (let i = 0; i < data.length; i += 4) {
    const lum = data[i];

    if (lum <= lower) {
      data[i + 3] = 0;
    } else if (lum <= threshold && feather > 0) {
      const alpha = ((lum - lower) / feather) * 255;
      data[i + 3] = Math.round(alpha);
    }
  }
}

Pixels below go fully transparent. Pixels between and get a linear alpha ramp. Pixels above are untouched. For t-shirt prep this knocks out studio backdrops while leaving hair and fabric edges soft, rather than the jagged bitmap look of a pure binary threshold.

Cubic splines, done properly

The obvious way to wire up a Photoshop-style curves tool is Catmull-Rom splines through the user's control points. Mostly works, except when two adjacent points have a steep slope difference: Catmull-Rom overshoots. Drag a shadow point down, the curve dips below zero before recovering. The LUT clamps negatives, so you get a flat black region where you wanted a gentle toe.

ScapeStudio uses monotone cubic Hermite interpolation via the Fritsch-Carlson method, which guarantees no overshoot:

tangents[0] = slopes[0];
tangents[n - 1] = slopes[n - 2];

for (let i = 1; i < n - 1; i++) {
  if (slopes[i - 1] * slopes[i] <= 0) {
    tangents[i] = 0;
  } else {
    tangents[i] = (3 * (dx[i - 1] + dx[i])) /
      ((2 * dx[i] + dx[i - 1]) / slopes[i - 1] +
       (dx[i] + 2 * dx[i - 1]) / slopes[i]);
  }
}

// Restrict tangents to the circle of radius 3
for (let i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
  const alpha = tangents[i] / slopes[i];
  const beta = tangents[i + 1] / slopes[i];
  const mag = alpha * alpha + beta * beta;
  if (mag > 9) {
    const tau = 3 / Math.sqrt(mag);
    tangents[i] = tau * alpha * slopes[i];
    tangents[i + 1] = tau * beta * slopes[i];
  }
}

The harmonic mean of slopes plus the radius-3 restriction is what makes it monotonic. The curve still passes through every control point exactly, still feels like Photoshop. It just cannot dip outside the range you drew. 256 evaluations per parameter change, a few microseconds total.

Non-destructive by buffer layout

Each pipeline stage reads from the previous stage's output and writes to its own buffer. The source is never touched. That matters for two reasons.

First, parameter changes only need to rerun from the earliest affected stage. Adjusting feather does not retouch the curves result; it clones the post-curves pixel data and applies threshold to the copy. After curves run, the print output is captured, then a fresh is allocated and thresholded independently for the t-shirt preview.

Second, the original image is still available at full resolution for export. The preview pipeline works on a downsampled 2000-pixel version for interactive feel; the export worker re-ingests the original bitmap, applies the same LUT and threshold values at full resolution, writes PNGs at 300 DPI. Same pipeline, different sampling.

The main-thread glue is deliberately thin but does one thing that matters: it debounces worker dispatch by 100ms:

export function processImage(
  sourceImage: ImageBitmap,
  curves: CurvePoints,
  threshold: number,
  feather: number,
  onResult: ProcessCallback
): void {
  if (debounceTimer) clearTimeout(debounceTimer);

  debounceTimer = setTimeout(() => {
    currentCallback = onResult;
    const lut = generateCurveLUT(curves);
    const w = getWorker();
    w.postMessage({ type: "process", imageBitmap: sourceImage, curveLUT: lut, threshold, feather, previewMaxSize: 2000 });
  }, 100);
}

Without this, dragging a slider fires dozens of worker dispatches per second. The worker processes one at a time, a queue builds, the preview falls behind. 100ms is long enough to coalesce a drag gesture, short enough that the output feels live.

One worker instance is reused across the session. Worker startup costs a few hundred milliseconds; you only pay it once.

The export worker is the same pipeline at full resolution, looped over configured sizes, written into a zip client-side:

for (const size of sizes) {
  const canvas = new OffscreenCanvas(widthPx, heightPx);
  const canvasCtx = canvas.getContext("2d")!;
  canvasCtx.drawImage(sourceImageBitmap, srcX, srcY, srcW, srcH, 0, 0, widthPx, heightPx);

  const imageData = canvasCtx.getImageData(0, 0, widthPx, heightPx);
  applyGrayscale(imageData.data);
  applyCurveLUT(imageData.data, curveLUT);

  canvasCtx.putImageData(imageData, 0, 0);
  const printBlob = await canvas.convertToBlob({ type: "image/png" });
  files.push({ name: `print/${fileName}_${label}_${widthPx}px.png`, blob: printBlob });
}

Each size gets a fresh at target pixel dimensions (cm at 300 DPI), the cropped source draws into it, the pipeline runs, produces a PNG. The t-shirt output clones the buffer, thresholds, exports separately. All blobs go into a JSZip folder and save as one archive. No server round trip. A 20-photograph batch at six sizes produces 240 PNGs and never leaves the browser.

What 60fps actually demands

The interactive budget is 16.6ms per frame. The worker pipeline on a 2000-pixel preview takes 30-50ms depending on image and device. Over budget for a single frame, which is why the main thread never waits on it. The drag gesture updates React state at 60fps from input events; the worker processes the latest coalesced state on its own clock; the result paints when it arrives. The preview trails the drag by one or two frames, the UI never stutters.

Moving the pipeline off the main thread is not an optimisation. It is the architectural choice that makes everything else possible. Once pixel loops live in a worker, the main thread only schedules messages and paints bitmaps. The curves handle stays under your cursor. The tab does not beachball on a 24-megapixel shot.

Purpose-built beats general-purpose. Four things, in a worker. Enough.

items.title: Three Records Your Support Team Needs After a Background Job Fails
items.author: Khakan Ali
items.content:
Conceptual recovery view. The lab stores accepted input and row results and derives the outcome; recovery-owner tracking is not implemented. Catalog data is fictional; the code and process-exit tests ran locally.

When a customer asks whether to upload a failed import again, the worker's health check cannot tell support what already changed. A retry count cannot answer that question either. The useful evidence is the accepted input, the committed work and the outcome derived from those records.

Here is a runnable catalog importer that makes those questions inspectable. The supplier and product data are fictional. The local implementation and failure tests were executed with Python 3.13.3 and SQLite 3.49.2; they are not a customer deployment or a distributed-system benchmark.

The lab uses one supplier's catalog in one disposable SQLite file. It deliberately keeps the catalog update and the completed-row result in the same database. There is no queue or external inventory API.

Run an import, then deliver it again

Save the three files in the appendix together: , and . Python's standard library supplies all dependencies. Use a new disposable database, never a production or shared one. From that directory, run:

python3 -m unittest -v test_importer
python3 -c 'import sys, sqlite3; print(sys.version); print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)'

The captured implementation suite passed all four tests. The version command lets you record your own environment rather than assume it matches the lab. For a manual delivery and replay, create a fresh directory:

lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
python3 importer.py --db "$lab_dir/catalog.sqlite" --id batch-7 --input sample.json
python3 importer.py --db "$lab_dir/catalog.sqlite" --id batch-7 --input sample.json

Each delivery should print:

{"import_id": "batch-7", "completed": 2, "total": 2, "outcome": "complete", "ack": true}

This output was observed for the first delivery in the captured run. Identical replay also completed; test-only audit triggers recorded zero additional catalog writes. Merely seeing two catalog rows would not prove that: an upsert could rewrite the same rows without increasing their count.

The field is a printed illustration of where acknowledgment would occur. It does not acknowledge a message to a real broker.

1. Record exactly what was accepted

The table stores the caller's import ID, the original file bytes, their SHA-256 hash and the expected row count. Acceptance commits separately before processing begins, so an accepted import can exist with no completed rows.

For the supplied file, the captured record is:

import_id: batch-7
payload_sha256: ce9147caac49d6b749fdbfa4fe343823f094b8e100c6225347f94154263a47a2
row_count: 2

The ID belongs to one exact delivery payload. Reuse it for a redelivery of those bytes. A corrected file needs a distinct ID; changing even whitespace under the existing ID is rejected by the code. The altered-input test changes a price from 1299 to 1300 cents, confirms a nonzero exit containing , and checks that prior records are unchanged.

Validation happens before acceptance. The payload must be a nonempty array; each row must have exactly , and . Names and SKUs must contain non-whitespace text, prices must be nonnegative integers, and the file cannot contain duplicate SKUs. This makes row position a usable work identity within this immutable file. It is not a general identity for a product across future imports.

The stored bytes are immutable by application contract. This code does not prevent an administrator from directly altering the database.

Each row is identified by , enforced as the primary key of . The worker starts before checking whether that row is complete.

If a result already exists, it skips the catalog write. Otherwise, it upserts the product and inserts the completed-row record, including the resulting SKU, name and price, within that transaction. Commit makes both changes visible together. The exception handler rolls back before propagating an ordinary failure; the full code below preserves that handler and the replay check.

This implementation uses SQLite's single-writer behavior for coordination. SQLite's transaction documentation explains that starts a write transaction immediately and can fail if another writer is active. The connection waits up to 15 seconds for a lock. That is bounded waiting, not unlimited recovery or a throughput claim.

In the duplicate-worker test, two fresh worker processes target the same import and local database. A third connection holds a write transaction while the test checks that both workers are still running. After releasing it, both workers complete. Audit triggers count exactly two catalog writes for the two input rows.

That observation is narrower than claiming the workers can run all their writes in parallel: SQLite serializes them. Longer contention can still fail.

The importer counts completed rows and compares that count with the accepted row count. It prints only when those counts agree. There is no independent success flag that can get ahead of row processing.

The captured catalog contains , Steel bottle, at 1299 cents and , Canvas bag, at 850 cents. Each has a completed-row result with the corresponding values. Support can inspect the records without relying on a process that may have disappeared:

python3 - "$lab_dir/catalog.sqlite" <<'PY'
import json
import sqlite3
import sys
with sqlite3.connect(sys.argv[1]) as db:
    for table in ('imports', 'catalog', 'completed_rows'):
        sql = {
            'imports': 'SELECT import_id, payload_sha256, row_count FROM imports',
            'catalog': 'SELECT sku, name, price_cents FROM catalog ORDER BY sku',
            'completed_rows': 'SELECT import_id, row_number, sku, result FROM completed_rows ORDER BY row_number',
        }[table]
        print(table, json.dumps(db.execute(sql).fetchall()))
PY

The completed result describes what that import committed. A later import with a different ID can update the same SKU, so an older result is not proof of the catalog's current value. This lab does not solve ordering between different imports or prevent an older delivery under a different ID from overwriting newer data.

The tests launch real Python subprocesses and use at two explicit failure points. Each retry runs in a fresh process against the same temporary database. These are abrupt process exits, not operating-system crashes or power-loss tests.

Before the first row commits, the process exits with code 71. The accepted import remains, but the catalog and completed-row tables both contain zero rows. A fresh retry completes both rows. Support's next action follows from that saved state: resume the accepted import using the same ID and bytes.

After the first row commits, the process exits with code 72 before printing the acknowledgment. There is no stdout, but one catalog row and one completed result survive. The retry reaches two completed rows, and an audit trigger observes zero updates to the already committed row. Missing acknowledgment therefore does not mean no work committed.

The suite also checks identical replay, altered-file rejection, and competing workers. Its captured summary is:

competing workers: both ack complete; 2 catalog writes, 2 completed rows
crash after commit: exit=72, before restart catalog=1 completed=1 ack absent; restart=2/2, committed row rewrites=0
crash before commit: exit=71, before restart catalog=0 completed=0; restart=2/2
normal/replay/altered: 2 completed, replay catalog writes=0, mismatch rejected

Run the supplied suite to exercise these cases safely; it creates isolated temporary databases. The crash flags are test hooks, not operating instructions for valuable data.

Where this recovery argument stops

The catalog write and result share one local transaction. A remote inventory update cannot join it. If a remote request succeeds and its response is lost, a missing local result does not establish whether repeating that request is safe. That boundary needs the provider's idempotency contract and a reconciliation process, with an owner for unresolved outcomes.

This lab has not tested SQS, PostgreSQL, multiple hosts, network filesystems or machine power failure. requests SQLite's commit synchronization; it is not protection against every storage failure. Production ingestion, access controls, migrations and monitoring are omitted. No end-to-end exactly-once guarantee follows from these tests.

A recovery screen built on these records could show the accepted identity, which rows committed, and which remain. A conflicting payload should remain a conflict. An uncertain remote action should remain unresolved. Neither should become a green success badge merely because another worker started.

Save each block under the stated filename. Keep byte-for-byte if comparing its hash with the captured run, including its final newline. The importer uses the same SQL schema shown in its constant; no separate setup command is needed.

[
  {"sku":"SUP-101","name":"Steel bottle","price_cents":1299},
  {"sku":"SUP-202","name":"Canvas bag","price_cents":850}
]

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Local SQLite illustration; a delivery is acknowledged only after all rows finish."""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import os
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

SCHEMA = '''
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS imports (
  import_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payload_sha256 TEXT NOT NULL, payload BLOB NOT NULL,
  row_count INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(row_count > 0)
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS catalog (
  sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(price_cents >= 0)
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS completed_rows (
  import_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES imports(import_id), row_number INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sku TEXT NOT NULL, result TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(import_id, row_number)
);
'''


def connect(path):
    db = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=15, isolation_level=None)
    db.execute('PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON')
    db.execute('PRAGMA synchronous=FULL')
    db.executescript(SCHEMA)
    return db


def load_payload(path):
    raw = Path(path).read_bytes()
    rows = json.loads(raw)
    if not isinstance(rows, list) or not rows:
        raise ValueError('payload must be a non-empty array')
    seen = set()
    for row in rows:
        if (not isinstance(row, dict) or set(row) != {'sku', 'name', 'price_cents'}
            or not isinstance(row['sku'], str) or not row['sku'].strip()
            or not isinstance(row['name'], str) or not row['name'].strip()
            or type(row['price_cents']) is not int or row['price_cents'] < 0
            or row['sku'] in seen):
            raise ValueError('invalid row or duplicate SKU')
        seen.add(row['sku'])
    return raw, rows


def deliver(db, import_id, raw, rows, crash=None):
    if not import_id.strip():
        raise ValueError('empty import ID')
    digest = hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
    db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE')
    try:
        existing = db.execute('SELECT payload_sha256, payload FROM imports WHERE import_id=?', (import_id,)).fetchone()
        if existing and (existing[0] != digest or existing[1] != raw):
            raise ValueError('import ID already belongs to different bytes')
        if not existing:
            db.execute('INSERT INTO imports VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)', (import_id, digest, raw, len(rows)))
        db.commit()
    except BaseException:
        db.rollback()
        raise
    for number, row in enumerate(rows, 1):
        db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE')
        try:
            completed = db.execute('SELECT 1 FROM completed_rows WHERE import_id=? AND row_number=?', (import_id, number)).fetchone()
            if not completed:
                db.execute('INSERT INTO catalog VALUES (?, ?, ?) ON CONFLICT(sku) DO UPDATE SET name=excluded.name, price_cents=excluded.price_cents', (row['sku'], row['name'], row['price_cents']))
                result = json.dumps({'sku': row['sku'], 'name': row['name'], 'price_cents': row['price_cents']}, sort_keys=True)
                db.execute('INSERT INTO completed_rows VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)', (import_id, number, row['sku'], result))
                if crash == 'before-commit' and number == 1:
                    os._exit(71)
            db.commit()
            if not completed and crash == 'after-commit' and number == 1:
                os._exit(72)
        except BaseException:
            db.rollback()
            raise
    total, done = db.execute('SELECT i.row_count, count(c.row_number) FROM imports i LEFT JOIN completed_rows c ON c.import_id=i.import_id WHERE i.import_id=? GROUP BY i.import_id', (import_id,)).fetchone()
    print(json.dumps({'import_id': import_id, 'completed': done, 'total': total, 'outcome': 'complete' if done == total else 'incomplete', 'ack': done == total}))


def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    p.add_argument('--db', required=True)
    p.add_argument('--id', required=True)
    p.add_argument('--input', required=True)
    p.add_argument('--crash', choices=['before-commit', 'after-commit'])
    args = p.parse_args()
    raw, rows = load_payload(args.input)
    with connect(args.db) as db:
        deliver(db, args.id, raw, rows, args.crash)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

import json
import sqlite3
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SCRIPT = HERE / 'importer.py'
SAMPLE = HERE / 'sample.json'

class DeliveryTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.temp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='catalog-demo-')
        self.addCleanup(self.temp.cleanup)
        self.root = Path(self.temp.name)
        self.db = self.root / 'test.sqlite'

    def command(self, source=SAMPLE, *extra):
        return [sys.executable, str(SCRIPT), '--db', str(self.db), '--id', 'batch-7', '--input', str(source), *extra]

    def run_job(self, *args):
        return subprocess.run(self.command(*args), text=True, capture_output=True, timeout=30)

    def rows(self):
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db) as c:
            imports = c.execute('SELECT import_id,payload_sha256,row_count FROM imports').fetchall()
            catalog = c.execute('SELECT sku,name,price_cents FROM catalog ORDER BY sku').fetchall()
            completed = c.execute('SELECT import_id,row_number,sku,result FROM completed_rows ORDER BY row_number').fetchall()
        return imports, catalog, completed

    def assert_complete(self):
        imports, catalog, completed = self.rows()
        self.assertEqual(len(imports), 1)
        self.assertEqual(imports[0][2], 2)
        self.assertEqual(catalog, [('SUP-101','Steel bottle',1299),('SUP-202','Canvas bag',850)])
        self.assertEqual([r[:3] for r in completed], [('batch-7',1,'SUP-101'),('batch-7',2,'SUP-202')])
        for r in completed:
            self.assertEqual(json.loads(r[3])['sku'],r[2])
        return imports, catalog, completed

    def test_normal_duplicate_and_altered_input(self):
        first = self.run_job(); self.assertEqual(first.returncode, 0, first.stderr)
        self.assertEqual(json.loads(first.stdout)['outcome'], 'complete')
        original = self.assert_complete()
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db) as c:
            c.executescript('CREATE TABLE writes(sku TEXT); CREATE TRIGGER audit_update AFTER UPDATE ON catalog BEGIN INSERT INTO writes VALUES (NEW.sku); END; CREATE TRIGGER audit_insert AFTER INSERT ON catalog BEGIN INSERT INTO writes VALUES (NEW.sku); END;')
        repeat = self.run_job(); self.assertEqual(repeat.returncode, 0, repeat.stderr)
        self.assertEqual(self.rows(), original)
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db) as c: self.assertEqual(c.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM writes').fetchone()[0],0)
        altered = self.root / 'altered.json'; altered.write_text(SAMPLE.read_text().replace('1299','1300'))
        rejected = self.run_job(altered)
        self.assertNotEqual(rejected.returncode, 0)
        self.assertIn('different bytes', rejected.stderr)
        self.assertEqual(self.rows(), original)
        print('normal/replay/altered: 2 completed, replay catalog writes=0, mismatch rejected')

    def test_killed_before_commit(self):
        killed = self.run_job(SAMPLE, '--crash', 'before-commit')
        self.assertEqual(killed.returncode,71)
        imports, catalog, completed = self.rows()
        self.assertEqual((len(imports),catalog,completed),(1,[],[]))
        retry = self.run_job(); self.assertEqual(retry.returncode,0,retry.stderr)
        self.assert_complete()
        print('crash before commit: exit=71, before restart catalog=0 completed=0; restart=2/2')

    def test_killed_after_commit_before_ack(self):
        killed = self.run_job(SAMPLE, '--crash', 'after-commit')
        self.assertEqual(killed.returncode,72)
        self.assertEqual(killed.stdout,'')
        imports, catalog, completed = self.rows()
        self.assertEqual(len(imports),1); self.assertEqual(len(catalog),1); self.assertEqual(len(completed),1)
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db) as c:
            c.executescript('CREATE TABLE writes(sku TEXT); CREATE TRIGGER audit_update AFTER UPDATE ON catalog BEGIN INSERT INTO writes VALUES (NEW.sku); END;')
        retry = self.run_job(); self.assertEqual(retry.returncode,0,retry.stderr)
        self.assert_complete()
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db) as c:self.assertEqual(c.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM writes').fetchone()[0],0)
        print('crash after commit: exit=72, before restart catalog=1 completed=1 ack absent; restart=2/2, committed row rewrites=0')

    def test_competing_workers(self):
        # Seed schema and import before opening the gate, so the contention is on row transactions.
        import importer
        db=importer.connect(self.db)
        raw, rows=importer.load_payload(SAMPLE)
        db.execute('INSERT INTO imports VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)', ('batch-7',__import__('hashlib').sha256(raw).hexdigest(),raw,len(rows)))
        db.executescript('CREATE TABLE writes(sku TEXT); CREATE TRIGGER audit_insert AFTER INSERT ON catalog BEGIN INSERT INTO writes VALUES (NEW.sku); END; CREATE TRIGGER audit_update AFTER UPDATE ON catalog BEGIN INSERT INTO writes VALUES (NEW.sku); END;')
        db.execute('BEGIN IMMEDIATE')
        p1=subprocess.Popen(self.command(),stdout=subprocess.PIPE,stderr=subprocess.PIPE,text=True)
        p2=subprocess.Popen(self.command(),stdout=subprocess.PIPE,stderr=subprocess.PIPE,text=True)
        time.sleep(0.3)
        self.assertIsNone(p1.poll()); self.assertIsNone(p2.poll())
        db.commit();db.close()
        for p in (p1,p2):
            out,err=p.communicate(timeout=30); self.assertEqual(p.returncode,0,err);self.assertTrue(json.loads(out)['ack'])
        self.assert_complete()
        with sqlite3.connect(self.db) as c:self.assertEqual(c.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM writes').fetchone()[0],2)
        print('competing workers: both ack complete; 2 catalog writes, 2 completed rows')

if __name__=='__main__':unittest.main(verbosity=2)

items.title: Fig Announces Elastic Integration to Help Security Teams Protect Detection Coverage as Data Changes
items.author: Kevin John
items.content:
announced an integration partnership with on November 19, 2026, the company said in a press release. Fig helps security operations (SecOps) engineers map detection dependencies, identify breaks and validate changes before they reach production. The integration connects Fig with Elastic Security, which Elastic describes as an open, agentic security operations platform. It is designed to let security teams build, ship and run detection and response while seeing how changes to their data affect what they can detect.

, the partnership deals with a practical concern for organizations that rely on detection rules to flag suspicious activity. Those rules work only when the data feeding them arrives in the structure they expect, and that structure can shift over time. Fig and Elastic link upstream data changes to the downstream detections that rely on them, which gives engineers control over each change that touches security coverage.

What the Fig and Elastic Integration Does

Elastic Security gives customers a starting point through prebuilt integrations and detection rules that help establish coverage from day one. Fig picks up from there and helps SecOps engineers safeguard and expand that coverage as their environments evolve. Elastic Security supplies the platform and its prebuilt content, and Fig focuses on the dependencies that tie upstream data changes to the detections built on that data.

Gal Shafir, co-founder and chief executive officer of Fig, summed up how the two companies divide the work. "Elastic gives security teams control over their data, and Fig gives them control over the engineering around it," Shafir said.

Why Detection Coverage Can Erode Without Warning

Detection rules depend on specific fields and values to recognize an attack. A vendor may update its log format, a team may bring a new source online, or an upstream pipeline may be reshaped to manage cost and performance. In each case, the information a rule needs may stop arriving in the form it expects. These changes may be intentional and beneficial, but they often happen in tools owned by different teams.

The result is drift. Data keeps flowing and rules stay active, yet a rule can lose the information it needs to catch the attacks it was written to detect. The partnership is designed to help Elastic users understand these dependencies, identify where a change has affected detection coverage and follow a clearer path from discovering an issue to addressing its cause.

How Fig Maps an Elastic Environment

Fig connects to Elastic through a read-only application programming interface (API) key and retrieves the configuration of the Elastic environment. From that configuration, Fig's deterministic Security Data Lineage maps each source through pipelines, mappings and fields to the detection rules that use them.

With that map in place, engineers can see what each rule relies on before a change goes live. When a source, pipeline or mapping changes, Fig identifies the affected detections, pinpoints where the flow broke and recommends a fix. Engineers can then use that context to investigate the issue and assess the proposed repair.

Jamie Hynds, director of product at Elastic, explained the value from Elastic's side of the partnership. "Environments never stop changing, from vendor schemas and APIs to ETL tools and pipelines. Fig traces those changes to the detection rules that depend on them, so SecOps teams can adapt quickly and maintain detection coverage with Elastic Security," Hynds said. ETL stands for extract, transform and load.

Testing Changes and Shipping Them as Code

Elastic's prebuilt integrations and research-backed detection rules provide broad coverage out of the box. Elastic's Automatic Import feature and its artificial intelligence (AI) Agent help teams build new integrations and custom rules as their requirements grow. Fig works alongside those capabilities by testing changes against the organization's own data and environment context before anything reaches production.

Once a change is validated, engineers can . Taken together, these steps form an engineering workflow that ties each planned change to its expected effect on detection coverage. Teams can assess dependencies, test adjustments and manage deployment as they add sources, refine pipelines or expand use cases. Shafir presented that workflow as a way to keep pace without giving up visibility. "Teams can see how every source connects to every detection, test each change against their own environment and ship it as code. That lets them move quickly without losing sight of their coverage," he said.

Support for Organizations Moving to Elastic Security

The integration also covers platform migrations. For organizations moving from another security information and event management (SIEM) platform, Elastic's Automatic Migration translates existing detection rules. Fig then checks each translated rule against the data available in Elastic before cutover, flags rules that need rework and recommends fixes. This validation helps engineers see where translated detection logic and the destination environment's data need to be aligned before switching over. Existing Elastic users can apply the same checks when they introduce sources or change detection use cases.
